title: HyperPod Slurm Clusters Declare Node Software Through Managed Extensions
description:
TL;DR

  • A cluster extension is a software package that AWS manages on every node of a SageMaker HyperPod Slurm cluster, declared through an API or the console and then installed, updated and removed by the service on the whole fleet.
  • Amazon launched the feature in November 2026 with two extensions: sagemaker-observability, which ships node, GPU, EFA and Slurm metrics to CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, and sagemaker-user-management, which creates the same user and group IDs on every node and rules who may use SSH and sudo.
  • The extension service runs its software as root on every node, so CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension and DeleteClusterExtension belong with administrator permissions, and the post advises keeping them away from the cluster execution role because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use that role's credentials.
  • Status carries the operational weight: Creating or Updating while a change rolls out, Active when no node reports a problem, with ActiveCount and TotalCount showing whether every node has converged, and Degraded when some nodes failed.
  • Each extension has its own ARN, so a platform team can own user management while a monitoring team owns observability, and the post asks for one owner per component so a script and an extension never configure the same exporter.
  • Lifecycle scripts stay the right tool for organization-specific software such as security agents, license servers and storage layout, and the two approaches coexist as long as each component keeps a single owner.
  • Slurm's maintenance reservations provide a separately planned mechanism for fleet-level work: root or SlurmUser creates the reservation, the maintenance flag marks its purpose, and a reservation with nodes stays inside one partition.

Official AWS figure from the 20 November 2026 post: the declaration path from administrator to cluster, the validation step, and convergence of the extension onto every node group, including replacement nodes. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

Amazon Web Services published Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on 20 November 2026, and the launch starts with two extensions. Two extensions exist today. What matters is that the software on the nodes now has a declared, validated, reportable form, which is the layer that used to live in a script somebody edited on a Friday.

What a cluster extension owns on a HyperPod Slurm fleet

HyperPod already declares most of a cluster through an API: node roles and partitions, FSx for Lustre and OpenZFS mounts, minimum capacity, automatic topology management and deep health checks that stress GPUs and test NCCL connectivity. The post describes those as five layers that HyperPod applies once, when it provisions a node, and then names the sixth layer, the software that runs on the nodes, as the one that keeps changing for the life of the cluster.

Netics editorial visual, 21 November 2026: the two mechanisms side by side, with the behaviour that changes when a node is replaced.

The reason is mundane and familiar to anyone who has run a shared compute estate. Researchers join and leave, a team asks for deeper GPU metrics for a week, an exporter ships a fix. A script runs only when a node is provisioned, so each change means editing it and then replacing nodes or rerunning it across the fleet, and a mistake appears only when it executes on some node. The extension replaces that cycle with a declaration, a schema check and a status field.

Two extensions ship today: metrics, and identity across nodes

The observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter and Slurm job and cluster metrics, and sends them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. The user management extension creates users and groups with the same IDs on every node, controls who can use SSH and sudo per node type, registers users with Slurm accounting, and can connect the cluster to Active Directory through a directory service.

Official AWS console capture from the 20 November 2026 post: installing sagemaker-observability, with the metric level and collection interval as the settings a schema validates before anything reaches a node. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

Those two choices say something about where AWS sees the pain. FSx mounts, network topology and scheduler configuration already had declarative paths. Identity and telemetry are the parts that drift silently, because a mismatched UID shows up as an unreadable home directory months later and a missing exporter shows up as a gap in a dashboard nobody was watching. The post also notes that each extension has its own ARN, which turns one cluster into several ownership zones.

The service runs as root, so the API belongs to administrators

The post states the permission model in one sentence worth repeating to a security team: an extension runs software as root on every node. That makes the three management calls administrative operations, and the recommendation that follows is specific and easy to get wrong: keep CreateClusterExtension, UpdateClusterExtension and DeleteClusterExtension away from the cluster's execution role, because every user who can sign in to the nodes can use that role's credentials.

Official AWS console capture from the 20 November 2026 post: both extensions in one view, each with its version, status and configuration link. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

The execution role still needs a narrow set of permissions, and the list is a good map of what each extension touches. Observability needs CloudWatch or aps:RemoteWrite. User management needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for the Active Directory secrets, kms:Decrypt when those secrets use a customer managed key, and a shared file system for home directories. A team that grants all of it through one broad role gets the fleet-wide root access the post warns about, with the convenience of a single policy.

Schema validation deserves an honest reading here. HyperPod checks settings against the extension's schema and rejects a misspelled setting before anything reaches a node, which removes a whole class of failed rollouts. It cannot know whether a metric interval matches the cardinality your Prometheus can absorb, or whether the user list matches the directory your staff actually use. Those remain engineering decisions with an owner.

Official AWS figure from the 20 November 2026 post: the status progression from Creating through Active and Updating to Degraded, with a health issue that names the component, its effect on the cluster, the next step and the number of affected nodes. Source: aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-managed-cluster-extensions-for-observability-and-user-management-in-amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm, captured 21 November 2026.

Active status plus the node summary show whether every node reports the requested version

Status is where this design earns its keep. Creating or Updating marks a rollout in progress. Active status plus the node summary show whether every node runs the requested version and settings and none reports a problem. Degraded means some nodes failed or report an issue. Each health issue names the component, describes the effect on the cluster, gives the next step and counts the affected nodes.

Provisioning scripts provide no built-in inventory of what is installed. A team running an exporter through a provisioning script learns about drift from a dashboard gap, or from a researcher who notices a missing GPU counter. ActiveCount and TotalCount provide the fleet-wide check beyond the node you happened to log into, and they show when a fleet-wide change has converged.

Netics editorial visual, 21 November 2026: the layers HyperPod derives at provision time, and the software layer added in November 2026.

The console view also shows the ownership split working. A cluster running both extensions lists them separately, with versions, statuses and configuration links, which is what allows one team to own metrics and another to own identity without sharing an API call.

The continuing role of lifecycle scripts

The post is clear about the boundary: run extensions when HyperPod offers a managed capability, and keep custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts for organization-specific software and initialization. Security agents, license servers and the storage layout a data pipeline expects belong in the image, because only your team knows what they need.

The rule that makes coexistence work is ownership. A component should have one owner, and the post warns against managing the same exporter, user or service through both a script and an extension, since competing configurations cause installation and runtime conflicts. Migration advice follows the same logic: turn the capability off in the lifecycle scripts, upload them to S3 so new nodes skip it, and move one capability at a time.

The SageMaker AI developer guide page on cluster extensions, with the requirements, the two available extensions and their scope. Source: docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-slurm-extensions.html, captured 21 November 2026.

What Slurm's maintenance reservations explain about the timing

A fleet-wide software change on a shared cluster needs a window, and Slurm already has the mechanism for it. The scheduler's advanced reservation guide describes reservations created, updated and destroyed by root or the configured SlurmUser through scontrol, a maintenance reservation created with the maint flag, and the rule that a reservation containing nodes stays inside a single partition; the guide's own example reserves the whole machine at 16:00 for 120 minutes with the maint and ignore_jobs flags.

The scheduling consequence is practical. HyperPod uses Slurm maintenance reservations to keep jobs off nodes during deep health checks; the extension guide says extension rollout itself does not hold back job scheduling. A team that pairs the extension update with a reservation it controls gets a predictable drain, and one that skips the reservation finds out how a degraded extension behaves while jobs are running.

Netics editorial visual, 21 November 2026: the part of the configuration a schema settles, and the part that needs a decision from the team that runs the cluster.

The launch is worth adopting for the two components it covers today, and the design is worth copying for the question it asks about every other component on the nodes: who owns it, how often does it change, and does a status field exist that says whether the whole fleet agrees. Teams running their own GPU estate outside a managed cluster face the same question with fewer defaults, which is the territory the self-hosted infrastructure and cloud exit page explores. For a separate SageMaker topic, see SageMaker's cross-region inference router.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: LLM-as-a-Judge Position Bias: Claude Flipped 103 of 400 Verdicts
description:
My new prompt won 63% of the time. I had the Slack message half-typed. Then I swapped which answer went first, ran the exact same 400 comparisons again, and the new prompt won 43%.

Same judge. Same pairs. Same rubric. The only change was which answer appeared under "Response A". That is LLM-as-a-judge position bias, and it had been quietly deciding my A/B tests for weeks.

TL;DR

  • I ran 400 pairwise comparisons with Claude as the judge, then ran all 400 again with the answer order swapped. 800 judge calls total.
  • 103 of 400 verdicts (25.75%) flipped when I swapped the order. 92 of those flips went to whichever answer was shown first.
  • The new prompt looked like a 63% winner. Counting only verdicts that survived the swap, it won 160 to 137, about 54%. A small edge, not a landslide.
  • On a blind sample I labeled myself, most flipped pairs were ones I'd call a tie. A flip is the judge's way of saying "I can't tell."
  • Fix: always judge both orders, treat disagreement as a tie, and give the judge an explicit TIE option.

What was I actually testing?

I was A/B testing two versions of a report-writing prompt. The system takes an interview transcript and writes a feedback report: what went well, what was weak, what to practice next.

This is the report generator inside Preterview, an interview prep tool I built and run (full disclosure: I built it). It runs voice mock interviews with three interviewer styles, scores a resume or portfolio, and ends with a written report, which is the part I was trying to improve. If you want to see what the reports look like, it's at preterview.com/en.

Prompt v2 was supposed to make reports more specific: quote the candidate's actual words, tie every criticism to a moment in the transcript. I generated reports from v1 and v2 for the same 400 transcripts, then asked Claude to pick the better one.

The obvious setup: new report in slot A, old report in slot B, ask "which is better?" One order, one verdict per pair. That single fixed order is exactly why v2 looked so good.

What is LLM-as-a-judge position bias?

LLM-as-a-judge position bias is the tendency of a model acting as an evaluator to prefer an answer because of where it appears in the prompt, not because of what it says. In pairwise comparisons, the judge favors slot A or slot B more often than the content justifies. It's a well-documented effect in the LLM evaluation literature, and I still walked straight into it.

The nasty part is that each individual verdict looks reasonable. The judge writes a confident paragraph explaining why Response A is more specific. You read it and nod. Nothing in a single output tells you the reasoning was built after the slot already won.

How did I measure it?

I ran every pair twice: once with v2 in slot A, once with v2 in slot B. Same system prompt, same rubric, forced choice between A and B. Here's the core of the harness:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

JUDGE_PROMPT = """You are grading two interview feedback reports
written for the same transcript. Judge on: specificity (quotes
the candidate's words), accuracy (claims match the transcript),
and actionability (clear next steps).

<transcript>{transcript}</transcript>
<response_a>{a}</response_a>
<response_b>{b}</response_b>

Reply with exactly one line: WINNER: A or WINNER: B"""

def judge(transcript, a, b):
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model=JUDGE_MODEL,
        max_tokens=20,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": JUDGE_PROMPT.format(
            transcript=transcript, a=a, b=b)}],
    )
    return msg.content[0].text.strip().split()[-1]  # "A" or "B"

def judge_both_orders(transcript, old, new):
    first = judge(transcript, a=new, b=old)    # new in slot A
    second = judge(transcript, a=old, b=new)   # new in slot B
    new_won_1 = first == "A"
    new_won_2 = second == "B"
    if new_won_1 and new_won_2:
        return "new"
    if not new_won_1 and not new_won_2:
        return "old"
    return "flip"

Each call carried a transcript excerpt plus two full reports, roughly 5,200 input tokens. 800 calls came to about 4.2M input tokens. Not free, but cheap next to shipping the wrong prompt to every user.

How many verdicts flipped when I swapped the order?

103 of 400 verdicts flipped, a 25.75% flip rate. One in four comparisons gave a different winner depending only on which report was printed first.

Here's the full breakdown:

Outcome Pairs
v2 wins in both orders 160
v1 wins in both orders 137
Flipped toward slot A 92
Flipped toward slot B 11
Total 400

So the flips weren't random noise. 92 of 103 went to whoever sat in slot A. If the judge were just uncertain and guessing, you'd expect something close to a 50/50 split between the two flip directions. 92 to 11 is a thumb on the scale.

Now look at what that did to the headline numbers:

  • Run 1 (v2 in slot A): v2 won 252 of 400. That's 160 consistent wins plus 92 slot-A flips. 63%.
  • Run 2 (v2 in slot B): v2 won 171 of 400. That's 160 plus the 11 slot-B flips. 42.75%.
  • Swap-consistent only: v2 won 160, v1 won 137. 53.9% of decided pairs.

My first run happened to put v2 in slot A. I was about to announce a 63% win rate for a prompt whose real edge was closer to 54%. If I'd randomly done it the other way around, I would have thrown out a prompt that was actually slightly better.

Are flipped verdicts just ties in disguise?

Mostly, yes. I took 50 random pairs, hid which prompt produced which report, and picked the winner myself before looking at any judge output.

  • 13 of the 50 had flipped verdicts, which tracks the 26% overall rate.
  • On the 37 pairs with a swap-consistent verdict, the judge agreed with me on 31 (84%).
  • Of the 13 flipped pairs, I marked 9 as "honestly, these are about the same."

That changed how I read the whole result. Position bias doesn't mostly override clear quality differences. It fills the vacuum when there isn't one. When two reports are close, the judge needs some tiebreaker, and the tiebreaker it reaches for is "the first one I read."

Which means a forced-choice prompt is lying to you twice. It hides ties, and then it resolves those hidden ties in a biased direction.

Does adding a TIE option fix position bias?

It helps a lot but doesn't eliminate it. I changed the output line to WINNER: A, WINNER: B, or WINNER: TIE and reran all 400 pairs in both orders.

  • 88 pairs got a TIE in at least one order.
  • Strict flips, where one order said A and the other said B, dropped from 103 to 31.

31 is still 31. The judge is still nudged by order on close calls, it just has a more honest exit now. That's why I don't trust a tie option by itself. The swap is the part that does the real work.

How should you run pairwise LLM evals now?

Here's my current setup, and it's the one I'd recommend to anyone A/B testing prompts with a model as the grader:

  1. Always judge both orders. It doubles the cost. Pay it. A single-order pairwise eval tells you about slot preference as much as about quality.
  2. Count a flip as a tie. Only swap-consistent verdicts go in the win column. Report the tie count next to the win rate so nobody reads 54% as 54-out-of-100-decisive.
  3. Offer an explicit TIE. It catches the close calls before they become flips.
  4. Hand-label a small blind sample. 50 pairs took me under an hour and told me more than the other 750 calls about what the judge's disagreement meant.
  5. Track the flip rate as a metric. If it jumps after you edit the judge prompt, your judge got worse, even if the win rates look exciting.

The thing I keep coming back to: none of this showed up in any single output. Every verdict came with a tidy justification. The bias only appeared when I ran the same question twice and compared.

So how bad is LLM-as-a-judge position bias with Claude?

In my setup, bad enough to flip a decision. Swapping answer order changed the winner on 103 of 400 pairwise comparisons (25.75%), and 92 of those flips favored the answer shown first. It turned a real 54% edge into either a 63% win or a 43% loss depending on which slot the new prompt landed in. The flips clustered on pairs that were close in quality, so the fix is cheap and mechanical: run every comparison in both orders, count disagreements as ties, give the judge a TIE option, and spot-check a blind sample by hand. If your LLM-as-a-judge eval only runs one order, your win rate is partly measuring position.

Written by the developer behind Preterview, an interview prep platform.

title: Hackers hijacked an IT partner's PC in 9 seconds through ScreenConnect
description:
On 12 Nov 2026, a technician at an IT support company joined a blank-named session in ScreenConnect, the remote-support tool. About 9 seconds later, the attacker's own ScreenConnect client was running on the technician's PC. The technician never saw a prompt.

The security firm Huntress published the case on 16 Nov ("CVE-2026-84869 in ScreenConnect Exploited to Run Malicious Files on MSP Technician Accounts", John Hammond). This article walks through what happened, why patching the server is not enough, and what to check today.

Why a technician's PC is the target

Huntress puts it plainly: "An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target."

In a normal session, the technician's host client and the guest machine can exchange files, and "the technician decides what moves and what runs." CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9), disclosed by ConnectWise on 8 Sep 2026 and added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 11 Sep, breaks that rule. Huntress's summary of the ConnectWise advisory: a guest could trigger file-transfer actions "that the technician's host client processed without authorization or confirmation, including running the file with elevated rights."

So the technician only has to join. Huntress notes the session can be an attacker-controlled machine, or "a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest."

The 9 seconds, step by step

Huntress's process telemetry from the technician's workstation (UTC, 12 Nov):

  1. 16:46:20.7 The host client runs a guest-pushed update_224ac089.bat from the client's Documents\...\Temp\ folder.
  2. 16:46:21.7 The script relaunches itself hidden through PowerShell and WScript.Shell.
  3. 16:46:22.2 It decodes a Base64 Telegram bot token and chat ID and reports the new victim to the operator.
  4. 16:46:22.6 Recon: reg query for the Windows product name and build, a check for an existing copy of its own client, and net session to test for admin rights.
  5. 16:46:23.9 curl downloads WindowsUpdate.msi from masterdarky[.]com into %TEMP%.
  6. 16:46:25.8 msiexec /a ... /qn unpacks the MSI as an administrative image, "which leaves no install record".
  7. 16:46:26.2 It sets the Secondary Logon service (seclogon) to start automatically and starts it.
  8. 16:46:28.3 runas /trustlevel:0x20000 and PowerShell Start-Process launch the payload.
  9. 16:46:29.1 WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe starts: a rebranded ScreenConnect client connected to the attacker's relay on port 8041.

The result, in Huntress's words: "The attacker now has their own remote-access client on the technician's machine that looks like legitimate ScreenConnect and named after Windows Update."

The trap: 688,000 requests, waiting for a join

How did the batch file get there? Huntress could see the delivery side in other servers' own databases. Across 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers between 20 Oct and 16 Nov, attacker guests made 688,000 "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat, from 29 source IP addresses. On the busiest server, 10 guest sessions from seven IPs made 70,414 requests over three weeks.

The exact file update_224ac089.bat was sprayed at five servers at 16:03 UTC on 12 Nov, 43 minutes before the compromise. Huntress assesses "with high confidence" that the spray operator and the masterdarky[.]com operator are the same.

Spray guests had blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames, claimed a client version matching the server's own build, and often had no preview image. On 27 spray sessions across 17 servers, the Company property was set to "crypto client".

Huntress also saw a guest that looked hand-driven push a harmless marker.txt two seconds after a technician joined, as a canary to prove the exploit worked, and an October attempt to drop Sync.bat into a technician's Startup folder through a ../ path.

Why patching the server is not enough

This is the line to forward: "Updating the server alone doesn't fix this, because the vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine."

ConnectWise's bulletin says cloud instances have already been updated to 26.6.5, and that ScreenConnect servers are not impacted. The fix that matters is on every technician's host client. In the cases Huntress studied, "many technicians were still on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after the fix shipped." The server's connection history records which client version each technician used, so the gap can be measured.

What to do today

  1. Update every technician's host client to 26.6.5 or later, plus any Access agents ConnectWise lists. If you can't today, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups.
  2. Hunt the server. On a copy of App_Data\Session.db, look for RanFiles (EventType 85) or SentFiles (86) events from a guest connection (ProcessType 2) while a host connection (ProcessType 1) was open. That overlap is the exposure.
  3. Hunt the technician PCs. Look for the ScreenConnect client running .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .vbs, .js or .txt files from Documents\*\Temp\, folders named %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<8hex>, and any ScreenConnect client whose command line points at a relay that isn't yours.
  4. If you find a hit, isolate the workstation, remove the rogue client, set seclogon back, and rotate every credential reachable from it: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault and customer admin accounts.
  5. Shrink the surface. Delete blank-named guest sessions that keep asking to run update*.bat (they come back), restrict who can join as a guest, and don't join unattended sessions you can't tie to a customer.

The wider point

What looks like a routine support session is, in reality, a file transfer and a download to the PC that holds the keys to every customer. Three of the nine steps went out to the internet: a report to a Telegram bot, an HTTPS download from the attacker's domain, and a relay connection to that same domain. Know what leaves your business on the web, and secure it.

Which do you check first after a report like this: the client versions on technician PCs, the server's session database, or outbound connections to relays you don't own?

Sources

  • Huntress, "CVE-2026-84869 in ScreenConnect Exploited to Run Malicious Files on MSP Technician Accounts", John Hammond, 16 Nov 2026: https://www.huntress.com/blog/cve-2026-84869-screenconnect-technician-exploitation
  • ConnectWise, "ScreenConnect 26.6.5 Security Patch" bulletin: https://www.connectwise.com/company/trust/security-bulletins/2026-09-08-screenconnect-bulletin
  • The Hacker News, "Hackers Exploit Critical ScreenConnect Flaw to Hijack MSP Technician PCs Without Warning", 23 Nov 2026: https://thehackernews.com/2026/11/hackers-exploit-critical-screenconnect.html

title: I built a time machine for a diamond factory, spec-first with Kiro
description:
I built a time machine for a diamond factory, spec-first with Kiro

Kiroween 2026, Frankenstein category. Live demo ·
3-minute video · Code

In a diamond factory, a rough packet takes about seventeen days to reach dispatch. The people who work on
it spend hours on it, not weeks. Every manager has a theory about the fix: more people, another shift, a faster
machine. Nobody can test a theory on last week and see what would actually have happened.

So I built RealityCheck. It replays what really happened in a factory, lets you stop at any recorded
moment, change one decision, and simulates the other future beside the one that happened. In the
demonstration, halving the time packets sit parked finishes the work about 30% sooner. Hiring three more
inspectors changes nothing but the cost, because that stage was never waiting for people.

The hard part wasn't the simulation. The hard part was keeping every number honest. This post covers how Kiro
helped with that.

A Frankenstein of five parts

RealityCheck is five parts that were never meant to share a body:

  • Skeleton: an append-only history in PostgreSQL. A database trigger refuses any edit to the past.
  • Heart: a discrete-event simulation engine in plain Java, with no framework and no randomness.
  • Blood: patterns from one real factory's month of data, published only as rounded aggregates.
  • Voice: an AI analyst (Claude) that explains results but is forbidden to calculate.
  • Face: a React app where every number is tagged Actual, Simulated or AI interpretation.

Stitching those together is where projects like this usually go wrong. The AI makes up a percentage, or the
simulation quietly uses a random seed. Or a chart shows a number nobody can trace. I wanted rules that
couldn't drift, and that's what Kiro gave me.

Steering: write the rules down once

Before any code, I wrote four steering documents in .kiro/steering/, about 560 lines in all. Kiro loads them
into every piece of work:

  • product.md: every number shown comes from the engine or recorded data. AI explains and never calculates. Simulation never alters recorded history.
  • simulation-rules.md: thirteen sections the engine must obey, covering determinism, event ordering, units, calendars and work in progress at the fork, plus the properties its tests must hold.
  • architecture.md: module boundaries, enforced by ArchUnit tests.
  • tech.md: the stack, and what not to add.

The surprise was how often these settled a design question before it became an argument. I needed per-stage
handling delays, and the obvious answer was a random number generator. But the steering says the engine is
deterministic: same input, same result, to the second. So the delay comes from a hash of the batch id
instead. That's realistic variation with no randomness, and every run reproduces exactly.

Specs: eleven features, requirements to tasks

Every feature has a spec in .kiro/specs/:

  • requirements.md, in WHEN/THE SYSTEM SHALL form;
  • design.md;
  • tasks.md.

There are eleven specs, 83 requirements and over 120 tasks. Each task names the requirements it satisfies
and the test that proves it.

Day to day, I worked task by task. I opened a spec's task list, asked Kiro to implement the next task against
its requirements, then checked the result against the acceptance criteria.

The best moment was spec 11, calibrating against a real factory. My first offline backtest showed that queues
on capacity couldn't explain how long packets sat in a department. Workers hold packets in parcels, so a packet
waits a day or two while the stage runs well below capacity. I updated the design in the spec first, adding
calibrated handling delays with a dated note explaining why. Only then did I change the engine. The spec
stayed the source of truth even when the data proved my first idea wrong.

When the build departed from a design, the spec was updated instead of left stale. Every tasks.md ends with
implementation notes recording what changed and why.

Hooks: checks on save

Five hooks in .kiro/hooks/ run on save, each scoped to a narrow file pattern:

  • the touched backend module's unit tests;
  • frontend lint and type-check;
  • an API contract check against docs/api.md;
  • a simulation-engine review, which checks engine changes against simulation-rules.md and decides whether the algorithm version must change;
  • an architecture-docs sync when migrations or Compose change.

The engine review hook was my favourite. Changing the engine without bumping its version would make old
results look comparable with new ones when they're not. The hook catches that at the moment of saving.

Custom agents and property-based tests

Five custom agents in .kiro/agents/ act as specialists:

  • simulation engineer;
  • database designer;
  • Java backend architect;
  • React UI/UX;
  • QA and testing.

Each is loaded with only its own steering and spec, so the UI agent never wanders into engine code.

Spec 07 requires the engine's correctness properties to be verified with property-based tests. There are
29 jqwik properties across 8 test classes. They cover:

  • determinism;
  • stone and carat conservation at every stage;
  • stage order;
  • capacity that never goes negative;
  • termination.

My favourite is property 10: adding capacity never increases completion time. It holds only in the
single-stage case. With several stages sharing pools, adding capacity can occasionally make the schedule
longer, which is a known scheduling anomaly. The steering says so plainly, and the engine reports it rather
than hiding it.

An AI that refuses to invent

The analyst is Claude, and the steering rule "AI never calculates" shaped all of it:

  • Claude sees only evidence keys from stored simulation results.
  • Every number it writes is checked against those results.
  • If an answer contains a figure the evidence can't support, it's replaced by a built-in analyst, and the screen says so.

In the demo, Claude says the evidence does not isolate a cause, and refuses to invent one. That's the answer I
wanted.

Honest accuracy

A simulator you can't check is just a story. RealityCheck has a backtest: it simulates past dates with no
changes and compares the result with what was recorded. On one real factory, imported privately, it's within
about a fifth on packets finished over a week. We publish exactly where it's wrong.

Our first real-data backtest actually looked better than that. The extract held only pieces that finished,
which flattered the result. We fixed the comparison window and published the less flattering numbers.

What I'd tell someone starting with Kiro

Write the steering first. The rules you'd normally keep in your head ("never fabricate a number", "the
engine is deterministic") become context for every task. That's what turned "AI on top of a simulation" into
something I can trust.

Try it at https://3-106-245-39.sslip.io, and the code, including the whole .kiro directory, is at
https://github.com/DRishu070501/RealityCheck.

#Kiro #Kiroween #KiroweenHackathon26

title: How I Built a Pure Client-Side Cross-Tab AI Bridge on Manifest V3 (Zero Backend Relays)
description:
Most AI browser agents today work in one of two ways:

  1. They spin up a remote cloud browser (expensive, blocked by corporate SSO/2FA).
  2. They pipe your active webpage DOM through their own backend servers before hitting an LLM API (huge privacy red flag, plus you have to pay for extra API keys).

I wanted something radically simpler and 100% private: use the web AI chats I already have open (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini, Kimi) to inspect and control another open, logged-in tab locally—with zero servers.

That's why I built TabWeaver (MIT licensed, zero build step, pure Manifest V3).

The Core Bottleneck: Raw HTML Destroys Token Budgets

If you grab document.documentElement.outerHTML from modern web apps like Google Analytics, Jira, or GitHub, you easily end up with 50,000+ characters of SVG paths, inline scripts, hidden nodes, and CSS noise.

To solve this natively in the browser, I wrote a Viewport & Overlay-Aware DOM Distiller (dom-distiller.js):

  1. Top-Layer Priority: Active modals, dialogs, and popovers get top extraction priority so search overlays aren't buried under static headers.
  2. Interactive Element Indexing: Visible buttons, links, inputs, and selects receive lightweight data-ext-elem-id anchors.
  3. Aggressive Noise Stripping: Tracking scripts, empty anchors, and hidden trees are stripped inside the client sandbox before serialization—cutting token usage by 80%+.

How the Dual-Tab Handshake Works

  1. Mention to Link: Type # or @ inside any of the 18 supported web AI composers. An inline tab picker pops up showing all open tabs in your current window.
  2. Visual Proof: The moment a target tab connects, TabWeaver renders a subtle Cyber Breathing Halo along the viewport border so you always know which tab is active.
  3. Structured Action Loop: The AI outputs compact JSON actions (click, fill, select, scroll, extract, navigate, finish), executed locally via chrome.scripting and action-executor.js.

Why "Logged-In Web Apps" Is the Sweet Spot

Because execution lives strictly inside your authenticated local Chrome profile:

  • You can summarize and analyze Google Analytics 4, Jira, Gmail, or internal dashboards behind logins without exposing cookies to any external relay.
  • You don't pay a cent for extra API wrappers—it runs directly on your existing ChatGPT / Claude / DeepSeek web session.

Try It & Inspect the Code

title: 0 FAIL, 12 Contradictions: How My Agent Memory System Lied to Me
description:
0 FAIL, 12 Contradictions: How My Agent Memory System Lied to Me

A green check is not the truth. The liar was my verifier.

Every number in this post points at a file or a command output in the repository. If it is not there, it is not here.

Note: the "12 contradictions" in the title belong to a different project — a learning project I audited. AHP's own cold reads found 8 / 3 / 5. Both teach the same lesson, so they are told together.

1. A green dashboard

Let me be concrete about what I built, otherwise the "gotcha" later lands soft.

I built a repo-local handoff protocol for AI coding agents, AHP (Agent Handoff Protocol) — a machine-checkable handoff protocol. It does not try to remember more. It answers one question: is the current state trustworthy, and can the next session pick it up?

Four files:

File Owns
AGENTS.md Agent entry point, boundaries, handoff contract
INDEX.md A file map — and no dynamic state
PROJECT.md Long-term decisions + a derived status block
HANDOFF.md Current work unit, exact pause point, next action, acceptance

Plus a status machine: PAUSED → ACTIVE → PAUSED / BLOCKED / COMPLETE / MONITORING. ACTIVE requires a future lease; PAUSED and COMPLETE must not keep an owner, a session, or a lease residue (SPEC.md §3).

Then twelve read-only gates, run in one command:

PASS CORE_FILES       core files present
PASS HANDOFF_SCHEMA   frontmatter is valid
PASS HANDOFF_TIME     timestamps are ordered
PASS LEASE            PAUSED has no residual lease
PASS VERIFY_COMMAND   verification command recorded
PASS HANDOFF_BODY     8 sections and next action are present
PASS HANDOFF_FRESH    sections 4-6 are fresh (0 days)
PASS INDEX_MAP        INDEX is a map and its links resolve
PASS PROJECT_SYNC     derived status matches HANDOFF
PASS MEMORY_LINKS     memory index and links are closed
PASS SECRETS          no high-confidence secret pattern found
PASS GIT_STATE        tree clean; timestamp matches the commit

[ahp] 0 FAIL / 0 WARN / 12 PASS / 0 SKIP

One number matters more than the others: fail-open gates are forbidden. Every gate needs a negative fixture that must turn red; a check with no failing fixture is a claim, not a check. The whole suite is 22 tests: 15 negative "must turn red" fixtures (one per gate), 6 CLI/scaffold tests, and 1 positive "a valid project should pass everything". npm test → 22/22.

That is where I thought the story ended.

Then I ran a cold read: a zero-context session that only got the four core files, and had to answer five questions — what is the current work unit and status, what is the exact next action, what was the last verification command and its result, what are the top three risks, and which statements in the four files contradict each other.

It found 12 contradictions.

The gates were 0 FAIL.

2. What the gates could not see

First, whose "12" this is: it belongs to another project — a learning project whose gates were all green while a zero-context reader found 12 contradictions in its four core files (docs/case-studies.md, case 8):

  • current_file named one file while §3 of the same document said "no file is being edited";
  • the acceptance criteria lived in two files — three items in one, four in the other;
  • the project documented three different verification command sets;
  • the long-term summary's "last updated" header was four days older than its own newest entry;
  • INDEX.md said "map and status" in one line and "map only" in another;
  • the status was ACTIVE with a lease that had expired 34 minutes earlier;
  • the recorded "last verification command" was a lifecycle command (ahp pause), not a verification.

The production project I audited was bigger: 70+ memory files, 279 wiki links, a 211 KB HANDOFF.md, a 185 KB long-term summary, 5 derived mirrors. It had the same disease: §1 said the work unit was accepted and pushed, while §2, §5 and the frontmatter still said "in progress, uncommitted files" — with a clean tree and the commit already on the remote. All gates green; the cold read found it.

Lesson one: structural checks are necessary but not sufficient. Eight sections can coexist with a contradiction. I wrote that into the protocol itself (docs/limits.md §2: "the worst failure is not a red gate — it is a green gate over a contradictory handoff").

What about my own repo? Same rules: zero context, four files only, one contradiction at a time.

  • v1: eight issues. A stale warning about the repo living inside a larger workspace git repo; an acceptance criterion that omitted the cold read; four different orderings of "test → cold read → commit/tag → article" across PROJECT.md and HANDOFF.md; a last_verified_command that recorded only ahp check when the real verification also ran npm test; a vague "finish the docs" when the docs were already written; and a missing statement that PROJECT.md's status block is derived.
  • v2: three issues. Release sequencing (requiring a clean tree before committing) and local-vs-remote tag ambiguity; and where the next work unit is opened.
  • v3: five more, smaller and semantic.

Eight, three, five — every single one was a documentation issue. The code was fine. The handoff was not.

That is exactly the failure AHP exists to catch, and it also showed that a cold read is not a one-off: it iterates, and every round produces something.

Where those contradictions ended up

The value of a cold read is not the discovery — it is that the same thing cannot happen twice. Every one of the 12 became either a gate assertion or a written "accepted, not fixed".

Three became gates, because the wording of the problem and the wording of the check are nearly identical:

Contradiction found Gate What the gate actually checks
current_file contradicts §3 HANDOFF_BODY if §3 says "none", current_file must be "none"
Status is ACTIVE but the lease expired LEASE ACTIVE requires a future lease_until; PAUSED/COMPLETE must not keep residues
The last verification command is a lifecycle command VERIFY_COMMAND last_verified_command cannot be ahp start/ahp pause-style

The rest did not become gates, not because they matter less, but because none of them can be machine-checked reliably:

Contradiction found Why no machine can check it
Three different verification command sets VERIFY_COMMAND inspects one field; it cannot see three documents each describing their own
Acceptance criteria split across two files, with different counts HANDOFF_BODY requires a numbered action in §4 and a non-empty next_action; it does not count acceptance items
The summary's "last updated" header predates its own newest entry HANDOFF_FRESH measures the age of dates in §4–§6 (threshold: 21 days); it does not compare a header against an entry
INDEX.md says "map and status" in one line and "map only" in another INDEX_MAP matches dynamic state rows; it does not recognise two different paraphrases of a policy

Those four became written acceptances instead of gates. A gate cobbled together to fit a case manufactures false greens — the one thing this whole design exists to prevent.

3. Worse: the verifier itself lies

The contradictions above were at least catchable by a cold read. The failures that actually scared me were of another kind: my negative tests told me a gate was broken, when my tests were the broken part.

Four real cases. All of them are in docs/lessons-from-production.md §3 and docs/case-studies.md.

3.1 The fixture was not past the threshold, so "red" was fake

The freshness gate fails above 21 days (the threshold comes from freshness.handoffDays in ahp.config.json). My negative fixture built a 20-day-old HANDOFF.md.

20 < 21, so the gate correctly emitted a WARN, not a FAIL. My test expected FAIL, so it could not turn red.

It looked like a broken gate. It was a bad fixture. Two fixes: push the fixture clearly past the threshold (40 days), or stop asserting the human-readable sentence.

3.2 The gate read the real repository, not the fixture

This one was worse. The fixture was written into a temp directory, but the git status and git log calls ran against the real project. The real repository was dirty at that moment, so the gate skipped itself and reported success.

The test said "not red". The gate logic was perfectly correct.

Fix: the test creates a temp git repo, passes the root explicitly, and every git command uses that root. Isolation is part of the test, not a convenience.

3.3 The assertion tested the message, not the gate

The gate printed 21 days; the test looked for 20 days. The test failed while the gate worked.

The reverse is worse: change the message and the test silently passes, so the gate is never exercised again — it becomes a decoration that can never fail.

Fix: assert the gate ID and status (LEASE / FAIL), use a regex for numeric details, and assert the exit code too.

3.4 A command named --check that wrote files

This one deserves its own paragraph.

A backup script took --check as an argument. Its behaviour: copy the source into the backup first, then enter the comparison branch, then report the resulting git differences. Result: it reported "10 differences" and left 10 files modified in the backup repository.

A check that writes is not a check. It is a migration wearing a misleading flag.

Fix: compare first, write only behind an explicit non-check flag, and verify git status before and after every --check.

AHP carries the same rule: gates must be read-only, and sync is the only thing that writes.

4. What I changed

Five moves, each of them turning a discovery into "this cannot happen again".

1. One current-state source. Dynamic state lives in HANDOFF.md and nowhere else. INDEX.md is a map, so the INDEX_MAP gate checks that it has not grown a status board. Long-term decisions live in PROJECT.md. The same fact is not allowed three homes.

2. Derive, do not duplicate. The status block at the top of PROJECT.md is generated from HANDOFF.md by ahp sync, not written by hand. Hand-written means it will drift, so ahp sync --check exists to catch the drift. Fields a tool can generate should not be maintained by discipline.

3. Negative tests are the product. Twelve gates, each with a fixture that must turn red. The cost is that I had to write 15 negative fixtures; the payoff is that every gate is still alive.

4. Isolated git fixtures. See 3.2.

5. The cold read is part of the protocol. A cold read is not "read the README and summarise it" — it is a zero-context session answering five specific questions. And every contradiction it finds must become either a gate assertion or a written acceptance. "Read it and forget it" is forbidden.

One more rule, borrowed verbatim from an external audit: every finding becomes either a gate/test or a written accepted risk, with a reason and a trigger for re-evaluation. It is the rule that stops "I know about this problem" from dying in a chat log.

5. What this does not fix (and what I will not claim)

It is easy to read the above as "install this and your memory system is safe". It is not. Stating the limits matters more than stating the wins.

  • Green is not true. The gates can see that a file exists, that the frontmatter is well-formed, that timestamps are ordered, that the lease has not expired, that the derived block has not drifted, that the index has not turned into a status board, and that no obvious key is committed. They cannot see whether next_action is the right next action, whether the recorded verification actually ran, whether two files contradict each other in prose, whether a remembered fact is still true in the world, whether a COMPLETE unit was actually accepted by a human, or whether the agent respected its boundaries. The worst failure is not a red gate — it is a green gate over a contradictory handoff.
  • Two models agreeing is not evidence. My workflow is one writer plus one independent reviewer: the reviewer is read-only, returns findings with file:line and evidence, and the primary adjudicates each one — fix it, turn it into a test/gate, or accept it in writing with a reason. The reviewer cannot merge. Tests and code always beat model consensus. Two models can also agree and both be wrong in the same way.
  • AHP is not a memory system. It does not replace Mem0 / Letta / Zep, does not do vector retrieval, does not do long-term memory extraction. It is four files, one status machine, a set of read-only checks, and one cold read.
  • AHP is not an access-control system. A lease is a soft lock, not authentication. It prevents accidents and low-grade concurrency, not malice.
  • AHP is not a security guarantee, and it is not an attack tool. It touches no live target and does not "hack things automatically". It just makes the handoff state harder to fool the next person.

One more thing I deliberately keep in the docs: docs/limits.md is not fine print at the bottom of a README. It is part of the protocol. A guarantee you cannot back is a disclaimer, and disclaimers are a form of dishonesty.

6. Try it yourself

You do not have to take my word. Use my repo as the target:

git clone https://github.com/cheah505-cyber/agent-handoff-protocol.git
cd agent-handoff-protocol
npm test                       # 22 tests, 15 of them negative fixtures
node bin/ahp.mjs check         # 12 gates
node bin/ahp.mjs init /tmp/demo && cd /tmp/demo
# now deliberately change HANDOFF.md's last_verified_command to "ahp pause"
# run check again and watch VERIFY_COMMAND turn red

Go further: stale the derived status block in PROJECT.md, run node bin/ahp.mjs sync --check and it fails; run node bin/ahp.mjs sync and it is repaired.

If you want to run the same checks against your own agent memory, I wrote them up as a practical, authorized-assessment checklist: docs/memory-security-checklist.en.md. Thirteen items, each with what to inspect, why it matters, what evidence to collect, and what counts as pass versus must-fix. It covers the memory inventory, poisoning, stale facts, hook injection, cross-agent trust, fail-open gates, checks that write, secrets, template supply chain, authorization scope, and report/retest.

Repo: https://github.com/cheah505-cyber/agent-handoff-protocol
Checklist: https://github.com/cheah505-cyber/agent-handoff-protocol/blob/master/docs/memory-security-checklist.en.md

The checklist is free and lives in the repository. If you want the packaged version (team rollout checklist + cold-read question card), leave an email and I will send it when it exists.

It is not an "automated scanner". It is a 2–5 day manual assessment process — use it only on systems you are authorized to assess.

7. One sentence

If this post leaves you with a single line, let it be this:

A handoff system is not a memory system; it is a truth-maintenance system.
The moment its checks stop being able to fail, it becomes another source of drift.

And the cheapest place to start is not a tool. It is this: the next time you hand off, let someone with no context read your state files. Whatever they cannot reconstruct is where your system is currently lying to you.

Appendix: where every number comes from

Number Source
12 gates, 0 FAIL node bin/ahp.mjs check; gate list in SPEC.md §6
22 tests (15 negative, 6 CLI, 1 positive) npm test
12 contradictions in the learning project docs/case-studies.md case 8
Cold reads 8 / 3 / 5 on AHP itself docs/lessons-from-production.md §3.7; HANDOFF.md §1
Production project: 70+ files, 279 links, 211 KB, 185 KB, 5 mirrors docs/lessons-from-production.md, preamble
21-day threshold / 40-day fixture ahp.config.json; docs/limits.md §3.1
20-day fixture docs/lessons-from-production.md §3.4; docs/case-studies.md case 3
--check left 10 files modified docs/lessons-from-production.md §3.5; docs/case-studies.md case 5
Lease expired 34 minutes earlier docs/case-studies.md case 6
5 derived mirrors docs/lessons-from-production.md §6
The five cold-read questions docs/limits.md §6; AGENTS.md handoff contract
