Thanks for reading!

title: AI is taking over your inbox. Google's and Microsoft's assistants were both fooled by one email
description:
Two years ago AI in email meant a button that fixed your grammar. Now the assistant reads the whole inbox before you do. It summarises threads, decides what is urgent, drafts the reply and, in some products, sends it.

That is useful. It also means the assistant reads text written by strangers, all day, and treats part of it as instructions. Google's and Microsoft's assistants have both been caught doing that in public. This post covers what is already running in your inbox, three documented cases, and five questions I now ask before I connect any AI to a mailbox.

I work on cloudmail, a webmail app with a built-in assistant and a connection for coding agents, so I have a side in this. The last section says what I run and what it does not fix. Product details and prices were checked on November 25, 2026.

AI is already in your inbox

  • Gmail. Thread summaries have been free for everyone since January 8, 2026. A beta called AI Inbox goes further: it shows "Suggested to-dos" and "Topics to catch up on" taken from your mail. On a personal account it needs a Google AI plan. Asking your inbox a question needs Google AI Pro, $19.99 a month.
  • Outlook. Copilot summarises threads and drafts replies. Microsoft 365 Copilot is an add-on at $30 per user a month, paid yearly.
  • Apple Mail. Mail on iPhone sorts incoming messages into categories by itself.
  • Agents. This is the newest part. Google now offers an MCP server for Gmail, which lets an outside AI tool search threads, apply labels, move mail to trash and create drafts. Claude's Gmail connector can "search and read emails", draft, and "send, reply to, and forward emails". AgentMail sells inboxes made for agents: 3 on its free plan, 10 for $20 a month.

So the question is no longer whether an AI reads your mail. It is what that AI is allowed to do after it reads a bad one.

Three times one email fooled the assistant

1. Gemini wrote a fake Google security warning (July 2025)

A researcher reported this through 0din, Mozilla's AI bug bounty programme. The attacker sends a normal-looking email with extra text at the end, hidden as white text on a white background and wrapped in a made-up admin tag. The victim sees nothing unusual. When they click "Summarize this email", Gemini reads the hidden text and obeys it.

The write-up's example makes the summary end with: "WARNING: Your Gmail password has been compromised. Call 1-800-555-1212 with ref 0xDEADBEEF."

There is no link and no attachment for a spam filter to catch. The warning appears in Gemini's own voice, inside Gmail. The write-up notes that similar attacks were first reported in 2024 and that Google had published mitigations, "but the technique remains viable today".

2. Copilot leaked data and nobody clicked anything (June 2025)

This one has a CVE number: CVE-2025-32711, published on June 11, 2025. Microsoft's description is one line: "AI command injection in M365 Copilot allows an unauthorized attacker to disclose information over a network." Microsoft scored it 9.3 out of 10, critical, and the score records that no action by the user is needed.

The researchers who found it, at Aim Security, named it EchoLeak. The attacker sends an email. Nobody has to open it. Later the user asks Copilot an ordinary question, Copilot pulls that email in as background, and the instructions inside it make Copilot send internal data out. Microsoft fixed it on its own servers and said it had not seen it used against customers.

3. Copilot summaries carried the attacker's link (March 2026)

Permiso, a security company, tested the three places where people summarise email with Copilot: the Summarize button in Outlook, the Copilot pane, and Copilot in Teams. Text that an attacker added to the end of an email could change what Copilot wrote. In their tests the summary could end with a section that looked like a Microsoft security notice, with a clickable link.

The results were not consistent. Their report says Outlook's button "sometimes flags, sometimes summarizes". Their point about why it works is the part I remember: people have been trained to distrust emails, and nobody has been trained to distrust the summary.

Why this keeps happening

A language model gets one long block of text. Your instructions and the stranger's email arrive in the same block. The vendor adds markers and filters to tell the two apart, and the attacker gets unlimited attempts to write around them. Each of the three cases above was fixed or reduced. The class of bug was not, because it is a property of how the model reads.

A fooled summary is bad. A fooled assistant that can send, forward or delete is worse. So the useful questions are about what the assistant can do, not about how good its filter is.

5 questions to ask before you connect an AI to your mailbox

1. Can it send, or only draft?

Google's Gmail MCP server has a tool to create a draft and no tool to send. Its docs say the draft "lets you review and send it from Gmail". That is the safe design.

Claude's Gmail connector can send. Its help page says that by default Claude "asks for your approval before each of these actions". In Auto mode the actions can run without asking, behind an automated check that, in the page's own words, "can miss risky actions".

2. Is the approval enforced by the server or by the assistant?

AgentMail's docs put this better than I can: "A draft is only an approval step if the agent cannot send on its own." If the same key that writes the draft can also call send, the review step is a habit and not a control.

3. Can the agent approve its own message, or change its own setting?

Look for an approve tool, or a settings call, that the agent's credential can reach. If either exists, an injected instruction can use it.

4. Is the message you approve the message that goes out?

If the agent can edit a held message after you have looked at it, you approved something else.

5. What can it read?

A token for one support mailbox limits the damage. A connection to your whole account does not. Ask too where the model runs and whether your mail is kept or used for training.

What I run

cloudmail is a webmail app that deploys into your own Cloudflare account. Its assistant and any outside agent work under the same rule, and the server enforces it.

A send made with an agent credential does not go out. The server stores the full message and answers pending_approval. The message waits in Pending approval until a person approves or rejects it.

Screenshot of cloudmail with sample data. Nothing here has left yet.

Checked against the five questions:

  • Send or draft: each mailbox has a mode. draft_only refuses sends, approve holds them and is the default, and auto is for a token that was given that scope on purpose.
  • Who enforces it: the server. It looks at which credential is asking, not at what the model says it intends.
  • Self-approval: there is no agent tool to approve a send. A token or connected app that tries to change a mailbox's mode is refused with person_required.
  • Same message: the hold stores the composed message. If the agent revises it after you looked, approval fails and you review the new version.
  • What it reads: a token can be confined to one mailbox. Summaries and labels run on Workers AI inside your own Cloudflare account.

The three send modes in cloudmail. Diagram drawn in code with AI.

Two more layers sit in front of that. Text from a sender reaches the agent inside markers that label it as untrusted data. A classifier scans what the agent is about to read, and if it flags a message, every send from that session is held for the next 30 minutes in every mode.

For an agent that has to run unattended, there is an inbox with a fixed list of recipients and an expiry:

cloudmail agent-inbox create --domain example.com --purpose "Invoice triage" \
  --send-mode auto --allow @partner.com --ttl-hours 24

That agent can send without approval, and only to that one domain. After 24 hours its token is revoked and its mailbox is deleted.

What this does not fix

  • The model can still be fooled. The markers and the classifier lower the odds, and neither is a guarantee. The hold decides what a fooled model is able to do.
  • A fake warning inside a summary, as in cases 1 and 3, is not stopped by a hold on sending. The summary card in cloudmail says "AI-generated, can be wrong", and you should read every AI summary that way, in any product.
  • A person can approve a bad message without reading it.
  • Approving is friction. You can exempt recipients you trust, and each exemption is a hole you made on purpose.

It is also not for everyone. cloudmail has no IMAP, so Apple Mail and Outlook cannot connect. It is email only. Your domain must use Cloudflare DNS. The code is public, and running it needs a licence key, $9 once for one domain or $29 once for unlimited domains.

The short version

AI in the inbox is here, and most of it helps. Before you connect an assistant, find out whether it can send, and who is able to stop it. If the answer is "the assistant decides", change that setting first.

More at trycloudmail.com. Docs and code: github.com/cloudmail-hq/cloudmail.

Disclosure: I work on cloudmail. This post was written with AI. The three cases come from the public write-ups by 0din, Microsoft and Permiso, and product details were checked against each vendor's own pages on November 25, 2026.

title: AI Agents Can Now Reverse-Engineer Your App in Hours. Here Is What Every Developer Needs to Know (And How to Defend Against It)
description:
Whether you're an indie hacker releasing a desktop Electron app, a mobile developer shipping on Android and iOS, or a SaaS engineer maintaining a mature frontend—there is a seismic shift underway in how software gets dissected.

You may have already seen repos like REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) trending on dev feeds. By tethering AI coding agents (like Claude Code) directly to professional reverse-engineering tools (Ghidra, Hopper, ASAR archive extractors) via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), these workflows automate what used to take veteran security researchers weeks of manually reading disassembly.

The Bottom Line: This isn't just a clever parlor trick for security demos. It fundamentally shifts the threat model for intellectual property, client-side security, and SaaS monetization.

Every developer on DEV needs to understand why this matters—and how to architect software so it doesn't become an afternoon cloning target for an AI agent.

Part 1: How AI-Driven Reverse Engineering Changes Everything

For decades, developers relied on an unwritten truce: security through obscurity. Just because someone could open browser DevTools or load a binary into Ghidra didn't mean many people would bother reading 50,000 lines of minified JavaScript or decompiled C++. It was simply too slow and expensive.

AI agents just broke that truce. Here is why the impact is so severe for everyday builders:

1. The Cost of Cloning Dropped to Near Zero

LLMs don't get tired, lose track of register states, or get intimidated by stripped symbols. With an MCP bridge to a disassembler or bundle unpacker, a single agent can:

  • Rapidly map your entire file hierarchy
  • Trace function call graphs automatically
  • Deduce variable roles from string references
  • Produce clean-room clones of your core features in a matter of hours

2. Automated Differential Testing Creates 1:1 Clones

Modern AI reversing pipelines don't stop at reading static code. They use automated testing oracles (like diff_test loops) to fire hundreds or thousands of inputs into your original binary, log every output and state mutation, and iteratively refine their rewritten code until it mirrors your app's behavior with 100% accuracy.

3. Client-Side Licensing, Paywalls, and Feature Flags Are Obsolete

If your desktop app, CLI utility, or mobile client verifies a license locally—or gates premium features behind a client-side check like this:

javascript
// ❌ Trivially bypassed by an AI agent in seconds
if (user.tier === 'pro' && verifyLocalLicenseKey(user.key)) {
unlockPremiumFeatures();
}
Consider it already bypassed. An AI agent can locate the validation branch, patch the binary, or extract the unlocked logic into a standalone script in minutes.

  1. Exposed Prompts, Heuristics, and Local Models

Many AI wrappers and local utilities bundle custom system prompts, scoring heuristics, pricing calculators, or fine-tuned weights directly inside the client package. Anything shipped to a user's disk or RAM is now trivially extractable and reusable by competitors.

  1. Faster Vulnerability Discovery for Attackers

On the offensive security side, the exact same tooling makes it easier than ever for bad actors to scan compiled binaries and thick clients for:
• Hardcoded API keys and internal endpoints
• Insecure deserialization flaws
• Broken client-side access controls

Part 2: How to Make Your Software "REA-Proof"

Reality Check: You cannot make client-side code 100% unhackable or irreversible. If a user's CPU has to execute instructions, someone with control over that machine can eventually inspect them.
Your goal isn't mathematical impossibility—it is destroying the economics and reliability of automated AI analysis. You want to strip away the clean, modular code structures that LLMs rely on while keeping your real crown jewels off the user's machine altogether.
Here is the 3-layer defense-in-depth blueprint your team needs:

Layer 1: Architectural Defense (The Only True Block)

Tools like REA depend on local artifacts—compiled binaries, .NET DLLs, mobile APKs, and unpacked Electron ASAR files. If your core logic never runs on the user's machine, there is nothing for Ghidra or an LLM to decompile.
• Treat the client strictly as a UI layer: Keep your web, mobile, or Electron app focused on rendering and user input. All meaningful state changes should happen on infrastructure you manage.
• Keep core logic on the backend: Place your pricing engine, recommendation algorithms, data parsers, AI system prompts, and license enforcement behind authenticated server APIs.
• Break traffic replay and differential testing: Because AI pipelines log network traffic to simulate your backend locally, enforce:
• Short-lived cryptographic tokens
• Server-side nonces & HMAC request signing
• TLS certificate pinning on mobile and desktop clients
If an agent cannot replay requests or mock your API responses, its automated testing loop stalls out.

Layer 2: Outwitting Static Decompilation & Exploding AI Context Windows

When code has to run locally—such as in offline-first apps, game engines, audio/video processors, or real-time tools—attack how LLMs read code. AI agents depend heavily on semantic names, modular functions, and predictable control flow.
• Strip out all symbols and metadata: Never ship .map source maps in production JS/Electron builds. Strip debug symbols from C/C++/Rust binaries, and strip reflection metadata in .NET and Java. When calculateSubscriptionDiscount() becomes sub_14008a2f0(), the LLM loses its primary semantic anchor.
• Flatten control flow and inject opaque predicates: Commercial protectors like VMProtect or Themida (native code), Jscrambler (JavaScript), and Dotfuscator (.NET) wrap clean if/else trees into massive, sprawling switch state machines filled with dead code branches. This massively inflates LLM token consumption, blows out context windows, and causes agents to hallucinate broken logic.
• Run your most sensitive functions in a virtual machine: Code virtualization compiles critical routines into custom bytecode executed by an embedded VM at runtime. When Ghidra decompiles the binary, it only sees the VM's instruction-fetch loop—never your actual business logic.
• Ditch plain-text wrappers in Electron: Unencrypted app.asar archives can be unpacked in seconds and read like open-source repositories. Package critical modules as native C++/Rust (.node) addons, obfuscated WebAssembly, or V8 bytecode (bytenode).

Layer 3: Runtime & Anti-Tampering Hardening

To stop automated agents from dynamically instrumenting your app at runtime to log inputs and outputs:
• Add anti-debugging and anti-instrumentation checks: Detect attached debuggers (IsDebuggerPresent on Windows, ptrace checks on Linux/macOS) and dynamic instrumentation frameworks like Frida.Pro Tip: Instead of crashing immediately (which pinpoints the exact check for the AI agent), silently degrade functionality or corrupt state later in execution.
• Enforce memory integrity and checksum verification: Cryptographically hash critical code segments in memory during execution to break automated binary patching.

Quick Hardening Reference by Stack

Target Stack Primary REA Attack Vector Highest-Impact Countermeasures
Electron / Web / JS
Unpacking .asar archives & reading AST/source maps Move logic to backend; delete .map files; native Rust/C++ addons or V8 bytecode (bytenode) + Jscrambler
Native (C / C++ / Rust)
Ghidra / IDA / Hopper decompilation & string analysis Strip symbols; encrypt strings; control flow flattening & virtualization (VMProtect / Themida)
Mobile (Android / iOS)
APK/IPA decompilation & MITM traffic capture R8/ProGuard full mode; native NDK for core logic; SSL pinning & Play Integrity / App Attest
.NET / Java
IL/Bytecode decompilation (dnSpy, ILSpy, JADX) Ahead-of-Time (AOT) native compilation; commercial obfuscators (Dotfuscator / DexGuard)

Pre-Release Security Checklist for Builders

Before you ship your next client build, run through this quick audit:
• [ ] Unpack your own production artifact (.asar, .apk, .exe, or JS bundle) to see what sits in plain sight.
• [ ] Verify .map files and debug symbols are stripped from all release pipelines.
• [ ] Audit client-side conditionals to ensure no paid features or business rules rely on local boolean flags.
• [ ] Move proprietary prompts, keys, and algorithms behind authenticated server endpoints.

title: WSP MCP: How AI Integration Is Transforming WordPress Website Management
description:
WordPress website management is becoming easier with the integration of artificial intelligence. Website owners, developers, and digital marketers are increasingly looking for ways to automate daily tasks, improve productivity, and manage their websites without spending hours working through the WordPress dashboard. One solution making this possible is WSP MCP, a free MCP plugin developed by WebSensePro.

WSP MCP connects popular AI assistants, including ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, and other compatible AI agents, directly to WordPress websites. It allows users to manage website content, update SEO settings, work with WooCommerce, and perform various administrative tasks through simple chat instructions.

What Is WSP MCP?

WSP MCP is a free WordPress plugin that uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect AI applications with WordPress websites. Instead of manually navigating different dashboard sections, users can communicate with an AI assistant and request specific website actions.

For example, users can ask an AI assistant to create a blog post, identify pages without meta descriptions, update product information, or organize website menus.

The plugin provides more than 200 tools covering different WordPress features and supported integrations. It does not require a separate paid subscription, companion plugin, or additional MCP Adapter.

Key Features of WSP MCP

One of the biggest advantages of WSP MCP is its extensive collection of website management tools.

  1. AI-Powered Content Management

Users can create, read, edit, and manage WordPress posts and pages through AI instructions. This can simplify content updates and help website administrators manage publishing tasks more efficiently.

  1. SEO Management

WSP MCP supports integrations with popular SEO plugins, including Yoast SEO and Rank Math. Users can retrieve and update SEO titles, meta descriptions, and focus keywords. These capabilities also extend to supported WooCommerce products and taxonomy terms.

  1. WooCommerce Store Management

Online store owners can use available tools to manage products, variations, orders, coupons, and other store-related information. Additional capabilities include sales reports, low-stock alerts, and product review moderation.

  1. Elementor Website Editing

For websites using Elementor, WSP MCP provides tools to inspect and modify page layouts, widgets, global styles, and page settings. This makes certain website design tasks easier to manage through AI.

  1. Plugin and Theme Management

The plugin provides tools for managing installed plugins and themes. Depending on the connected WordPress user's permissions, administrators can perform supported installation, activation, updating, and theme management tasks.

How Does WSP MCP Improve Website Productivity?

Managing a WordPress website often involves repetitive activities, including content publishing, SEO updates, product management, and website maintenance.

WSP MCP helps simplify these activities by allowing users to communicate their requirements in everyday language. Rather than manually locating individual settings, users can send instructions through their connected AI application.

For digital marketing agencies, this can make routine website management more convenient. Developers can also use supported tools to inspect website structures and perform certain updates without constantly switching between applications.

Security and User Control

Website security is important whenever AI tools are connected to a content management system.

WSP MCP includes individual controls for its available tools. Write-enabled abilities are disabled by default, allowing administrators to decide which actions an AI assistant can perform.

The plugin also uses WordPress user permissions and capability checks to restrict access. Its built-in Audit Log records AI tool activity, while the usage dashboard provides information about tool usage and response times.

These features help website owners maintain greater visibility and control over AI-assisted website management.

How to Connect WSP MCP to WordPress

Getting started with WSP MCP involves a few basic steps:

Install and activate WSP MCP on your WordPress website.

Open the MCP Settings section in your WordPress dashboard.

Enable the specific tools you want to use.

Visit the MCP Connection section and select your preferred AI application.

Follow the connection instructions and authorize access.

Start managing supported website tasks through AI prompts.

The plugin supports several AI applications, including ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Codex, Google Antigravity, OpenClaw, and OpenCode.

Who Can Benefit from WSP MCP?

WSP MCP can be useful for different types of WordPress users.

Website owners can simplify routine administration, while digital marketing professionals can manage supported SEO tasks more conveniently. Developers can use AI-assisted tools for website updates, and WooCommerce store managers can access supported e-commerce management capabilities.

Agencies managing multiple website responsibilities may also find AI integration useful for improving their daily workflows.

Final Thoughts

Artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities for improving website management. WSP MCP brings these capabilities directly into WordPress by connecting compatible AI assistants with more than 200 tools.

Its combination of content management, SEO integrations, WooCommerce functionality, Elementor support, and permission-based controls makes it a useful option for businesses and professionals exploring AI-powered WordPress automation.

Developed by WebSensePro, WSP MCP offers a free way to bring AI assistance into everyday WordPress workflows without requiring a separate paid plugin subscription.

title: ChatJimmy Explained: How Taalas Put Llama 3.1 8B Inside a Chip
description:
Type a question into chatjimmy.ai and the answer does not stream. It just appears, all at once, as if someone pasted it.

Most people assume a chatbot gets faster when it runs on a bigger GPU. ChatJimmy does not use a GPU at all. It runs on a chip called HC1, made by a Toronto startup named Taalas, and the AI model is not loaded into that chip. The model is part of the chip's wiring.

What ChatJimmy is

ChatJimmy is a free public demo. Taalas launched it on 19 February 2026, together with its first chip. The company's launch post calls the product "a hard-wired Llama 3.1 8B". Llama 3.1 8B is an open-weights model that Meta released in 2024. It is small and not new. The new part is the hardware.

You can check this yourself. The demo's /api/models endpoint returns one model, llama3.1-8B, "owned by Taalas Inc." Its health endpoint names the backend hardware talos003_llama3. Both were still true on 25 November 2026.

The headline number is speed:

  • Taalas claim: 17,000 tokens per second, per user. This was measured by Taalas's own lab, with 1,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens.
  • Independent check: Jaskamal Kainth sent the demo 12 prompts on 31 October 2026 and read the timing stats that every ChatJimmy reply includes. Long answers came out at about 15,600 tokens per second. A 1,227-token answer took about 80 milliseconds of chip time.

A token is a small piece of text, roughly three quarters of a word. For comparison, most chatbots you use every day write somewhere between dozens and a few hundred tokens per second.

One caveat: those 15,600 tokens per second come from the stats the demo reports about itself. Nobody has published an independent hardware test yet.

Why normal chatbots are slow: the memory wall

To understand HC1, you first need to know where the time goes on a GPU.

An AI model is mostly a huge list of numbers called weights. Llama 3.1 8B has about 8.03 billion of them. When the model writes text, it produces one token at a time. For each new token, it has to use every weight in the model once.

On a GPU, the weights live in memory chips next to the processor (called HBM, high-bandwidth memory). For every single token, all those weights travel from memory into the processor again. The math itself is fast. Moving the weights is slow. Engineers call this the memory wall.

The numbers make it clear. At 16-bit precision, each weight takes 2 bytes, so Llama 3.1 8B is about 16 GB. An NVIDIA H200 can read about 4.8 TB of memory per second. Divide one by the other:

  • 4.8 TB/s ÷ 16 GB = about 300 tokens per second for one user, at best.

That is a ceiling, not a typical result. Real systems land below it.

GPUs are not badly designed. They solve this with batching: one read of the weights serves many users at the same time, so total output across all users is high. But batching does not make the answer faster for you, the one person waiting in the chat window. It also does not help an AI agent that has to wait for each step before starting the next one.

How HC1 removes the wall

Taalas's idea is simple to say and hard to build: if moving the weights is the slow part, do not move them. Build them into the circuit.

Think of a music box. The song is not stored in a separate memory. It is the pins on the metal cylinder. The box plays that song instantly, every time, and it can never play a different one. HC1 is a music box for Llama 3.1 8B.

Here is what Taalas has said publicly about how it works:

  • Weights in mask ROM. Paresh Kharya, Taalas's VP of products, told The Next Platform that the weights are hard-coded into a "mask ROM recall fabric". Mask ROM is read-only memory whose contents are set by the photomasks used to manufacture the chip. It is the same idea as the ROM in old game cartridges: the data is part of the physical chip.
  • Storage and multiply in one transistor. CEO Ljubisa Bajic said the chip can "store four bits away and do the multiply related to it" with a single transistor. Taalas has not published the circuit. Bajic called it "a clever trick that we don't want to broadcast."
  • SRAM for what changes. Some things must change during a conversation. The chip keeps those in normal on-chip memory (SRAM). This includes the KV cache, which is the model's memory of the conversation so far, and small fine-tuning add-ons called LoRA adapters.

Why does a fixed weight save so much? A general multiplier circuit has to handle any number. If the weight is known when the chip is designed, most of that circuit can be removed. For example, multiplying by 4 is just a wire that shifts the bits. Multiplying by 5 is one shift plus one addition. This "constant multiplier" trick is old and well known in signal processing. Taalas's version is more advanced, but the principle is the same: the memory and the math become one small piece of circuit.

Once the weights stay still, very little data moves. Between two layers of the model, one token is a list of 4,096 numbers, about 8 KB. Compare that with 16 GB of weights. So HC1 does not need HBM, fancy packaging, or liquid cooling. Taalas says its system uses none of them.

The chip itself

From the Taalas products page and The Next Platform report:

  • Made on TSMC's 6 nm process
  • 815 mm² die, close to the largest chip a lithography machine can print
  • 53 billion transistors
  • About 200 W per card, according to Bajic
  • A server with ten cards uses about 2.5 kW

A quick calculation shows why the mask ROM trick matters. 53 billion transistors for 8.03 billion weights is about 6.6 transistors per weight, and that budget also covers the SRAM and all other logic. Normal SRAM needs 6 transistors per bit. At just 3 bits per weight, SRAM alone would need about 144 billion transistors, almost three times the whole chip.

How one chip design runs a different model

If the model is wired into the chip, a new model needs a new chip. Taalas says it has made this cheaper than it sounds.

A chip is built in layers: transistors at the bottom, then many layers of metal wiring on top. According to The Next Platform, switching HC1 to a different model changes only two metal layers. Everything else stays the same. Taalas says a model it has never seen before "can be realized in hardware in only two months."

So Taalas sells a platform (HC1, and next HC2), not one fixed product. Different models get "printed" onto the same base design.

The trade-offs

The speed is real, but it is bought with flexibility. These are the costs:

  • One model per chip, forever. The base weights cannot be updated. A better model means new chips.
  • Aggressive compression. Taalas's own post says the chip uses a custom 3-bit format, mixing 3-bit and 6-bit weights, which "introduces some quality degradations relative to GPU benchmarks." HC2 moves to standard 4-bit floating-point formats to fix this.
  • Short memory. The KV cache must fit in on-chip SRAM, which is small. In Kainth's tests, a prompt of about 6,000 tokens hit the message max context limit 6144 reached. Llama 3.1 normally supports 131,072 tokens. Taalas calls the context size "configurable", so other deployments may differ.
  • Speed does not add intelligence. It is still an 8B model, and it makes 8B-model mistakes. Taalas itself calls its debut model "clearly not on the leading edge."
  • The cost and power claims are self-reported. Taalas says HC1 is "nearly 10X faster than the current state of the art, while costing 20X less to build, and consuming 10X less power." Independent tests back up the speed. Nobody outside Taalas has checked the cost and power numbers.

How is this different from Groq or Cerebras? Those companies also avoid slow off-chip memory, but they keep weights in SRAM that is loaded at run time. Their hardware can run many models. HC1 trades that freedom for more speed per user and far fewer transistors per weight.

What happened next: AMD bought Taalas

Taalas built its first product with 24 people and $30 million of spending, out of more than $200 million raised, according to its launch post.

On 6 August 2026, AMD announced a definitive agreement to acquire Taalas. On 17 November 2026, AMD said the deal was complete. AMD plans to put the technology into its accelerator roadmap and build systems that combine it with AMD Instinct GPUs. AMD did not state the price in its announcement. Tech.eu reported the deal at about $2.9 billion.

Taalas's February roadmap planned a mid-sized reasoning model on HC1, then a frontier-class model across many HC2 cards. As of 25 November 2026, ChatJimmy still lists only llama3.1-8B.

My take

ChatJimmy is not a better chatbot. It is a demo of a different idea: for some jobs, a good-enough model that answers in milliseconds beats a smarter model that takes seconds.

That fits real products. Think of voice assistants, classifiers inside apps, or AI agents that need hundreds of model calls to finish one task. For those, waiting is the main cost, and HC1 removes most of it.

The big risk is time. Models improve every few months, and a chip with frozen weights cannot follow. Taalas is betting that a two-month turnaround is fast enough, and that many companies will keep using the same model for a long time once it works. AMD paying for that bet suggests it believes the idea has a place next to GPUs, not instead of them.

If you want to feel the difference, open ChatJimmy and ask for a 1,000-word essay. The interesting part is not the essay. It is that you never see it being written.

Key takeaways:

  • ChatJimmy runs Llama 3.1 8B on Taalas's HC1 chip, at a claimed 17,000 tokens per second and an independently observed ~15,600.
  • GPUs are slow for one user because every token needs every weight moved from memory. HC1 builds the weights into the chip, so nothing big has to move.
  • The price: one model per chip, 3-bit and 6-bit weights with some quality loss, and a short 6,144-token context on the demo.
  • A new model needs two new metal layers and about two months, according to Taalas.
  • AMD completed its acquisition of Taalas on 17 November 2026.

Sources:

  • Ljubisa Bajic, The path to ubiquitous AI, Taalas, 19 February 2026
  • Taalas products page (HC1 specs)
  • Timothy Prickett Morgan, Taalas Etches AI Models Onto Transistors To Rocket Boost Inference, The Next Platform, 19 February 2026
  • Jaskamal Kainth, Taalas HC1: How ChatJimmy Hardwires an LLM Into Silicon, 31 October 2026 (measurements)
  • AMD, AMD Acquires Taalas to Advance Compute Solutions for Rapidly Growing AI Inference Market, 6 August 2026
  • AMD, AMD Completes Acquisition of Taalas to Advance AI Inference Innovation, 17 November 2026
  • Tech.eu, AMD acquires AI chip startup Taalas for $2.9B, 23 November 2026
  • Meta, Llama 3.1 8B model card
  • NVIDIA, H200 specifications
  • chatjimmy.ai /api/models and /api/health endpoints, checked 25 November 2026

title: Astra’s ShellBench Lead Shows the Business Risk of Agent Harnesses
description:
Quick take

  • ShellBench evaluated 100 personal-assistant tasks across 12 models and five agent harnesses, totaling 53,100 runs.
  • Harness averages ranged from 42.9% for Claude Code to 45.2% for OpenClaw, while model choice had the larger overall effect.
  • GPT-6 Astra completed all three repeated attempts successfully only 48.8% of the time, despite its 62.5% ShellBench score.
  • The Wire urged caution because OpenClaw maintainers authored the study, its lead was 0.01 percentage points, and no significance test was reported.

Why it matters

For corporate buyers and investors, the decision shifts from comparing model scores to assessing complete agent workflows, tools, permissions, memory, safeguards and repeatable execution, because those factors affect review costs and deployment economics.

GPT-6 Astra topped a new benchmark of everyday AI agent work, but its lead depended on the surrounding software and came with a major reliability warning. The result suggests that buyers may be comparing complete agent systems, not models alone.

The leaderboard changes with the software

ShellBench results and repeat-completion rate — see the chart in the original article.

The commercial significance of ShellBench is not simply that GPT-6 Astra ranked first. It is that the ranking exposes how difficult it is to separate a model’s capability from the system that operates it.

The ShellBench research paper reports that GPT-6 Astra achieved a 62.5% score, narrowly ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 61.9%. Those figures present Astra as the leading model in the evaluation, but they do not produce a stable hierarchy across every operating environment.

Astra performed better than Fable 5.2 when both were run through the Pi harness. When the evaluation moved into Claude Code, however, Astra performed worse. The difference matters because an agent harness determines how a model receives instructions, accesses tools, retains context and handles failures. In practice, those layers can alter the product a customer experiences as much as the underlying model can.

The paper’s aggregate results point in a more complicated direction than the individual comparison. Across the tested systems, harness averages ranged from 42.9% for Claude Code to 45.2% for OpenClaw. The researchers concluded that model choice had a larger overall effect than harness choice. That finding supports the argument that stronger models still matter most, while also showing that the surrounding software can change the outcome for a particular model and task.

For companies buying agent technology, this distinction has direct economic consequences. A model provider can claim leadership on a benchmark, but customers do not purchase an abstract model score. They purchase a workflow that must open the right email, update the right calendar entry, interpret a receipt, manipulate a spreadsheet and avoid exposing confidential information. If the harness changes those outcomes, then model rankings are only one part of the competitive picture.

A benchmark built around operational mess

The OpenClaw project announcement describes ShellBench as an evaluation of 100 personal-assistant tasks involving emails, calendars, spreadsheets, receipts, phishing attempts and sensitive information. The benchmark covered 12 models and five agent harnesses across 53,100 runs.

That design makes ShellBench more relevant to deployment decisions than a clean coding test would be. Many commercial agent failures will not come from an inability to generate a syntactically correct function. They will come from ambiguity, incomplete information, misplaced trust or an unsafe action taken at the wrong moment.

A receipt may contain several plausible totals. An email may request a payment while carrying signals of phishing. A calendar task may require interpreting a vague instruction and checking for conflicts. A spreadsheet assignment may demand both accurate manipulation and judgment about which data should remain private. These are workflow problems, not isolated prompts.

This is where the harness becomes strategically important. Tools, permissions, memory and safeguards determine how much freedom an agent has and how easily it can recover from an error. A more capable model may still be a worse business product if its operating environment gives it poor context, weak guardrails or an unreliable way to verify completed work.

The benchmark therefore complicates the usual model race. Model developers want their systems judged as the source of intelligence. Platform companies and harness developers have an incentive to show that orchestration, tooling and safety controls create a separate competitive moat. ShellBench gives evidence to both sides.

Astra’s reliability problem is larger than its lead

Astra’s headline score hides a more troubling operational result. It completed all three repeated attempts successfully less than half the time, with a 48.8% rate for completing every attempt.

That consistency measure may matter more to enterprise buyers than a narrow lead over Fable 5.2. An assistant that succeeds spectacularly on one run but fails on a repeat attempt can create review costs that erase the value of automation. Human operators must check its work, retry tasks and investigate whether a failure came from the model, the harness or the external tool.

For unattended agents, reliability is not a secondary quality. It is the foundation of the business case. A company can tolerate occasional imperfection in a drafting assistant because a person reviews the output. It has far less tolerance for an agent that manages email, updates records or handles sensitive information without predictable behavior.

The 48.8% result also changes how Astra’s 62.5% score should be interpreted. Astra may have the highest measured task performance, but customers evaluating deployment need to ask how often the system completes a workflow correctly and repeatedly. The most valuable model may not be the one with the highest average score. It may be the one that produces fewer expensive surprises.

The benchmark itself is now part of the competition

The only outside reaction supplied for this story is critical. On The Wire argued in its analysis of ShellBench that the comparison deserves caution because OpenClaw maintainers authored the study. The publication also noted that OpenClaw led by only 0.01 percentage points, that no significance test was reported and that rankings changed when certain criteria were removed.

That critique does not invalidate the results, but it highlights a central measurement problem. Changing a harness also changes its prompt, tools and runtime, according to The Wire’s account. If so, a harness comparison is not a controlled comparison of interfaces alone. It is a comparison of complete systems with different operating assumptions.

The supplied material contains this critical view, and no opposing outside response was provided. The absence of a second perspective makes methodological scrutiny especially important, rather than a reason to dismiss the benchmark.

For investors and corporate buyers, the practical lesson is straightforward. AI leaderboards should be read as evidence about a configured product, not as a pure ranking of intelligence. The durable advantage may belong to the company that combines a strong model with dependable memory, effective tools, careful permissions and repeatable execution.

Astra currently leads the ShellBench score, but its inconsistent completion rate leaves room for competitors to win on deployment economics. If Fable 5.2 or another model can deliver slightly lower peak performance with stronger reliability, its total cost of ownership may be lower. The next phase of the agent market will be decided less by who wins a single benchmark and more by who can turn messy, high-risk tasks into dependable business processes.

Sources

  • arxiv.org (primary)
  • openclawd.baby (primary)
  • onthewire.ai (primary)
