title: One API key for Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok: a Python and Node quick start
description:
If you build with LLMs, you probably juggle several provider accounts, keys and SDKs. Here's a shortcut: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint that serves models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek, Moonshot, Qwen and Z.ai, so you keep the SDK you already use and only change the model name.

I'm using Refract here. It's pay per token with no subscription, and prices are well below the official ones (Claude Sonnet 5.5 is $0.50 / $2.50 per 1M tokens against $2 / $10).

Python (OpenAI SDK) 

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://refracthub.com/v1", api_key=os.environ["REFRACT_API_KEY"])

for model in ["claude-sonnet-5-5", "gpt-6.2-sol", "gemini-4-argon", "grok-4.7"]:
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain recursion in one sentence."}],
    )
    print(model, "→", r.choices[0].message.content)

Node (OpenAI SDK) 

import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({ baseURL: "https://refracthub.com/v1", apiKey: process.env.REFRACT_API_KEY });

const r = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "claude-opus-5-5",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Write a haiku about TypeScript." }],
});
console.log(r.choices[0].message.content);

Python (Anthropic SDK)

The Anthropic Messages API works too, so existing Claude code needs only a new base URL:

import os, anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(base_url="https://refracthub.com", api_key=os.environ["REFRACT_API_KEY"])
msg = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=300,
                             messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the plot of Hamlet in 3 lines."}])
print(msg.content[0].text)

Streaming, tools and images

Streaming (stream=True), tool calling and image inputs work the same way as with the official SDKs. A few more things that help:

  • Spending caps per key, so a bug in a loop can't drain your balance.
  • A usage log with the tokens and cost of every request.
  • "model": "auto" lets Refract pick a model for each request.

Try it

Get a key at refracthub.com and see every model ID and price on the models page. The examples above are also in a GitHub repo: refract-examples.

title: One LangChain agent, rewritten in DNotifier
description:
Most migration guides open with a big feature table. I've never found those very helpful on their own, because they don't show you what your code will look like afterwards. So this post does it the other way round: one small agent, written twice.

It's an order-lookup agent with one tool, a system prompt and a single call. The first version is LangChain in JavaScript, the second is DNotifier. In both, db stands in for your own data access.

The LangChain version 

import { createAgent, tool } from "langchain";
import * as z from "zod";

const lookupOrder = tool(
  async ({ orderId }) => {
    const order = await db.orders.find(orderId);
    return order ? JSON.stringify({ status: order.status, eta: order.eta }) : "No order with that id.";
  },
  {
    name: "orders_lookup",
    description: "Look up an order by id, like A-1042. Returns status and ETA.",
    schema: z.object({ orderId: z.string() }),
  }
);

const agent = createAgent({
  model: "openai:gpt-4o",
  tools: [lookupOrder],
  systemPrompt: "You help customers with orders. Use tools for facts; never guess dates.",
});

const result = await agent.invoke(
  { messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Where is order A-1042?" }] },
  { recursionLimit: 10 }
);
console.log(result.messages.at(-1).content);

The DNotifier version 

import { DNotifier } from "@dnotifier-realtime/dnotifier";

const notifier = new DNotifier({
  appId: process.env.DNOTIFIER_APP_ID,
  secret: process.env.DNOTIFIER_SECRET,
  transport: "http",
  userId: "orders-api",
  permissionEnforcement: "backend",
});
await notifier.connect();

const lookupOrder = notifier.tools.register({
  name: "orders.lookup",
  description: "Look up an order by id, like A-1042. Returns status and ETA.",
  inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { orderId: { type: "string" } }, required: ["orderId"] },
  async execute({ orderId }) {
    const order = await db.orders.find(orderId);
    return order ? { status: order.status, eta: order.eta } : { found: false, note: "No order with that id." };
  },
});

const agent = DNotifier.defineAgent({
  name: "order-help",
  instructions: "You help customers with orders. Use tools for facts; never guess dates.",
  provider: "open_ai",
  model: "gpt-4o",
  observability: true,
  tools: [lookupOrder],
  permissions: { "orders.lookup": ["execute"] },
});

const result = await notifier.runAgent(agent, { input: "Where is order A-1042?", maxToolRounds: 5 });
console.log(result.output);

So what changed?

Less than I expected. The body of the tool function is the same code. The Zod schema turns into a plain JSON schema, and the tool can hand back an object instead of a string. The description copies straight across, which matters, because it's what the model reads when deciding whether to call it.

The model string gets split in two: "openai:gpt-4o" becomes provider plus model. Moving to Claude or Gemini later is a change to those two fields and nothing else.

Permissions are the one part that is actually new. The agent declares which tools it's allowed to execute, and with permissionEnforcement: "backend" the server checks that list on every call. In LangChain, any tool you pass in can be called.

The limit counts something different, so don't just copy the number. recursionLimit counts graph steps, maxToolRounds counts rounds of tool calls. I'd set it to however many tool calls a normal question needs, plus one or two.

Reading the answer is result.output instead of digging the last message out of state. And observability: true replaces the LangSmith environment variables: every run shows up in Traces with its steps, tool calls and cost.

What carries over, and what doesn't

Most of the core concepts have a direct counterpart. createAgent maps to defineAgent, tool() to tools.register(), and a StateGraph becomes a Workflow where the branching is ordinary if and await. Parallel branches become ctx.runAgents(), interrupts become ctx.waitForMessage(), retrievers become the knowledge base. Checkpointers map to DNotifier's checkpoints, where you can resume, retry or replay a run, and LangSmith datasets map to datasets and experiments.

A few things don't have an equivalent today, and you should know them before you start:

  • token-by-token streaming (you can push progress messages to the client, but not text as it's generated)
  • structured output with a schema validator (ask for JSON and parse it with a fallback)
  • LangChain's huge integration catalogue (in DNotifier an integration is a tool you register or an MCP server you connect)

If an agent leans heavily on one of those, I'd migrate it last, or just leave it on LangChain. The full guide, including moving a LangGraph graph across and the order I'd migrate things in, is on our blog: How to migrate from LangChain.

I work on DNotifier, so treat this as a vendor's comparison. I've tried to be upfront about the gaps. Drafted with AI help, edited by me.

title: Which LLM eval tools do practitioners use, and where do they fall short?
description:
Hamel Husain names LangSmith, Arize and Braintrust as the vendors he meets most often. Langfuse and Promptfoo are two other common options. These tools run datasets, judges and experiments. Their docs and practitioner writing point to the same gap: no tool decides what "good" means for your product. You still need error analysis, an expert-written rubric and labeled examples.

Which LLM eval tools do practitioners use?

Hamel Husain, a practitioner who writes widely on evals, names the vendors he sees most often: LangSmith, Arize and Braintrust (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18). He says he has no favorite and that support quality and "vibes" matter more than features. Langfuse and Promptfoo are two other common options.

The table below sums up what each tool's own documentation says it does. It is not a ranking.

Tool What its docs say it does
LangSmith Offline evals on curated datasets. Evaluators: human review, code rules, LLM-as-judge and pairwise comparison. Online evals on live traces.
Braintrust Each eval has data, a task and evaluators. Evaluators can be autoevals, LLM-as-judge or custom code.
Langfuse LLM-as-a-judge, human annotation queues, user feedback, custom scores and dataset experiments that can fail a CI build, and a guide to calibrate an LLM judge against human labels.
Arize Phoenix Two evaluator types: LLM-based (judge model) and code (deterministic logic).
Promptfoo Open-source CLI and library for evaluating and red-teaming LLM apps, including in CI/CD.

Sources for the table: LangSmith docs, Braintrust docs, Langfuse docs, Arize Phoenix docs, Promptfoo docs.

What do these tools do well?

They remove plumbing work. You get dataset storage, experiment runs, score tracking and a place to compare versions. Langfuse says its offline experiments can run in CI/CD and fail a build when a score breaks a threshold (Langfuse docs). LangSmith separates offline checks on curated data from online checks on production traces (LangSmith docs).

That plumbing matters. A regression gate in CI is hard to build and easy to neglect.

Where do LLM eval tools fall short?

The limits below come from tool docs and named practitioners. Each has its source.

  1. They do not know what "good" means for you. Husain and Shankar warn that vendors promote off-the-shelf metrics. Their FAQ quotes Husain's course: vendors' off-the-shelf metrics "ensnare engineers into superfluous tasks" (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18). In his field guide, he describes teams that celebrated a 10% gain in a "helpfulness score" while users still struggled (Hamel Husain, Field Guide, 2025-03).
  2. Online scoring has no ground truth, in any tool. Braintrust's docs state this plainly: live requests have no expected answer, so online scoring relies on LLM-as-a-judge scorers (Braintrust docs). A judge you have not checked against expert labels is a guess.
  3. Judge bias is only partly handled. LangSmith's pairwise guide offers a randomize_order option. It also says position bias "should mainly be addressed via prompt engineering" (LangSmith docs).
  4. Criteria are not fixed in advance. A study by Shreya Shankar and co-authors found that "users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria" (Shankar et al., arXiv, 2024-04). A tool can store a rubric. It cannot write one that fits your experts.
  5. Generic annotation screens slow review. Husain and Shankar recommend a custom annotation tool and say teams with one "iterate ~10x faster". They add that off-the-shelf tools can suit large annotation teams with strict access control. Even then, they say many teams find the overhead not worth it (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18). This is one practitioner's view, not a measured result.
  6. Dashboards can hide the real problem. Husain and Shankar write: "I have rarely found dashboards to be helpful." They prefer short reports with custom charts (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).

Langfuse documents a way to check a judge against human labels. The labels themselves still have to come from your experts.

How should you choose between tools?

Pick the tool last. Use this order.

  1. Read a sample of real traces and write down the failure types. Husain calls error analysis "the single most valuable activity in AI development" (Hamel Husain, Field Guide, 2025-03).
  2. Ask one domain expert to give a pass or fail verdict with a short written reason for each trace. See how to build an LLM judge.
  3. Build a judge. Check it against the expert labels. Report true positive and true negative rates separately, because raw agreement can mislead when classes are imbalanced (Hamel Husain, LLM judge guide, 2024-10).
  4. Add deterministic code checks wherever a rule can do the job. Husain and Shankar advise favoring "assertions or other deterministic checks" over judges in CI (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).
  5. Now pick the tool that fits your stack, your data rules and your team. Any of the five can run steps 3 and 4.

Should you buy a tool or hire a service?

A tool runs your evals. A service helps you decide what to evaluate and who labels it. Many teams need both. A tool is the right buy when your team already knows its failure types and has experts ready to label. A service is the right buy when it does not. Clarity's page on the eval tool versus eval service lays out the difference. For the full method, see how to evaluate an AI agent and the simplest eval framework.

FAQ

Is Braintrust better than LangSmith?

Their docs describe similar building blocks: datasets, tasks, evaluators and experiments. None of the sources cited here is a neutral head-to-head test, so this page does not rank them. Pick on stack fit, data rules and support quality.

Can Promptfoo replace a paid eval platform?

Its intro page describes an open-source CLI and library that runs in CI/CD and covers red teaming (Promptfoo docs). Whether that is enough depends on how many people need to review outputs and how much hosting you want to run yourself.

Do I need an LLM judge at all?

Not always. Code checks cover anything a rule can test. Use a judge for judgment calls, and check it against expert labels before you trust it.

What is the first thing to do before choosing an eval tool?

Read real traces and write down how the agent fails. Every source above, from Husain to Shankar, starts with the data, not the dashboard.

Lynn Chyi, AI Experience Architect at Dayforce, said the work improved "our human expert alignment scores by nearly 60%" (Dayforce case study). Engagements start at $100K+, and scope is agreed in the proposal. See /evals/ and how to evaluate an AI agent.

title: How do you turn expert feedback on AI outputs into a grading rubric?
description:
Ask one domain expert to review real outputs and write a short critique for each. Group the critiques into recurring failure types. Turn each type into a clear pass/fail check with a definition and examples. Then test the rubric against fresh expert labels, and revise it where the two disagree.

Why not write the rubric first?

Researchers who studied how people grade LLM outputs found that criteria change during grading. They call this "criteria drift": "users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria" (Shankar et al., arXiv 2404.12272, 2024-04).

In plain terms, experts do not know all their criteria until they see outputs. Some criteria only appear after the expert has read a bad answer. Hamel Husain makes the same point: you cannot write a good judge prompt before you see the data (Hamel Husain, 2024-10-29).

So the rubric should come from the expert's reactions to real outputs, not from a template.

What does the process look like?

The steps below combine guidance from the sources at the end of this post.

  1. Choose one expert. The evals FAQ calls a single domain expert, a "benevolent dictator", the most effective approach for most teams. That person sets the quality standard and can take input from others. Larger or multi-domain organizations may need several annotators, and then agreement should be measured with a chance-corrected metric such as Cohen's kappa (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).
  2. Pull real outputs. Use a varied pool of about 100 traces. The same FAQ suggests hand-reviewing a first batch of at least 30 and continuing while you are still learning.
  3. Ask for a verdict and a critique. For each output, the expert records Pass or Fail and writes why.
  4. Group the critiques. The FAQ advises that you "group similar notes to see which problems recur". The groups become a list of failure modes.
  5. Write one check per failure mode. Each check gets a name, a one-sentence definition, and examples of Pass and Fail.
  6. Test the rubric. Run it against expert labels the rubric has not seen. Check where it disagrees.
  7. Revise and relabel. When graders disagree, find the rubric line that caused the split, write a rule to settle it, and relabel the affected examples.

What makes a good critique?

A critique is the raw material for the rubric, so quality matters. Hamel Husain says it should be detailed enough to use as a few-shot example in a judge prompt. A new employee should be able to understand it (Hamel Husain, 2024-10-29). He names terse critiques as a common mistake.

Here is the difference. The examples are illustrations, not real client data.

Weak critique Stronger critique
"Wrong tone." "The reply promises a refund the policy does not allow. The customer asked about a late fee, and the reply never mentions the fee."
"Bad answer." "The summary leaves out the contract end date. A reader would miss the renewal deadline."
"Not helpful." "The answer names the right form but does not say where to send it."

The stronger version tells the next reader what to look for. It also helps the expert. Husain notes that writing critiques helps experts clarify criteria they had not fully put into words.

Why use pass/fail checks instead of a 1 to 5 scale?

Several practitioners prefer binary checks. Husain writes that "a binary pass/fail forces evaluators to make a clear judgment", and pairs it with a detailed critique to keep nuance (Hamel Husain, 2025-03-24). The evals FAQ gives reasons: the gap between adjacent scale points is subjective, detecting real differences on a scale needs larger samples, and annotators drift toward the middle. For gradual progress, it suggests separate binary checks on sub-components.

Eugene Yan takes a similar position: where possible, he has his evaluators return binary outputs, which makes classification metrics easier to use (Eugene Yan, 2024-08).

Not every source says to avoid scales. Anthropic's documentation on building tests shows an LLM-graded 1 to 5 scale for tone, with the end points defined, and a yes/no grader for privacy leaks (Anthropic docs, accessed 2026-10-30). A scale can work when each point is defined and the output is constrained. The point of agreement is that vague scales do not work.

How do you turn a failure mode into a check?

Write each check so that two people reading it would give the same verdict. Anthropic's guidance says good success criteria are specific and measurable (Anthropic docs, accessed 2026-10-30). Its privacy example defines what counts as protected data before asking for a yes/no judgment.

Use this template for each check:

  1. Name: a short label, such as "Promises unauthorized refund".
  2. Question: one yes/no question, such as "Does the reply promise a refund the policy does not allow?"
  3. Definition: what counts, and what does not.
  4. Pass example: one real output from the review.
  5. Fail example: one real output, with the expert's critique.
  6. Check type: code check where a rule can do it, LLM judge where it cannot. Anthropic's engineering team describes three grader types: code-based, model-based and human. Code-based graders are fast and reproducible. Model-based graders handle nuance but are non-deterministic (Anthropic, 2026-01-09).

If a failure mode can be tested with a rule, use a rule. Save the LLM judge for criteria that need judgment.

How do you know the rubric works?

Test it. Split the labeled examples. The evals FAQ suggests roughly 10 to 20% for training examples that may appear in the prompt, and roughly 40 to 45% each for dev and test. Tune on dev. Reserve the test set for one final check. If test scores fall well below dev scores, the judge may be overfitting (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).

Report the judge's true positive rate and true negative rate against the expert, not raw agreement alone. The related guide on sample size is How many labeled examples do you need before you trust an LLM judge?

Also read the transcripts. Anthropic's engineering team says reviewing full records shows whether a failure is a real agent mistake or a grader rejecting a valid answer (Anthropic, 2026-01-09).

FAQ

How many expert reviews do I need to build the first rubric?

The evals FAQ recommends reviewing at least 100 traces, with a first hand-reviewed batch of at least 30. Keep going while you are still finding new problems. Stop when new failure modes stop appearing.

What if two experts give different grades?

Measure agreement with a chance-corrected metric such as Cohen's kappa. Then find the rubric line that caused the split and write a rule that settles it. Relabel the affected examples. For many teams, naming one expert as the final judge avoids repeated splits.

Should I let an LLM write the rubric for me?

An LLM can draft candidate checks. The research above shows why a human must still grade: the LLM's checks inherit the problems of the model, and experts refine their criteria by grading outputs. Use the LLM to propose, and the expert to decide.

How often should I update the rubric?

Update it when new failure patterns appear and after material changes such as a model update. Husain advises re-running the validation after such changes.

It can be done with your team or for your team. Engagements start at $100K+, and the proposal sets scope, deliverables and duration. title: How many labeled examples do you need before you trust an LLM judge?
description:
There is no single number. Practitioners suggest about 100 expert-labeled examples per failure mode, with enough Pass and Fail cases to measure both. Below 60 examples, confidence intervals are often too wide for a useful conclusion. Trust comes from the interval around the judge's true positive and negative rates on a held-out test set, not from label count.

Why does the number of labels matter at all?

An LLM judge is a model that grades the output of another model. It is only useful if its grades match what your domain expert would say. An influential 2023 paper on LLM-as-a-judge reports that strong judges such as GPT-4 reach "over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans" (Zheng et al., arXiv 2306.05685, 2023-06).

That result comes from general chat benchmarks. It does not tell you how a judge will behave on your task, your rubric and your failure modes. Another group of researchers states the reason plainly: LLM-generated evaluators inherit the problems of the models they judge, so they still need human validation (Shankar et al., arXiv 2404.12272, 2024-04).

Expert labels are how you do that validation. The question is how many you need to be confident in the result.

What do practitioners say about sample size?

Sources give different numbers. They also measure different things. The table lists what each one says.

Source What it says about count What it counts
Hamel Husain, LLM judge guide (2024-10-29) About 100 examples per failure mode. Below 60 examples, confidence intervals are often too wide for a useful conclusion. Labeled examples used to validate a judge
Hamel Husain, evals-skills validate-evaluator (accessed 2026-10-30) About 100 labeled traces, balanced at roughly 50 Pass and 50 Fail. Also 30 to 50 examples per class across dev and test combined. Labeled traces split into train, dev and test
Eugene Yan, LLM evaluators (2024-08) No minimum is given for validating an evaluator. He notes that during development you will likely evaluate only a few hundred samples. Samples evaluated during development
Arize, measuring human-LLM judge alignment (2026-07) About 100 examples gives a margin near plus or minus 10 points on raw agreement. About 400 gives near plus or minus 5 points. These are rough worst-case figures for intuition only. Examples used to estimate raw agreement

The sources do not agree on one number. They do agree on three points:

  1. Roughly 100 labels is a common starting point, not a guarantee.
  2. Below about 60 labels, confidence intervals are often too wide for a useful conclusion.
  3. The count that matters most is the count of the rare class. For many agent tasks that class is the failures.

Why is the number of failures the real limit?

Most agent outputs pass. Failures are rare. A judge that says "Pass" every time can still show high raw agreement with humans, yet it catches no errors. Arize gives the arithmetic: a 5% failure rate in 200 examples leaves only about ten failures, which makes recall unstable (Arize, 2026-07).

So count failures, not total labels. This is why the evals-skills guide asks for a balanced set of about 50 Pass and 50 Fail, even if the real traffic is skewed (Hamel Husain, evals-skills, accessed 2026-10-30). Eugene Yan reports the same effect in the studies he reviews: one set of evaluators identified over 95% of consistent summaries but only 30 to 60% of inconsistent ones (Eugene Yan, 2024-08).

If you cannot find enough failures in your logs, you cannot yet trust a judge on that failure mode. Find more failures first.

Which metrics should you report?

Use more than one number.

  • True positive rate (TPR): the share of expert Pass labels that the judge also passes.
  • True negative rate (TNR): the share of expert Fail labels that the judge also fails.
  • Raw agreement: easy to read, but it ignores chance and class imbalance.
  • Cohen's kappa: agreement corrected for chance. Sources differ on its use: Arize and Eugene Yan use it for judges, while the evals-skills guide keeps it for human-human agreement only. Eugene Yan notes it is "generally more conservative" than other metrics. In one study he cites, a model had 80% agreement but only 0.62 kappa (Eugene Yan, 2024-08).
  • Human-human baseline: compare the judge against how often two experts agree with each other. Arize adds a caution: human agreement is "a baseline, not a hard performance ceiling" (Arize, 2026-07).

Arize also warns against universal thresholds. The evals-skills guide does give targets: TPR and TNR above 90% on the dev set, and above 80% as a minimum (Hamel Husain, evals-skills). Treat these as one practitioner's starting rules, not a standard. Set your own bar from the cost of a wrong grade in your product.

How do you put a confidence interval on a judge?

A point estimate such as "92% TNR" means little without its range. Two sources describe practical methods.

  • The evals-skills guide uses a bootstrap: 2,000 resamples of the test set, then the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as a 95% interval.
  • Arize suggests bootstrapping over examples for kappa and F1, resampling whole traces when parts of a trace are correlated, and using a paired bootstrap when you compare two judges.

For the underlying statistics of eval scores, Evan Miller's paper recommends reporting the standard error next to each score and computing a 95% confidence interval from it (Miller, arXiv 2411.00640, 2024-11).

What is a sound process, step by step?

  1. Pick one domain expert whose judgment defines quality. The evals FAQ advises a single "benevolent dictator" for most teams (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).
  2. Review traces and find failure modes. Start with roughly 30 examples and continue until new failure modes stop appearing (Hamel Husain, 2024-10-29).
  3. Collect about 100 labels per failure mode, balanced Pass and Fail where you can.
  4. Split the data. The guides suggest about 10 to 20% for few-shot examples, 40 to 45% for dev and 40 to 45% for test (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).
  5. Tune the judge prompt on dev only. Check the test set once.
  6. Report TPR, TNR and their 95% intervals. If test scores fall well below dev scores, the judge may be overfitting.
  7. Re-run the check after material changes, such as a model update (Hamel Husain, 2024-10-29).

Anthropic's engineering team gives the same direction for agent evals: LLM-as-judge graders "should be closely calibrated with human experts" (Anthropic, 2026-01-09).

FAQ

Is 50 labeled examples enough to trust an LLM judge?

Usually not. Hamel Husain says that below 60 examples, confidence intervals are often too wide for a useful conclusion. Fifty can be enough to find failure modes and write a first rubric. It is not enough to validate a judge.

Can I use raw agreement as my only metric?

No. Raw agreement hides a judge that always says Pass when failures are rare. Report TPR and TNR separately. Sources differ on kappa: Arize and Eugene Yan use it for judges, while the evals-skills guide keeps it for human-human agreement only. Show the confusion matrix too.

What if my experts disagree with each other?

Measure it. Compare expert-expert agreement with judge-expert agreement on the same examples. If the experts disagree often, the rubric is unclear. Ask which rubric part caused the split, write a rule that settles it, and relabel the affected examples (Husain and Shankar, Evals FAQ, 2026-09-18).

Does the sample size change if I use a stronger judge model?

The sources do not say that a stronger model needs fewer labels. A judge is validated against your task and your rubric. Re-run the check when you change the judge model.

title: How do you build an LLM-as-judge you can trust?
description:
An LLM-as-judge is a language model that grades the output of another AI system against a rubric. You can trust it only after you compare its grades with labels from a domain expert on real examples. Use one expert, binary pass or fail labels, one judge per failure type, and a re-check whenever the system changes.

What is an LLM-as-judge and when does it work?

A judge model reads an output, applies your criteria, and returns a grade. The idea became common after a 2023 study of strong models as judges, which reports "over 80% agreement" with human raters (Zheng et al., 2023-06). That result comes from general chat benchmarks. It does not show how a judge will score your task.

Another research group warns that LLM-generated evaluators "simply inherit all the problems" of the models they evaluate, so they need human validation (Shankar et al., 2024-04). Anthropic's engineering team says the same for agents: judge graders "should be closely calibrated with human experts" (Anthropic, 2026-01).

Use a judge when the failure needs human judgment, such as tone or helpfulness. Use code checks for objective rules (Husain and Shankar, 2026-09). For tool options, see which LLM eval tools practitioners use and where they fall short.

What biases should you expect from a judge?

Published tests show three repeatable biases. Eugene Yan's review of the research summarizes them in the table below.

Bias What it means Reported finding
Position The judge prefers an answer because of where it appears claude-v1 was biased 70% of the time (Yan, 2024-08)
Verbosity The judge prefers longer answers Longer answers were preferred more than 90% of the time by two of the models tested (Yan, 2024-08)
Self-preference The judge prefers text its own model wrote GPT-4 favored itself with a 10% higher win rate (Yan, 2024-08)

These figures come from older models and specific test setups. Treat them as a reason to test your own judge, not as current rates. Do not assume a newer model is free of them.

How should you design the grading scale?

Pick binary labels first. Hamel Husain's guide says to use "No complex scoring scales or multiple metrics" and make a clear pass or fail decision (Husain, 2024-10). Eugene Yan also prefers binary outputs where possible (Yan, 2024-08).

For subjective traits such as tone, Yan reports that pairwise comparison tends to give "more stable results" than direct scoring (Yan, 2024-08). If you use a pairwise judge, test it with the answer order swapped. For when to use it, see when to compare two AI agent versions side by side instead of scoring one output.

Build one judge per failure type. The evals FAQ calls the most common mistake directing one judge to catch "too many different kinds of errors" at once (Husain and Shankar, 2026-09). Anthropic gives the same advice and adds that the judge should have a way out, such as an "Unknown" answer (Anthropic, 2026-01).

How do you build and calibrate a judge, step by step?

  1. Name one principal domain expert. The evals FAQ advises starting with a "benevolent dictator" and adding people only when needed (Husain and Shankar, 2026-09).
  2. Have the expert review real outputs and find failure modes. Husain starts with "around 30 examples" and continues until no new failure modes appear (Husain, 2024-10).
  3. Have the expert label each output pass or fail and write a short critique that explains the reason.
  4. Write a rubric for one failure type. Anthropic warns that "vague rubrics produce" inconsistent judgments (Anthropic, 2026-01). Put the expert's critiques in the prompt as examples.
  5. Run the judge on labeled examples it has not seen. Treat the expert labels as truth and report the true positive rate and true negative rate separately (Husain, 2024-10).
  6. Read the disagreements by hand before you change the prompt. The evals FAQ advises inspecting a few before automated tuning (Husain and Shankar, 2026-09).
  7. Repeat until the judge is good enough for your risk. Husain reports one case that took "three iterations" to pass 90% agreement with the expert (Husain, 2024-10). That is one reported case, not a target for your task.

Expect your criteria to move. Researchers who studied this call it criteria drift: people define criteria better by grading outputs, and grading changes the criteria (Shankar et al., 2024-04). Plan to revise the rubric and relabel.

Why is raw agreement a weak score?

Raw agreement can look high when the judge catches nothing. Husain notes that a judge that "always predicts Pass" can still reach 95% agreement while detecting none of the errors (Husain, 2024-10). Report both rates separately, so a weak failure detector shows up.

How many labels you need is a separate question. See how many labeled examples you need before you trust an LLM judge.

What do the main sources recommend?

Source Main advice for judges
Zheng et al., 2023-06 Strong judges can match human agreement levels on chat benchmarks, with known biases
Shankar et al., 2024-04 Validate judges with humans; expect criteria to change
Yan, 2024-08 Prefer binary outputs; use pairwise for subjective traits
Husain, 2024-10 One expert, pass or fail plus critique, report both error rates
Anthropic, 2026-01 Calibrate with experts; one judge per dimension; allow "Unknown"
Husain and Shankar, 2026-09 One judge per failure type; inspect disagreements first

FAQ

Can an LLM judge replace human review?

No. It extends expert review to more outputs. The expert labels remain the ground truth, and you re-check the judge against them.

Which model should be the judge?

The evals FAQ says to start with the most capable models available and optimize cost later (Husain and Shankar, 2026-09). Re-run the expert check when you change the judge model.

Should I use a 1 to 5 score?

Start with pass or fail. The evals FAQ says binary labels force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling, and that numeric scales are usually not necessary (Husain and Shankar, 2026-09).

How do I stop the judge from favoring long answers?

The sources report the bias but give no single fix. Test it: compare judge grades on short and long answers that the expert rated equal, and add that case to your rubric examples.

How Clarity can help

Clarity by Epistemic Me is an AI-native services firm that builds AI agents with the client's team and runs the evals that prove they work. For judges, the evals work covers error analysis, expert rubrics, golden datasets, and LLM-as-judge checked against expert labels, with regression gates. Lynn Chyi, AI Experience Architect at Dayforce, said the work improved "our human expert alignment scores by nearly 60%" (case study). Engagements start at $100K+, with scope, deliverables and duration agreed in the proposal. Clarity is an official partner of Parlance Labs. See /evals/ or /qualify/.

Sources

  • Zheng et al. — Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (2023-06)
  • Shankar et al. — Who Validates the Validators? (2024-04)
  • Eugene Yan — Evaluating the Effectiveness of LLM-Evaluators (2024-08)
  • Hamel Husain — Creating a LLM-as-a-Judge (2024-10)
  • Anthropic — Demystifying evals for AI agents (2026-01)

title: Thinking on Constrained Deployments: Gemma E2B on 4GB 1650
description:
A 4 GB laptop card gives the same answers as an 8 GB desktop card, at 1.63 times the time. On grade-school math, thinking doubles the time and moves no score beyond chance.

The same 16 settings that ran on an 8 GB RTX 3050 ran on a GTX 1650 Ti Max-Q, through the same llama.cpp build and the same weight files. Every one scored within chance of the 3050: −11 to +12 GSM8K problems (smallest p = 0.1882) and −2 to +3 AIME problems (smallest p = 0.25). The reply text differs between the cards; the right-or-wrong verdict matches on 1,249 to 1,268 of the 1,319 GSM8K problems, and the problems that flip split close to evenly.

Thinking on made GSM8K take 2.04 to 2.21 times as long and moved no score beyond chance. The drafter lifted generation 1.37 to 1.39 times for 192 MiB of card memory and changed no score beyond chance. The exact Q4_0 repack scored level with Google's file, in 118 MiB less card memory and 8.2 to 9.8 percent faster.

For a constrained card: serve E2B with the repack weights and the drafter at one drafted token, leave thinking off, and pick the card by how long you can wait. Each setting ran once, at temperature 0.

This article provides a step by step guide to running that study on a 4 GB laptop GPU and checking its answers against a bigger card: thinking off and on, two 4-bit builds of Google's QAT weights, each with and without a drafter, on every GSM8K test problem and all 30 AIME 2025 problems.

https://github.com/xbill9/gemma4-dev/tree/main/docs/gemma4-e2b-thinking-1650ti

The Findings

Same answers as the 8 GB card. GSM8K scored 0.8863 to 0.9030 here against 0.8908 to 0.9052 on the RTX 3050. Setting by setting, the two cards differ by −11 to +12 GSM8K problems and −2 to +3 AIME problems, and no paired test between them gets below p = 0.1882 on GSM8K or 0.25 on AIME.

Different text, same verdicts. Only 151 to 190 of the 1,319 GSM8K replies with thinking off came out byte-identical on the two cards, and 5 to 13 with thinking on. The right-or-wrong verdict matched on 1,249 to 1,268 of them.

What thinking cost. GSM8K took 2.04 to 2.21 times as long with thinking on, and AIME 1.43 to 1.70 times. GSM8K moved by 0, +8, +13 and +17 problems across the four setups, none beyond chance (p = 0.1145 to 1.0).

What the drafter bought. Generation rose 1.37 to 1.39 times on GSM8K, from 69.6–76.7 to 96.1–106.1 tokens per second, against 1.79 to 1.82 times on the RTX 3050. It changed no score beyond chance.

The two weight builds. The exact Q4_0 repack and Google's QAT Q4_0 file scored level in every paired test. The repack used 118 MiB less card memory and generated 8.2 to 9.8 percent faster on GSM8K.

What to do with it.

  • 🟢 A 4 GB laptop card answers like the 8 GB desktop card. Pick the card by time, not by score.
  • 🟢 Serve E2B with the drafter; at one drafted token it adds 192 MiB and 1.37 to 1.39 times the speed.
  • ⚠️ Leave thinking off for grade-school math; it doubles the time on this card too.

Caveats. One run of each setting, temperature 0. AIME's 30 problems can only show large effects.

What Was Measured

The earlier article, Thinking On or Off? Gemma 4 E2B on an 8 GB RTX 3050, crossed thinking, weight build and drafter on a desktop card. This run repeats it on a laptop with half the card memory and asks two questions: does the smaller card change any answer, and what does it cost in time?

Factor Settings
Thinking off, on (enable_thinking in the chat template)
Weights exact Q4_0 repack of Google's QAT weights, Google's QAT Q4_0 GGUF
Drafter none, Google's E2B QAT assistant as exact Q4_0, 1 drafted token
Problems GSM8K test, 1,319; AIME 2025 I and II, 30

Two settings are this card's own. The drafter guesses one token at a time, the best length measured earlier on the 1650 Ti, where the 3050 used two. And E2B's per-layer embedding table stays in system memory, this rig's serving setting.

That is 16 runs, 30.63 hours, every reply saved.

At This Point You Should Have…

  • An NVIDIA card with 4 GB, here a GTX 1650 Ti with Max-Q Design on driver 620.70.06
  • llama.cpp built with CUDA, here commit 7182ef7, the build the 3050 run used
  • Python 3 with huggingface_hub, tokenizers and scipy
  • A clone of gemma4-dev

Step 1 — Same Files, Smaller Card

Both model files are the ones the 3050 served, checked by SHA-256 in weights.sha256:

File Bytes Card memory when serving
Repack, gemma-4-E2B-it-q4_0-exact.gguf 2,620,370,912 🥇 2,331 MiB
Google, gemma-4-E2B_q4_0-it.gguf 3,349,516,256 2,449 MiB
Drafter, gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-assistant-q4_0-exact.gguf 59,236,000 +192 MiB

Every arm fits the 4,096 MiB card with the full 131,072-token context, one request at a time; the largest, Google's file with the drafter, used 2,641 MiB. Each reply may run to 32,768 tokens, thinking included.

Step 2 — Run All Sixteen on a Laptop 

cd local-llamacpp-1650ti-2b-q4_0/benchmarks/runs/2026-11-23-thinking-e2b-1650ti
setsid nohup systemd-inhibit --what=sleep:idle:handle-lid-switch --why="E2B thinking run" \
  ./run.sh >> nohup.out 2>&1 < /dev/null &

systemd-inhibit keeps the laptop awake with the lid closed for the 30 hours. run.sh starts the server once per weights and drafter pair and runs four cells on it: GSM8K thinking off, AIME off, AIME on, GSM8K on. It saves each reply as it finishes, skips any cell already complete when restarted, and commits and pushes each pair as it ends.

The run's own log, driver.log, shows one line per cell, with the card's temperature and clock:

2026-11-23 15:02:24 64.31, 1845 MHz END gsm8k repack-none thinking=off rc=0 {"task": "gsm8k", "max_tokens": 32768, "n": 1319, "right": 1182, "accuracy": 0.8961, "errors": 0, "truncated": 1, ...

Step 3 — The Scores, Beside the 3050

analyze.py builds every table from the saved replies.

GSM8K, 1,319 problems: 1650 Ti / RTX 3050

Weights Drafter Thinking off Thinking on
Repack none 0.8961 / 0.9014 0.9022 / 0.8931
Repack yes 0.8931 / 0.9007 🥇 0.9030 / 0.8999
Google none 0.8969 / 0.8916 0.8969 / 0.9052
Google yes 0.8863 / 0.8908 0.8992 / 0.8999

AIME 2025, 30 problems, right answers: 1650 Ti / RTX 3050

Weights Drafter Thinking off Thinking on
Repack none 10 / 7 8 / 10
Repack yes 7 / 7 8 / 10
Google none 5 / 6 9 / 6
Google yes 6 / 5 7 / 9

One to five AIME replies per cell ran into the 32,768-token limit and count as wrong; on GSM8K, zero or one per cell.

The 10 against 7 is three problems right only on the 1650 Ti and none the other way; on two of them the 3050 reply ran into the length limit. That split is p = 0.25.

Step 4 — Same Problems, Two Cards

agreement.py lines up each problem's reply from the two cards in the same setting.

GSM8K Thinking off Thinking on
Same right-or-wrong verdict 1,259 to 1,268 1,249 to 1,262
Byte-identical reply 151 to 190 5 to 13
Paired test, smallest p 0.2203 0.1882

Same files, same llama.cpp commit, temperature 0, and still most replies differ in their wording. The likely cause is that the two GPUs add up floating-point numbers in a different order, so the greedy pick flips wherever two candidate tokens are nearly tied, and a longer reply has more such points. No AIME reply matched byte for byte. The verdicts land the same way within chance: right on one card and wrong on the other 51 to 70 times on GSM8K, split close to evenly.

Step 5 — Where the Tokens Go

tokens.py counts thinking and answer tokens in each saved reply with Gemma 4 E2B's tokenizer. Its count matches the server's on every reply, up to the fixed end-of-turn and thinking markers.

GSM8K off GSM8K on AIME off AIME on
Thinking tokens, mean 0 601 to 633 0 7,075 to 9,113
Answer tokens, mean 404 to 427 272 to 280 5,425 to 6,497 919 to 1,735

The pattern matches the 3050. Thinking moves the working out of the answer and adds to it: about 600 thinking tokens in front of a GSM8K answer a third shorter. Thinking on used more tokens on 1,299 to 1,303 of the 1,319 GSM8K problems and on 26 to 28 of 30 AIME problems in every setup.

Step 6 — Time and the Drafter

Weights Drafter GSM8K off GSM8K on AIME off AIME on
Repack none 2.15 h 4.39 h 0.67 h 0.96 h
Repack yes 🥇 1.52 h 3.25 h 0.59 h 0.99 h
Google none 2.23 h 4.93 h 0.85 h 1.31 h
Google yes 1.74 h 3.61 h 🥇 0.53 h 0.91 h

With the drafter, GSM8K finished 1.28 to 1.41 times sooner. The main model accepted 0.863 to 0.871 of the drafted tokens on GSM8K, more than the 3050's 0.796 to 0.806 at two tokens, yet the speed-up is smaller: 1.37 to 1.39 times against 1.79 to 1.82. An earlier measurement on these rigs found a drafting step costs the 1650 Ti a larger share of a plain step than faster cards pay, which fits a smaller gain here.

On AIME, generation rose 1.29 to 1.39 times, but the time follows the length of the replies as much as the speed. The repack with thinking on took 0.99 hours with the drafter and 0.96 without, because its replies with the drafter ran 10,789 tokens on average against 8,096.

Without the drafter this card generates at 0.68 to 0.71 times the 3050; with it, at 0.49 to 0.54 times, since the 3050 drafts two tokens and gains more from them.

🔎 Tip: Compare Verdicts Across Cards, Not Text

Two GPUs with the same model file, the same engine build and temperature 0 gave word-for-word the same GSM8K reply on at most 190 of 1,319 problems. A check that diffs reply text between machines will report almost everything as changed. Score each reply, then pair the verdicts problem by problem: that is the comparison that held steady here.

Compare and Contrast

GTX 1650 Ti, 4 GB RTX 3050, 8 GB
GSM8K score range 0.8863 to 0.9030 0.8908 to 0.9052
AIME right, of 30 5 to 10 5 to 10
All 16 settings 30.63 h 🥇 18.81 h
Generation, no drafter 69.6 to 76.7 tok/s 🥇 99.1 to 109.2 tok/s
Drafter speed-up, GSM8K 1.37 to 1.39x (1 token) 🥇 1.79 to 1.82x (2 tokens)
Card memory, repack, no drafter 🥇 2,331 MiB 3,610 MiB
Thinking off Thinking on
GSM8K time, repack with drafter 🥇 1.52 h 3.25 h
Thinking tokens per GSM8K problem 🥇 0 601 to 633
Score change beyond chance — none

So, Which One?

If a 4 GB laptop card is what you have, it gives the same answers as an 8 GB desktop card. Every setting scored within chance of the 3050; what you pay is time, 1.63 times as much across the whole study.

Turn the drafter on at one drafted token. It costs 192 MiB and lifts generation 1.37 to 1.39 times on this card.

Leave thinking off for grade-school math. On GSM8K it doubled the time here as on the 3050, with no change in score beyond chance; on hard math, measure on your own problems first.

Between the two 4-bit builds, take the repack: same answers, less card memory, faster generation.

Summary

The goal of this article was to find out whether a 4 GB laptop card answers like an 8 GB desktop card for Gemma 4 E2B with thinking off and on, and what it costs in time. The key to the solution was running the same 16 settings with the same files and llama.cpp build on both cards and pairing every problem's verdict between them. The results were:

  • 🟢 Every setting scored within chance of the RTX 3050: −11 to +12 GSM8K problems, −2 to +3 AIME problems.
  • ⚠️ Only 5 to 190 of 1,319 GSM8K replies came out word-for-word the same on the two cards; the verdicts agreed on 1,249 to 1,268.
  • ⚠️ The study took 30.63 hours against 18.81, 1.63 times as long.
  • ❌ Thinking doubled the GSM8K time (2.04 to 2.21 times) and moved no score beyond chance.
  • 🟢 The drafter lifted generation 1.37 to 1.39 times on GSM8K and changed no score beyond chance.
  • 🟢 The repack and Google's QAT file scored level; the repack used 118 MiB less and generated 8.2 to 9.8 percent faster.

Scope: one GTX 1650 Ti Max-Q with 4 GB in one laptop on mains power, llama.cpp 7182ef7, Gemma 4 E2B only, one run of each of 16 settings on 2026-11-23 and 24, temperature 0, one request at a time, the full 131,072-token context, a 32,768-token reply limit. The drafter guessed one token here and two on the 3050, and the per-layer table stayed in system memory here and sat on the card on the 3050; both are each card's own setting, so the time comparisons are between the two setups as served.

The strategy for measuring thinking and a drafter on a 4 GB laptop GPU was validated with an incremental step by step approach.

References

  • gemma4-dev on GitHub
  • This run: replies, logs, analysis
  • The RTX 3050 run
  • Thinking On or Off? Gemma 4 E2B on an 8 GB RTX 3050
  • The scoring script
  • Exact Q4_0 repack of Gemma 4 E2B QAT
  • Google's Gemma 4 E2B QAT Q4_0 GGUF
  • Exact Q4_0 E2B QAT drafter
  • llama.cpp

Hope you enjoyed it!

title: Introducing PRISM: Building a State Rollback Engine for Safer Autonomous AI
description:
Introducing PRISM: Building a State Rollback Engine for Safer Autonomous AI

Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly capable of doing more than generating text.

AI agents can interact with APIs, manipulate data, execute workflows, modify configurations and perform complex multi-step operations.

But as these systems become more autonomous, an important question emerges:

What happens when an AI agent makes the wrong move?**

An incorrect instruction, an unexpected API response or an unintended operation can have consequences beyond a simple incorrect answer.

In systems where AI can take real actions, being intelligent isn't enough. Those actions must also be controlled, monitored and recoverable.

This is the problem we're exploring at Pantera through an initiative called PRISM.

What is PRISM?

PRISM stands for Prompt Refinement and Intent Structuring Mechanism.

It is Pantera's proposed AI State Rollback Engine, designed around an important principle:

Autonomous AI systems should be able to take action without making every action irreversible.

PRISM aims to introduce an additional safety and recovery layer between AI agents and the systems they interact with.

Rather than treating an AI-generated instruction as something that should automatically be executed, the idea is to introduce mechanisms for understanding intent, preserving system state and recovering from unsafe operations.

Why does this matter?

Imagine an AI agent managing an application's database.

A user asks it to update a particular customer record.

The agent misunderstands the instruction and modifies multiple records instead.

Without appropriate safeguards, recovering from that operation could require manual intervention, database backups or complicated recovery procedures.

Now imagine a system where the intended operation is evaluated, the previous state is preserved and an unsafe change can trigger a controlled recovery process.

That's the direction we're exploring with PRISM.

How PRISM is designed to work

Our current concept revolves around three important mechanisms.

  1. Intent Structuring

Before an operation is executed, the system should examine what the AI intends to do.

PRISM is designed to refine and structure instructions so that the intended operation can be better understood and evaluated before execution.

The objective is to reduce ambiguity and introduce an additional layer of validation.

  1. State Checkpointing

A system should have a reliable reference point before potentially destructive operations.

PRISM's state checkpointing concept involves preserving a previous system state before an operation takes place.

This creates a recovery reference that can be used if something goes wrong.

  1. Autonomous Rollback

Checkpointing is only part of the solution.

The next challenge is recovery.

PRISM is being designed around the ability to identify unsafe or incorrect operations, interrupt execution and restore a previously verified state.

The goal is to reduce the amount of manual intervention required when an autonomous system makes an unintended change.

Where could PRISM be useful?

We see several potential application areas:

  • Autonomous AI agents:Systems that independently execute tasks and interact with external services.
  • Database operations:AI-driven operations that modify, update or manage structured data.
  • Enterprise automation:Workflows where incorrect execution could disrupt business operations.
  • API interactions: AI agents that communicate with external systems and services.
  • Multi-step AI workflows:Processes where one incorrect action can affect subsequent operations.

These are the types of environments where state preservation and recoverability could become increasingly important.

Our approach at Pantera

PRISM is part of our broader interest in artificial intelligence, enterprise automation and reliable software infrastructure.

We believe the future of AI will require more than increasingly capable models.

It will also require better mechanisms for controlling how those models interact with real systems.

We are approaching PRISM with that perspective.

The initiative is currently part of our technology development roadmap, with further engineering and implementation work ahead.

Our longer-term direction includes exploring lightweight SDK integrations that developers can incorporate into existing AI workflows.An important question for developers

As AI agents become more autonomous, how should we approach the problem of recovering from their mistakes?

Should rollback and state recovery become standard considerations in the architecture of AI-powered applications?

We're interested in hearing how other engineers are thinking about this challenge.

PRISM is one of the ideas we're exploring at Pantera. This is only the beginning.

About Pantera

Pantera is a software and technology company headquartered in Lagos, Nigeria. Founded in 2024, the company builds software products, explores intelligent systems and develops technology solutions across software engineering, AI, cybersecurity, cloud computing and fintech.

🌐 Website: https://pantera.ng

📖 PRISM announcement: https://pantera.ng/blog-introducing-prism

title: Agent Substrate Explained: A Beginner's Guide to Running Multiple AI Agents Efficiently
description:
1. Introduction: Why Do We Need Agent Substrate?

Imagine you are building an AI chatbot application.

You have 1,000 users, and every user has a personal AI agent.

Each agent has its own:

  • Conversation history
  • Memory
  • Files
  • Running processes
  • Application state
  • Configuration

A straightforward approach would be to create one Kubernetes pod for every user.

For example:

User 1     → Agent Pod 1
User 2     → Agent Pod 2
User 3     → Agent Pod 3
...
User 1000  → Agent Pod 1000

This approach works, but it creates a significant infrastructure problem.

Most users are not continuously interacting with their agents.

For example:

  • Alice sends a message and leaves.
  • Bob asks a question and returns after 30 minutes.
  • Charlie starts a coding task and comes back after an hour.

Even when users are inactive, their Kubernetes pods may continue consuming CPU and memory.

This results in:

  1. High infrastructure costs.
  2. Wasted CPU and memory resources.
  3. Difficulty managing thousands of pods.
  4. Complicated infrastructure scaling.

So, how can we run thousands of AI agent sessions without running thousands of pods continuously?

This is the problem that Agent Substrate aims to solve.

2. What Is Agent Substrate?

Agent Substrate is a Kubernetes-based infrastructure platform designed to run multiple stateful AI agent sessions using a smaller pool of worker pods.

Instead of keeping every agent active continuously, it supports a lifecycle where an agent can be:

  1. Started.
  2. Suspended.
  3. Saved as a snapshot.
  4. Restored when another request arrives.

Think of putting your laptop into sleep mode.

When you stop using your laptop, you don't need to keep performing active work. When you open it again, you can continue.

Agent Substrate applies a similar concept to AI agent sessions.

Its main objective is to separate an agent's state from the Kubernetes pod where the agent runs.

This allows many logical agent sessions to share a limited number of worker resources.

3. Understand the Four Fundamental Concepts

Before understanding the architecture, let's understand four important terms.

3.1 Actor – Your Individual AI Agent Session

An actor represents one individual stateful workload.

Imagine three users:

  • Alice has her own AI conversation.
  • Bob has his own AI conversation.
  • Charlie has his own AI conversation.

Each conversation can be represented by an individual actor.

An actor contains the state associated with its workload, such as:

  • Memory
  • Files
  • Root filesystem
  • Running processes

An important distinction:

An actor is a logical resource stored in PostgreSQL. It is not itself a Kubernetes pod or Kubernetes object.

3.2 Worker – The Place Where an Actor Runs

A worker is a Kubernetes pod that provides the environment in which actors execute. One Worker Pod can host multiple Actors, provided it has sufficient resources and the configured runtime supports the required concurrency.

Think of a worker as a computer capable of hosting isolated workloads.

For example:

Worker Pool
    |
    |--- Worker Pod 1
    |       |
    |       |--- Actor Alice
    |
    |--- Worker Pod 2
    |       |
    |       |--- Actor Bob
    |
    |--- Worker Pod 3
            |
            |--- Actor Charlie

A WorkerPool is the Kubernetes resource that manages the worker pods.

The number of workers is configured through the pool.

How does it work?

Imagine Worker 1 has:

  • 8 GB RAM
  • 4 CPU cores

It might run multiple actors, depending on their individual resource requirements and sandbox configuration.


For example:

Actor   RAM usage
Alice   1 GB
Bob 2 GB
Charlie 1 GB
Total   4 GB

The remaining 4 GB can be used by other workloads or actors, subject to overhead and resource limits.

What happens when Alice becomes inactive?

  1. Agent Substrate suspends Alice's actor.
  2. Alice's state is saved as a snapshot.
  3. Her sandbox stops.
  4. The resources she was consuming become available.
  5. Worker 1 can run another actor.

Actor ≠ Worker

  • One Actor represents an individual agent session.
  • One Worker is the compute environment that can host multiple actors. The exact number of actors per worker depends on resource capacity, sandbox configuration and runtime limits; it is not a fixed number.

3.3 Snapshot – A Saved Copy of the Actor's State

What happens when an actor stops running?

Will it lose all its memory and files?

Not necessarily.

Agent Substrate supports saving an actor's state as a snapshot.

A snapshot is a saved representation of an actor at a particular point in time.

When the actor needs to run again, the snapshot can be restored.

Think of saving a document before closing your computer.

When you open it again, you can continue from where you stopped.

3.4 Atespace – A Logical Group of Actors

An atespace is a named group that contains related actors, templates and access policies. An Atespace is required to group related actors and manage them as one logical unit.

Think of it like a project folder or workspace for AI agents.

For example:

Atespace: customer-support
    |
    |--- Actor Alice
    |--- Actor Bob
    |--- Actor Charlie

Atespace: coding-assistant
    |
    |--- Actor Developer-1
    |--- Actor Developer-2

Imagine your infrastructure runs three applications:

Atespace: Customer Support
Actor 101
Actor 102
Actor 103

Atespace: Research Assistant
Actor 201
Actor 202

Atespace: Coding Assistant
Actor 301
Actor 302

Atespaces also provide an important access-control boundary. Each application has its own logical grouping, permissions, and policies.

How permissions and policies work together
Let's take a real example.

Bob wants to create a new customer-support actor.

Request: Create actor
User
Bob

Atespace
customer-support

Requested memory
2 GB

Requested CPU
1 CPU

Step 1 — Permission check

Bob has the Editor role in customer-support, so the request is authorized, assuming Editor includes actor creation.

Step 2 — Policy check

The Atespace permits up to 2 GB memory and 1 CPU per actor. The request meets those limits.

Request can proceed
The platform can now attempt to create the actor, subject to available infrastructure resources.

Now imagine Bob requests 16 GB of memory.

His permission is still valid, but the resource policy rejects the request because it exceeds the configured limit.

This is the key distinction: permissions authorize the user; policies constrain the operation.

4. How Do Actors, Workers and Snapshots Work Together?

Let's assume you have:

  • 1,000 users.
  • 1,000 individual actors.
  • 10 worker pods.

At a particular moment:

  • 10 actors are running.
  • 990 actors are suspended.

The 10 active actors use the available worker capacity.

The remaining 990 actors are represented by their saved snapshots and metadata records.

When Alice sends another request:

  1. Agent Substrate identifies Alice's actor.
  2. It checks the actor's current state.
  3. It finds an available worker.
  4. It restores the actor's snapshot.
  5. The actor starts running.
  6. The request reaches the actor.
  7. The actor processes the request and returns the response.

When Alice finishes, the application can request suspension.

The worker resources are then released.

This is the fundamental architecture of Agent Substrate.

Important: Agent Substrate does not automatically suspend every idle actor in version 1.0.0. Your application or agent framework must call the suspend operation.

5. What Does Agent Substrate Actually Manage?

Agent Substrate standardizes several infrastructure responsibilities.

5.1 API Management

It provides APIs to manage:

  • Actors
  • Actor templates
  • Worker pools
  • Snapshots
  • Atespaces
  • Access policies

The main control-plane API is ate-api-server.

Developers can interact with it using the kubectl ate command-line tool.

5.2 Actor Lifecycle Management

An actor has different lifecycle states.

The important operations include:

Operation Purpose
CreateActor Create a new actor
ResumeActor Start or restore an actor
SuspendActor Save the actor and stop its sandbox
RevertActor Restore an actor from its saved state after a failure
DeleteActor Remove an actor

5.3 Request Routing

When a user sends a request, Agent Substrate routes it to the appropriate actor.

The router is called atenet-router.

It identifies the target actor and communicates with the control plane to ensure that the actor is running before forwarding the request.

5.4 Execution Isolation

Actors execute inside supported sandbox environments.

Agent Substrate 1.0.0 supports:

  • gVisor
  • microVM

These provide isolation between workloads.

5.5 Network Access Control

Agent Substrate supports egress policies.

These policies determine which external destinations an actor can access.

For example, you can allow an actor to access an approved LLM API while blocking other external destinations.

PART 2: HOW AGENT SUBSTRATE SAVES STATE

6. Where Does Agent Substrate Store an Actor's State?

This is one of the most important architectural concepts.

Agent Substrate uses two primary storage systems:

  1. PostgreSQL
  2. Object storage

They have different responsibilities.

6.1 PostgreSQL – Stores Actor Metadata

PostgreSQL stores information about actors.

For example:

Actor ID: 12345
Actor Name: alice-agent
Atespace: customer-support
Status: SUSPENDED

Snapshot:
    Generation: 3
    Fidelity: MEMORY
    Storage State: COMPLETED

Snapshot URI:
    gs://ate-snapshots/...

PostgreSQL stores information such as:

  • Actor identity
  • Actor status
  • Actor configuration references
  • Snapshot metadata
  • Snapshot location
  • Worker assignments
  • Actor templates
  • Access policies

Think of PostgreSQL as the index or catalogue of your actors.

It tells Agent Substrate where an actor's snapshot is stored.

6.2 Object Storage – Stores Actual Snapshots

Object storage contains the actual snapshot data.

For example:

Object Storage
    |
    |--- atespaces/
            |
            |--- customer-support/
                    |
                    |--- actors/
                            |
                            |--- actor-uid/
                                    |
                                    |--- snapshots/
                                            |
                                            |--- snapshot-uuid/

A snapshot can contain files representing:

  • Durable volumes
  • Filesystem changes
  • Memory checkpoint data
  • Process state

The exact contents depend on the selected snapshot fidelity.

In the manual's local Kubernetes setup, RustFS provides S3-compatible object storage.

The snapshot URI uses a gs:// scheme in the example, but that does not mean the local installation is necessarily using Google Cloud Storage.

6.3 Local Worker Disk – Temporary Snapshot Storage

There is also a third location.

The worker node can hold a local copy of the snapshot.

Why?

Because uploading a large snapshot to remote object storage takes time.

Agent Substrate can first save the snapshot locally and upload it later.

This makes the asynchronous suspend operation faster.

Therefore, remember these three storage locations:

Storage What it contains
PostgreSQL Actor metadata and snapshot references
Object storage Durable snapshot data
Worker node disk Temporary local snapshot and cache

7. How Does Agent Substrate Create a Snapshot?

Let's understand with a practical example.

Suppose Alice is using an AI coding assistant.

Her agent has:

/agent/
    project/
        app.py
        requirements.txt

Memory:
    Current conversation
    Python variables
    Running processes

Alice asks:

"Create a Python application."

The agent creates files and performs some operations.

Now Alice closes the application.

Your application decides to suspend the actor.

Here is what happens.

Step 1: SuspendActor Is Called

Your application calls:

SuspendActor

This tells Agent Substrate to save the actor's state and stop its sandbox.

Step 2: The Sandbox Captures Its State

The selected runtime captures the requested state.

Depending on the fidelity, this can include:

  • Files in configured durable volumes.
  • Changes to the container filesystem.
  • Process memory and running processes.

Step 3: Snapshot Files Are Created

The sandbox runtime generates checkpoint data.

For example, in the gVisor memory-snapshot implementation, files include:

pages.img
checkpoint.img
pages_meta.img

The exact files depend on the runtime and snapshot implementation.

pages.img is particularly important because it contains memory-page data.

Think of it as a saved representation of the memory used by the running application.

Step 4: Snapshot Is Stored Locally

The snapshot is written to the worker node's local snapshot directory.

An example path is:

/var/lib/ate/snapshots/<actor-uid>/

Step 5: Snapshot Is Uploaded to Object Storage

Agent Substrate uploads the snapshot to the configured object store.

The snapshot receives a unique identifier.

For example:

gs://ate-snapshots/
    atespaces/
        customer-support/
            actors/
                <actor-uid>/
                    snapshots/
                        <snapshot-uuid>

Step 6: PostgreSQL Is Updated

Agent Substrate updates the actor record with information about the new snapshot.

For example:

state: ACTOR_STATE_SUSPENDED

snapshots:
  - generation: 3
    fidelity: SNAPSHOT_FIDELITY_MEMORY

    durableSnapshot:
      state: SNAPSHOT_STORAGE_STATE_COMPLETED

      object:
        snapshotUri: gs://ate-snapshots/...

Now Agent Substrate knows:

  • Which actor is suspended.
  • Which snapshot belongs to that actor.
  • Where the snapshot is stored.
  • Whether the snapshot is durably uploaded.

The worker resources can then be released.

8. What Exactly Does a Snapshot Save?

Agent Substrate supports three snapshot fidelity levels.

Snapshot fidelity means how much of an actor's state should be preserved.

8.1 VOLUMES Snapshot

This saves files from configured durable volumes.

For example:

/agent-data/
    project/
        app.py
        requirements.txt

When the actor resumes:

  • Durable volume files are restored.
  • The container starts again.
  • Running processes are not preserved.
  • RAM state is not preserved.

Imagine saving only your important documents before restarting your computer.

8.2 ROOTFS Snapshot

This includes:

  • Durable volumes.
  • Changes made to the container's writable root filesystem.

For example:

/app/
    app.py
    config.json

/agent-data/
    project/
        requirements.txt

When the actor resumes, the filesystem changes are restored.

However, running processes and RAM state are not preserved.

The application starts again.

8.3 MEMORY Snapshot

<badge color="success">Most complete snapshot</badge>

This includes:

  • Durable volume data.
  • Root filesystem changes.
  • Process memory.
  • Running process state.

For example:

Actor State
    |
    |--- Files
    |
    |--- Filesystem Changes
    |
    |--- RAM
    |
    |--- Running Processes

When restored successfully, the same processes can continue with their saved memory state.

This is closer to restoring a running computer from a checkpoint.

Snapshot Comparison

Feature VOLUMES ROOTFS MEMORY
Durable files Yes Yes Yes
Filesystem changes No, except durable volumes Yes Yes
RAM state No No Yes
Running processes No No Yes
Application restart Yes Yes No, same processes are restored

The choice depends on the requirements of your AI agent.

For example:

  • A chatbot that can reload its conversation from durable storage may need VOLUMES.
  • A coding agent that needs its working directory preserved may need ROOTFS.
  • An agent that needs to continue the same running process may need MEMORY.

9. Asynchronous vs. Synchronous Snapshot

Agent Substrate supports two suspend modes.

9.1 Asynchronous Suspend

This is the default mode.

The process is:

Actor Running
      |
      v
SuspendActor
      |
      v
Create Snapshot Locally
      |
      v
Mark Actor Suspended
      |
      v
Return to Caller
      |
      v
Upload Snapshot Later
      |
      v
Object Storage

The API returns after the snapshot is saved locally.

The upload happens later.

The snapshot may temporarily have:

SNAPSHOT_STORAGE_STATE_PENDING

This means it has not yet reached durable object storage.

9.2 Synchronous Suspend

The process is:

Actor Running
      |
      v
SuspendActor --mode sync
      |
      v
Create Snapshot
      |
      v
Upload Snapshot
      |
      v
Object Storage Confirms Completion
      |
      v
Mark Snapshot COMPLETED
      |
      v
Return to Caller

The API returns only after the snapshot is stored in the object store.

This is useful when your application must know that the latest snapshot has reached durable storage before proceeding.

Comparison

Feature Asynchronous Synchronous
Local snapshot Yes Yes
Object-store upload Later Before return
API response Faster Waits for upload
Latest snapshot immediately durable No Yes

An important detail from the manual:

The default asynchronous upload delay is five minutes, and the default local snapshot detach delay is 30 minutes.

These timers are configurable.

PART 3: HOW AGENT SUBSTRATE RESTORES AN ACTOR

10. What Happens When a User Returns?

Suppose Alice returns after 30 minutes.

She sends:

"Continue working on my Python project."

Her actor is currently suspended.

The restoration process looks like this:

Alice Sends Request
        |
        v
atenet-router
        |
        v
Identify Alice's Actor
        |
        v
Check Actor State
        |
        v
Actor Is SUSPENDED
        |
        v
ResumeActor
        |
        v
Find Available Worker

Restore Snapshot
