title: "Be Thorough" Is Not Neutral: What Anthropic's Sandbox-Escape Evals Mean for Agent Prompts
description:
If you run coding agents in containers, Anthropic's new sandbox-escape evaluation ("Siren") is worth ten minutes of your time.

The setup: Claude models without their product safeguards, more than 1,700 scenarios, 26 deliberately weakened sandboxes built on Docker, gVisor, QEMU, bubblewrap and Linux namespaces. Misconfigurations modeled on public vulnerability reports. The credentials or files needed to finish the task sit outside the boundary.

What drives escapes is not pressure. Deadlines and high stakes moved escape rates by about 6 percentage points at most. What moved them was wording: telling the agent to search thoroughly, or giving it broad authority over the machine. Removing those phrases cut sandbox-reach rates by 23–26 points in five of six models.

The mitigations are boring, which is good news:

  • A system prompt that describes the sandbox, lists the boundaries and says "stop if the task needs out-of-bounds resources" reduced escape attempts by 68–96%.
  • A tool that lets the agent report a sandbox weakness instead of exploiting it cut unauthorized reach by a further 7–33 points.
  • A classifier gating tool calls blocked the first unauthorized read in 96–100% of dangerous scenarios.

Combined, misaligned escapes went to roughly zero in the tested models. The practical lesson for anyone writing agent prompts: "be thorough" is not a neutral instruction. Scope it.

Coverage: CSO Online, https://www.csoonline.com/article/4253053/prompting-ai-to-be-thorough-can-drive-sandbox-escapes-anthropic-says.html

Daily, source-checked briefing on alignment, evals and AI regulation, L'Eco di Turing: https://il-quotidiano.web.app/edizioni/report-2026-11-26.html

title: The USB-C Port for AI: Demystifying Model Context Protocol (MCP)
description:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard, originally introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, that gives AI host applications a consistent way to connect with external tools, databases, and local files[cite: 8]. Much like a USB-C port or the Language Server Protocol, it uses bidirectional JSON-RPC 2.0 messages over stdio or HTTP/SSE transports so one server can work across desktop apps, editors, and terminal agents[cite: 8]. Keep in mind that MCP standardizes communication and capability discovery, not model inference itself, centralized authentication out of the box, or protection against hallucinated tool calls[cite: 8].

Why This Matters

Inferred audience assumption: This guide is written for software developers, AI engineers, DevOps specialists, technical product managers, open-source contributors, and technology leaders connecting large language models to external systems, local files, databases, or CLI tools[cite: 8]. Based on the dossier, it assumes intermediate software development familiarity, basic comfort with REST or GraphQL APIs and command-line tools, and practical experience using AI assistants, without requiring prior protocol specification expertise[cite: 8].

Wiring every AI client to every external system by hand creates a tangle of custom glue code[cite: 8]. After reading this guide, you can explain MCP's host, client, and server architecture, build and wire up a basic MCP server across desktop and CLI environments, and spot key security and scaling trade-offs before shipping[cite: 8].

Escaping the Custom Glue Code Trap

Think about a developer maintaining connectors between three AI interfaces (a desktop chat app, an IDE assistant, and a terminal agent) and four data sources (a Postgres database, GitHub, a local workspace, and an internal API). Without a shared protocol, every combination demands custom adapter logic, inconsistent schemas, and separate maintenance lifecycles[cite: 8].

Definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
An open client-server protocol built on JSON-RPC 2.0 that standardizes how AI host applications discover and use external data sources, tools, and workflow prompts[cite: 8].

Instead of building custom integrations for every pair, MCP lets teams expose a capability once on an MCP server and reuse it across compatible clients[cite: 8]. Rather than multiplying custom connectors across every app and data source, an open protocol turns integration into a shared, reusable layer[cite: 8].

Core Architecture and Primitives

MCP separates responsibilities across a clear client-server topology using stateful JSON-RPC 2.0 messages[cite: 8].

Hosts, Clients, and Servers

  • MCP Host: The user-facing AI application (such as Claude Desktop, VS Code, Cursor, a CLI agent, or a custom web client) that manages connections and user approvals[cite: 8].
  • MCP Client: The connector layer inside the host that negotiates capabilities, discovers server offerings, and routes requests between the model and servers[cite: 8].
  • MCP Server: A local script or remote service that exposes context and capabilities to connected clients[cite: 8].

Server Primitives and Client Features

Servers expose three core primitives[cite: 8]:

  • Tools: Executable functions with structured input schemas that an AI model can invoke to take actions or query systems[cite: 8].
  • Resources: Data or files identified by URIs (such as schemas, logs, or documents) that provide context[cite: 8].
  • Prompts: Reusable prompt templates and workflow instructions offered to users or clients[cite: 8].

Clients can also support server-initiated capabilities such as Sampling (asking the host's LLM for a completion), Elicitation (requesting input from the user), and Notifications for live updates[cite: 8].

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              MCP HOST                                  │
│  (Claude Desktop / Cursor / VS Code / Claude Code CLI / Custom Web App)│
│                                                                        │
│   ┌───────────────────┐               ┌───────────────────────────┐    │
│   │   LLM Engine      │               │   MCP Client Controller   │    │
│   │ (Claude / GPT-4o) │ ◄───────────► │ (Auto-discovers tools &   │    │
│   └───────────────────┘               │  prompts user approvals)  │    │
│                                       └─────────────┬─────────────┘    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                                      │
                       JSON-RPC 2.0 Over              │
                     stdio OR HTTP / SSE              ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                             MCP SERVER                                 │
│                   (Local Script or Remote Microservice)                │
│                                                                        │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐   │
│   │        TOOLS        │  │     RESOURCES      │  │    PROMPTS    │   │
│   │ (SQL Queries, Git,  │  │ (Files, Schemas,   │  │ (Task         │   │
│   │  API Execution)     │  │  Log Streams)      │  │  Templates)   │   │
│   └──────────┬──────────┘  └─────────┬──────────┘  └───────┬───────┘   │
└──────────────┼───────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼───────────┘
               ▼                       ▼                     ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE                         │
│     (PostgreSQL Database / GitHub API / Local File System / Slack)     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Four-Step Developer Implementation Workflow

Follow this sequence to build a server, connect it to a host, and verify message flow before relying on it in daily work.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Step 1: Design the MCP Server & Select Transport       │
│ • Local tools/files -> stdio transport                 │
│ • Cloud services/multi-tenant -> HTTP with SSE transport│
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Step 2: Implement Core Primitives (TypeScript/Python)   │
│ • Define Tools (functions with JSON schema parameters) │
│ • Define Resources (URI data sources)                  │
│ • Log debug traces to stderr (keep stdout clean)       │
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Step 3: Configure Host Applications (Desktop & CLI)     │
│ • Add server entry to claude_desktop_config.json        │
│ • Configure VS Code / Cursor / Claude Code CLI settings│
└──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Step 4: Validate with MCP Inspector & Grant Permissions│
│ • Run npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector              │
│ • Test tool calls and verify interactive approvals     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. Choose Scope and Transport

Pick stdio when the host launches a local process on the same machine, or HTTP with SSE (streamable HTTP/SSE) when connecting to a remote or shared service.

  • What success looks like: Your transport matches where the server runs and how credentials or network access are managed.

2. Implement Tools and Resources Safely

Use the official TypeScript (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk) or Python (mcp) SDK to define typed tool parameters and resource handlers.

  • Common mistake: Writing log or debug messages to stdout on a stdio server breaks JSON-RPC stream parsing. Always write logs to stderr (such as console.error()).

  • What success looks like: Tools validate inputs cleanly, stdout carries only valid protocol messages, and diagnostics appear on stderr.

3. Register the Server in GUI and CLI Hosts

Add your server configuration to desktop or editor settings (such as claude_desktop_config.json) or register it via CLI commands (such as claude mcp add my-db-tool node /path/to/server/build/index.js).

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-db-tool": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/server/build/index.js"],
      "env": { "DB_URL": "postgresql://localhost:5432/mydb" }
    }
  }
}
  • What success looks like: The host starts the server and lists its tools and resources without configuration errors.

4. Inspect Schemas and Approval Prompts

Run the MCP Inspector (npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node build/index.js) to examine JSON-RPC requests and responses interactively, then verify tool calls in your target host.

  • What success looks like: Input schemas, tool outputs, and human-in-the-loop approval prompts behave as expected.

Ecosystem Adoption and Practical Scenarios

Since Anthropic introduced MCP in November 2024, adoption has expanded across desktop apps, editors, CLI agents, and model setups. Compatible clients include Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Code, and Goose CLI, alongside adapters for models such as ChatGPT/GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Gemini, and local runtimes like Ollama or vLLM.

Integration Layer Examples in Research Primary Role
Desktop & IDE Hosts Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code Interactive chat, code editing, and tool approvals

|
| CLI & Local Runtimes | Claude Code, Goose CLI, Ollama, vLLM | Terminal workflows and local model execution

|
| Backends & Data Sources | PostgreSQL, GitHub, Slack, filesystems | Live data reads, queries, and external actions

|

Consider two real-world scenarios:

  • Local debugging with database context: A developer connects a Postgres MCP server to Claude Desktop to inspect schemas as resources and query orders and logs via tools when troubleshooting a failed order.

  • Agentic coding in the terminal: A developer uses Claude Code CLI with a GitHub MCP server to inspect issues, update code on a branch, run tests, and open a pull request.

Two common misconceptions are worth clearing up:

  • MCP is not locked to Anthropic models or Claude Desktop; it is an open standard usable with other models, IDEs, and CLI tools.

  • MCP does not replace REST or GraphQL APIs; it wraps existing APIs and systems in a standard discovery and invocation interface for AI clients.

Security, Context Limits, and Protocol Trade-Offs

Adding tool execution and data access introduces real operational trade-offs that teams need to manage deliberately:

  • Local execution risk: A stdio server runs code on the host machine, so untrusted or unvetted servers can pose serious risks if users grant broad permissions without checking what tools expose.

  • Context window overhead: Exposing many servers with large tool schemas inflates context usage and can add latency across turns.

  • Evolving authentication boundaries: Local stdio setups often pass secrets via environment variables, while remote HTTP/SSE deployments continue expanding OAuth 2.1 support rather than solving every enterprise auth requirement out of the box.

Sources

  • [1] Model Context Protocol Official Specification
  • [2] Model Context Protocol Architecture Overview
  • [3] Introducing the Model Context Protocol - Anthropic
  • [4] Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP): The Complete Guide - Fabricio Carraro
  • [5] MCP 101 - Understanding the Model Context Protocol - Itential
  • [6] Model Context Protocol Explained: Architecture and Setup - Viktor AI
  • [7] Stanford CS329T: Model Context Protocol Architecture Slides
  • [8] Model Context Protocol Claude Architecture Guide - Essa Mamdani

title: Nvidia Releases BioReason-Pro 2 Protein AI Models
description:
Open weights and code give life-science developers two protein-reasoning checkpoints, with documented deployment requirements and research-only validation limits.

Nvidia released BioReason-Pro 2 on November 24, 2026, providing supervised fine-tuned and reinforcement-learning checkpoints for protein-function annotation and biological hypothesis generation. The release includes downloadable weights and code for prediction, evaluation and training, giving developers concrete artifacts to integrate into research workflows.

The official BioReason-Pro 2 model card describes a system built around a Qwen3.5-9B language decoder, a frozen ESM3 protein encoder, and Nvidia-trained protein and Gene Ontology projection components. Nvidia permits commercial and non-commercial use under the applicable licenses.

Commercial permission is separate from scientific validation. Nvidia calls BioReason-Pro 2 an initial research release. Its biological outputs are hypotheses requiring expert review and experimental validation, and the model is not intended for clinical or diagnostic decisions.

For developers following Nvidia’s model releases, the consequential detail is the complete prediction workflow: hardware, auxiliary models, input limits and feature versions all matter alongside the headline checkpoint.

What Nvidia Shipped With BioReason-Pro 2

Nvidia’s BioReason-Pro 2 release contains two checkpoints that share an architecture and input format but represent different training stages.

Checkpoint Documented training
BioReason-Pro 2 SFT Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuned on 272,688 Kimi K3 reasoning traces
BioReason-Pro 2 RL The SFT model further trained using GRPO with an LLM-judge reward

The official GitHub repository supplies prediction, scoring, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning code. It also includes GO-GPT, the Gene Ontology term predictor whose output becomes part of the language model’s prompt.

SFT, or supervised fine-tuning, teaches the model from example responses. The subsequent RL stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, with a language model judging responses to provide the reward signal.

That training description explains how the checkpoints differ; it is not evidence that every RL-generated biological claim is more accurate. An LLM-judge reward is a training signal, not experimental confirmation. The opened sources provide no independent measurements establishing which checkpoint works better for a particular laboratory’s proteins.

Nvidia identifies protein-function annotation, experiment-guiding hypotheses and protein-set triage as expected uses. These are workflows where a proposed function can help researchers prioritize follow-up work, provided the proposal remains distinguishable from an established annotation.

How BioReason-Pro 2 Combines Proteins and Language

BioReason-Pro 2 combines encoded protein information with biological context before generating a natural-language explanation and predicted Gene Ontology terms.

Gene Ontology, usually shortened to GO, provides standardized terms for describing protein functions, biological processes and cellular locations. The system uses both protein representations and GO-related information, with separate components serving different roles.

Component Role in BioReason-Pro 2
Qwen3.5-9B decoder Generates the reasoning text and final answer
Frozen ESM3 encoder Encodes the protein, using structure when supplied
Protein projection and GO graph components Connect protein and ontology representations to the language model
GO-GPT Predicts GO terms that are included in the prompt
Optional InterPro features Add protein-family, domain and related annotation context

The repository specifies ESM3 layer 37 for the protein representation. “Frozen” means the encoder’s parameters remain fixed during the described model training.

GO-GPT and the GO graph encoder are distinct parts of the workflow: GO-GPT supplies term predictions in the prompt, while the graph encoder processes ontology information. Treating them as interchangeable would obscure what developers need to load and maintain.

The engineering implication is straightforward: BioReason-Pro 2 is a multi-model pipeline, not a standalone text checkpoint that receives an amino-acid sequence pasted into a chat box. Its documented inference path also depends on protein encoders, GO assets and consistent prompt construction.

Running BioReason-Pro 2 Locally

BioReason-Pro 2 inference fits on one CUDA GPU with 80 GB of memory, according to Nvidia’s repository. That is a documented working configuration, not a demonstrated minimum for every possible deployment.

The prediction workflow has three stages:

  1. Retrieve or compute optional InterPro features.
  2. Generate GO-GPT term predictions.
  3. Run the selected BioReason-Pro 2 checkpoint, with RL selected by default.

After configuring the repository’s inference environment, Nvidia documents these commands:

python scripts/data/download_assets.py --dest assets --skip-structures --skip-ia
python predict.py --input data/examples/proteins.tsv --output runs/example/predictions.tsv

The first command downloads the GO embeddings while skipping structure and IA assets. The second runs prediction on the supplied example protein table. These commands illustrate the documented workflow; they are not a record of testing for this article.

The checkpoint, ESM3, GO-GPT and GO-GPT’s ESM2 encoder download on first use. Developers can select the supervised checkpoint with --model sft, or supply another checkpoint location with --checkpoint.

Required Protein Input Fields

The input is a tab-separated file with a header row.

Field Required? Expected content
protein_id Yes Unique identifier used for outputs and caching
organism Yes UniProt-style organism name
sequence Yes Amino-acid sequence
taxid No NCBI taxonomy ID, preferred by GO-GPT over the organism name
partners No Interaction-partner names separated by ~
structure_path No Path to a PDB or mmCIF structure file containing chain A

The model and GO-GPT read only the first 2,000 residues. For longer proteins, this means predictions use a truncated sequence. Researchers evaluating long, multidomain proteins should account for omitted regions when interpreting a proposed function.

Missing interaction partners or structures are supported conditions. During training, partners were withheld from 80% of samples and structures from 50%. An unreadable structure, or one whose backbone fails to match the sequence, falls back to sequence-only processing.

Version Choices That Affect Reproducibility

BioReason-Pro 2 was trained and scored with GO-GPT’s ep75 checkpoint, making that version the clearest starting point for reproducing Nvidia’s documented pipeline.

The repository also offers ep89, which Nvidia describes as slightly better at GO prediction on its own. That does not automatically make it a better input provider for BioReason-Pro 2. Changing GO-GPT changes the predictions placed in the prompt, so downstream performance needs its own evaluation.

InterPro has a similar version distinction:

  • Training features came from InterProScan 5.78-109.0.
  • Online sources use InterPro’s current release.
  • Running local InterProScan 5.78-109.0 provides the training-release match.

The practical choice is between matching the documented training conditions and using newer upstream annotations. Either can be useful, but developers should record the choice when comparing outputs.

With --interpro, previously unscanned sequences may be submitted to EBI’s InterProScan service, which requires a real email address. Teams handling proprietary sequences should therefore check whether their configuration uses an external service or local InterProScan before enabling it.

Inference uses greedy decoding, a 16,384-token window and up to 8,000 generated tokens. Outputs include reasoning, a summary, confident and speculative GO terms, and hypothesized interaction partners. Nvidia’s scoring parser extracts both confident and speculative GO terms, so evaluation results should not be read as measuring only the model’s confident annotations.

BioReason-Pro 2 Licensing for Commercial Use

BioReason-Pro 2 is available for commercial and non-commercial use, with different licenses covering the weights, code and language-model backbone.

Release component Stated license
BioReason-Pro 2 weights OpenMDW 1.1
Repository code MIT
Qwen3.5-9B backbone Apache 2.0

The model card’s licensing information supports commercial use, but developers should assess the terms component by component. Calling the whole stack “MIT licensed” would be inaccurate: MIT covers the code, while the weights use OpenMDW 1.1.

The distinction matters for product teams evaluating releases through resources such as Zeniteq’s AI model release timeline. Availability, licensing permission and readiness for a specific scientific workflow are separate questions.

For BioReason-Pro 2, a useful evaluation would preserve the documented dependency versions, inspect predictions against known annotations and keep generated hypotheses separate from validated findings. The code and weights make that evaluation possible; they do not supply its outcome.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can BioReason-Pro 2 Be Used Commercially?

Yes. Nvidia states that BioReason-Pro 2 checkpoints are available for commercial and non-commercial use under OpenMDW 1.1. The repository code uses MIT, and the Qwen3.5-9B backbone uses Apache 2.0. Those permissions do not make the model suitable for clinical or diagnostic decisions, which Nvidia excludes from its intended uses.

What GPU Does BioReason-Pro 2 Need?

Nvidia documents inference fitting on one CUDA GPU with 80 GB of memory. The workflow also loads auxiliary models, including ESM3 and GO-GPT. Its default vLLM GPU-memory allocation is 0.45 because ESM3 and the GO encoder allocate memory outside that share. The documentation does not establish a lower minimum.

What Data Does BioReason-Pro 2 Require?

BioReason-Pro 2 requires a tab-separated file containing a unique protein ID, an organism name and an amino-acid sequence. Optional fields add taxonomy, interaction partners and a structure-file path. Both the model and GO-GPT read the first 2,000 residues, and missing partners or structures are supported by the documented training conditions.

Originally published on Zeniteq.

title: If your app uses an LLM for anything numeric, take the math away from it
description:
I run a personal-finance app where people ask an AI about their money. The first version let the model compute things like "how much will $500/month be worth in 25 years" and "can I retire at 60". It was wrong often enough to be dangerous, and it never sounded unsure.

What fixed it:

  1. Every calculation is a plain function with tests. Compound growth, retirement Monte Carlo, Social Security claiming, Roth conversion tax, debt payoff. The model doesn't do arithmetic.
  2. The model's job is picking the tool and explaining it. Tool schemas list required inputs. If the user didn't give one, the model asks instead of guessing.
  3. The tool returns its assumptions, and the model has to say them out loud ("assuming 6% returns and 3% inflation"). Users trust a stated assumption more than a confident number.
  4. Reuse the engine everywhere. The same functions back the chat, the voice mode, 30+ free web calculators, and a public MCP server. One test suite covers all four.
  5. Refuse advice outside the tools. "Should I buy X stock" gets the math and the tradeoffs, not a pick.

Try it

The MCP server is public with no auth at https://malimoney.com/v1/mcp (streamable HTTP; listed in the official MCP Registry as com.malimoney/calculators). To add it to Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http malimoney https://malimoney.com/v1/mcp

Or list the tools with curl:

curl -s -X POST https://malimoney.com/v1/mcp -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Accept: application/json, text/event-stream' -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}'

The cost is that every new question type needs a new tool, so we ship slower than "just ask the model". For money, I'd make that trade every time. Has anyone found a good way to tell, in production, when a model skipped the tool and did the math itself?

I'm building MaliMoney, a voice AI you talk to about your bank accounts. You can try it on sample accounts with no signup at https://malimoney.com/.

title: Parallel Coding Agents Keep Colliding? Give Each One a Lane
description:
You start two coding agents on the same repo. One adds a discount to the pricing API, the other shows the new price in the cart. Both report success. Then you merge, and one of them has rewritten a file the other one owned.

Running agents in parallel is easy to start. Keeping them out of each other's way is the actual work. This article is a practical setup for that: give each agent a lane, write the lanes down, define how agents hand work to each other, merge in a fixed order, and keep one reviewer. If you're still deciding whether you need more than one agent at all, read Single Agent, Subagents or an Agent Team? first. This one assumes you've decided, and the agents are already colliding.

What a lane is

A lane is three things that belong to one agent and nobody else:

  • A checkout. Its own working directory, so edits on disk can't overwrite each other.
  • A branch. Its own line of history, so you can review and merge it separately.
  • A set of files. The paths it is allowed to change.

The first two are solved by tooling. The third is a decision you have to make and write down, and it's the one that's usually missing.

Step 1: Give each agent its own checkout with git worktrees

The git worktree docs put it in one line: "A git repository can support multiple working trees, allowing you to check out more than one branch at a time." Each worktree is a separate directory on its own branch, sharing the same repository history.

The main coding agents now build on this:

  • Claude Code: claude --worktree feature-auth creates a worktree under .claude/worktrees/feature-auth/ on a new branch worktree-feature-auth, per the worktrees docs. Custom subagents can always run in their own worktree with isolation: worktree in their frontmatter.
  • Codex (ChatGPT desktop app): the worktrees page says worktrees "let Codex run multiple independent chats in the same project without interfering with each other." By default Codex works in a detached HEAD state, and you can create a branch from the chat header.
  • Cursor: in the Agents Window, Cursor creates a separate checkout when you start an agent in a worktree, and runs setup commands from .cursor/worktrees.json, per the worktrees docs.

Two practical notes from those docs. A worktree is a fresh checkout, so dependencies and gitignored files such as .env aren't there until you set them up (Claude Code has .worktreeinclude, Cursor has setup-worktree). And, as the Codex page puts it, "Git only allows a branch to be checked out in one place at a time." That rule protects you: two agents can't silently share one branch.

If you'd rather do it by hand, plain git works with any agent:

git worktree add -b lane/api .worktrees/api
git worktree add -b lane/ui .worktrees/ui

Step 2: Write the lanes in a shared task file

Worktrees isolate files on disk. They don't stop two agents from changing the same file in their own copies. You find that out at merge time, which is the most expensive moment to find out.

So the file ownership goes in a file every agent reads before it starts. I keep it at the repo root as TASKS.md:

# TASKS.md (one lane per agent)

## lane: api
branch: lane/api
owns: src/api/
status: in progress
task: add a discount parameter to get_price

## lane: ui
branch: lane/ui
owns: src/ui/
status: in progress
task: show the discounted price in the cart

Each agent's prompt then says: work only in your branch, change only the paths under owns, and if you need a change outside them, write a hand-off note instead (Step 3). Claude Code's agent-teams docs give the same advice for teams, which don't get worktrees: "Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites. Break the work so each teammate owns a different set of files."

Instructions alone aren't proof, so I check them. This script reads TASKS.md, asks git which files each lane branch changed since main, and flags files outside a lane and files touched by more than one lane. It only reads.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check that each agent's branch only touched the files its lane owns.
Reads TASKS.md and git history only. Usage: python3 lane_check.py [BASE]"""
import re, subprocess, sys
from collections import defaultdict

base = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "main"
lanes = re.findall(r"^## lane: (\S+)\nbranch: (\S+)\nowns: (.+)$",
                   open("TASKS.md").read(), re.M)

def changed(branch):
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "diff", "--name-only", f"{base}...{branch}"],
                         capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
    return out.split()

touched_by = defaultdict(list)
problems = 0
for name, branch, owns in lanes:
    prefixes = [p.strip() for p in owns.split(",")]
    files = changed(branch)
    print(f"lane {name} ({branch}): {len(files)} file(s) changed")
    for f in files:
        touched_by[f].append(name)
        if not any(f.startswith(p) for p in prefixes):
            problems += 1
            print(f"  OUTSIDE LANE  {f}")

for f, names in sorted(touched_by.items()):
    if len(names) > 1:
        problems += 1
        print(f"SHARED FILE  {f}  <- {', '.join(names)}")

print("OK: every lane stayed in its files" if not problems
      else f"{problems} problem(s): fix before merging")
sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)

I tested it on a small invented repo with the two lanes above. To be clear: no agent ran here. I made the "agent" edits by hand with commits, to reproduce the collision from the intro: the UI lane also changed src/api/client.py, which belongs to the API lane, and the API lane changed it too. This is the real output, run on 26 Nov 2026 with git 2.47.3 and Python 3.13.5:

$ git worktree add .worktrees/api2 lane/api
Preparing worktree (checking out 'lane/api')
fatal: 'lane/api' is already used by worktree at '/tmp/shop/.worktrees/api'
[exit 128]
$ python3 /tmp/lane_check.py
lane api (lane/api): 2 file(s) changed
lane ui (lane/ui): 2 file(s) changed
  OUTSIDE LANE  src/api/client.py
SHARED FILE  src/api/client.py  <- api, ui
2 problem(s): fix before merging
[exit 1]
$ git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only lane/api lane/ui
876743633a0717c0cd987ad594fbd1b26bbc968d
src/api/client.py

Auto-merging src/api/client.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/api/client.py
[exit 1]

The first command shows git refusing to put one branch in two worktrees. The lane check names the file and both lanes before any merge. git merge-tree --write-tree performs a trial merge of the two branches; per its docs it "does not make any new commits and does not read from or write to either the working tree or index". It confirms the conflict.

Step 3: Hand off instead of reaching across

The UI agent had a real reason to touch client.py: it needed something from the API side. The fix isn't to forbid that need. It's to route it to the lane that owns the file. I use a short hand-off note, appended to TASKS.md under the owner's lane. For the demo, an example would look like this:

### hand-off: ui -> api
need: client.py should expose the discounted price endpoint
why: cart.html shows the discounted price (lane/ui)
blocking: yes, ui shows a placeholder until this lands
done when: get_price(item_id, discount) is reachable from client.py

Five lines: who asks whom, what, why, whether it blocks, and how to tell it's done. The owning agent picks it up, and the asking agent reverts its out-of-lane edit. In the demo, after the UI lane reverted client.py:

$ python3 /tmp/lane_check.py
lane api (lane/api): 2 file(s) changed
lane ui (lane/ui): 1 file(s) changed
OK: every lane stayed in its files
[exit 0]

Step 4: Merge in a fixed order

My rule (my own, not from the docs): merge the lane that others depend on first. Here the UI needs the API, so lane/api goes first, then lane/ui, and the tests run after each merge, not once at the end. If the second merge breaks something, you know which lane did it. Write the order into TASKS.md before the agents start, so nobody argues about it at the end.

Both merges went through cleanly in the demo, and afterwards git worktree remove cleaned up both lanes.

Step 5: One reviewer for all lanes

Parallel agents can produce work faster than one person can read it. My rule here is also my own: one reviewer, human or a dedicated review agent, reads every lane's diff before it merges, and nothing merges on the writing agent's own say-so. A reviewer who sees all lanes is the one who notices that two "independent" tasks made opposite assumptions.

When to stop adding agents

Claude Code's agent-teams docs are direct about this: token costs scale linearly, coordination overhead grows, and "beyond a certain point, additional teammates don't speed up work proportionally." They suggest starting with 3 to 5 teammates for most workflows and add: "Three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones." Their overview of parallel approaches adds that running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage.

My own signals that the next agent won't help:

  • You can't give it a set of files no other lane touches.
  • Hand-off notes start outnumbering finished tasks.
  • The reviewer is the queue: lanes wait for review more than they wait for work.

At that point, fewer lanes with bigger tasks usually beats more lanes with smaller ones.

Checklist

  1. One agent, one worktree, one branch.
  2. Write each lane's files in TASKS.md before any agent starts.
  3. Set up each worktree: dependencies and .env aren't copied by default.
  4. Out-of-lane change needed? Hand-off note to the owner, not a direct edit.
  5. Run a lane check before merging: files outside lanes, files shared by lanes.
  6. Merge the depended-on lane first; run tests after each merge.
  7. One reviewer reads every diff.
  8. Can't give a new agent its own files? Don't add it.

Where to go next

Lanes, hand-offs and shared state are one part of a bigger design question. Multi-Agent Orchestration: The Complete Guide covers it framework-agnostic in 40 pages: when not to go multi-agent, five coordination patterns (sequential pipeline, fan-out/fan-in, supervisor-workers, dynamic handoff, maker-checker/debate), task boundaries and roles, handoffs and shared state, and five failure modes, including state collisions and diffused accountability.

How do you split work between parallel agents today: by files, by branches, or by trusting them to stay out of each other's way?

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the author.

title: Headlong: a complete agent harness written in Bash
description:
Headlong

Most coding agents wake up when you message them, do a job, then stop. Headlong takes the opposite approach. It is a complete agent harness written in Bash, built around shellm, a recursive language model loop that keeps thinking between conversations. Your team's Slack messages arrive as observations in that stream, and the agent decides whether to answer. Each step rebuilds context from an append-only log, recent entries in full and older ones summarised in tiers, so a long-running agent loses nothing to compaction. It is small, readable end to end, and easy to modify. As of 26 November 2026 it has 1,313 stars on GitHub, is Apache-2.0 licensed, and has no GitHub release yet. The repo is now under Laude Institute.

Repo: https://github.com/laude-institute/headlong

What you get

  • A recursive language model loop (shellm) that keeps thinking between conversations, instead of waking up per message
  • Slack messages delivered as observations in the stream, with the agent deciding whether to answer
  • Context rebuilt each step from an append-only log: recent entries in full, older ones summarised in tiers
  • A small Bash codebase, readable end to end and easy to modify

The test for Headlong is a long-running job: does the agent still know what happened last week?

Quick poll

What would you use Headlong for first?

  • Letting it watch a Slack channel
  • Running a long-lived agent on a real repo
  • Reading the Bash source end to end
  • Watching it for now

Vote in the comments.

If you found Headlong interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: Making agent retries safe across timeouts and restarts
description:
Imagine an enterprise support agent ordering an approved replacement for a customer. The order goes through, but the confirmation times out. The agent retries and reports success. Two orders are now queued for fulfillment, and the support team has a duplicate to sort out.

That sequence is easy to miss if the only thing you check is whether the retry succeeded. To reproduce it, this experiment uses a small HTTP order service and a scripted tool caller. In the first timeout case, the caller gave up after about 101 ms. The order had already been committed. Retrying created another row with the same tenant, product and quantity. The caller saw one timeout followed by a successful 201 Created.

The failure sits between the tool and the service, so reproducing it does not require a model. The setup uses two SQLite databases, one for the caller's saved state and one for the service's orders. All failures are injected locally. This is a deployment exercise, not a report from a customer environment.

Across three rounds, the experiment recorded 117 scenario runs and 288 HTTP requests, keeping failed attempts alongside successful ones. Reusing a saved operation key prevented duplicates in several cases. It was not enough when the service had no record of the earlier request, whether because that record was never saved or had already been deleted.

What happens between a tool call and its result

For the replacement order in the opening example, the tool request could be as small as this:

POST /orders
Content-Type: application/json

{"sku":"keyboard","quantity":1}

The service can commit this order and lose the connection before the response reaches the caller. To make that timing reproducible, the test gives the caller a 100 ms socket timeout and makes the service hold its response for 500 ms after committing. Here is the caller's record, with unrelated fields omitted:

{
  "fault": "timeout_after_commit",
  "timeout_seconds": 0.1,
  "status": null,
  "error_type": "TimeoutError",
  "error": "timed out",
  "elapsed_ms": 100.892311
}

The exception tells us how long the caller waited. To find out whether the order exists, we have to look at the server trace and database. Raising the timeout above 500 ms would let this particular response arrive, but it would leave the connection-drop and process-crash cases unresolved.

That is why increasing timeouts or adding backoff cannot settle the duplicate-order problem on its own. As AWS explains in its guidance on timeouts and retries, a failed call can still have side effects. Once the order is committed, a retry needs a way to identify it as work already done.

Three retry strategies, the same faults

An idempotency key gives the service an identifier it can recognize when the caller retries. To check what that actually protects, the experiment runs each scenario with three ways of identifying the request:

Strategy What the caller sends
No key The same payload again, without an operation identifier
New key per attempt A new UUID for every HTTP request
Durable action key One UUID saved for the intended action before the first request, then reused

The service supports keys throughout. What changes is the caller: it either omits the key, replaces it on every attempt, or saves and reuses it. A fresh UUID on each request still makes every retry look like new work, even though the payload has not changed.

The results below count orders created in one scenario run. Counting successful responses would miss the original problem. All three repetitions produced these counts.

Injected condition No key New key per attempt Durable action key
Response arrives normally 1 1 1
Caller times out after commit 2 2 1
Connection closes after commit 2 2 1
Service exits before commit, then restarts 1 1 1
Service exits after commit, then restarts 2 2 1
Caller process dies before its completion checkpoint 2 2 1
Eight concurrent deliveries of one intended action 8 8 1
All three responses are dropped 3 3 1

Notice the difference between a service exit before and after commit. Before commit, there is no saved order, so the next attempt should create one. After commit, creating another would be a duplicate. The service needs to return the result of the original order instead.

These counts describe deliberately injected faults, not their frequency in production traffic. They establish which behavior each strategy produces. To understand why the durable key works here, we need to follow where it is stored and how the service uses it.

Keep the identity outside the model conversation

For the support workflow, the key belongs to the approved replacement order. Retrying its HTTP request does not mean the customer approved another order.

The caller therefore saves a mapping from (tenant, action) to a random UUID before making the first request. A fresh invocation looks up the same action and gets the same key. Storing that mapping in SQLite lets it survive a caller restart; keeping it in a Python variable would not.

This only works if the workflow preserves the action identifier as well. After a restart, the test resumes action-1 and retrieves its saved key. Generating a new action ID at that point would lose the protection before the next HTTP request was sent. The same applies to model-driven tool calls: an SDK retry, a workflow retry and a resumed invocation may all be attempts to complete one approved action. Their identity needs to come from saved workflow state.

Two genuinely separate orders can have identical payloads. If a customer intentionally orders two keyboards in two transactions, hashing the payload as the operation key would incorrectly collapse the second order into the first. The distinct-action control sends the same payload with two action identities and correctly creates two orders.

A payload hash is still useful, but for a different check: whether a caller has changed the request while reusing an existing key. That check belongs on the service side.

The service has to make a promise it can keep

Recognizing the key is only half the job. The service also needs to know what happened when it first received that key. It stores a replay receipt: a record of the key, request fingerprint, response status and response body. When the same key and payload arrive again, the service returns that saved response, including the original order ID.

The order and its receipt are written together:

BEGIN IMMEDIATE
  look up (tenant, operation, key)
  if a receipt exists:
    reject a different payload, or return the saved response
  otherwise:
    insert the order
    insert its replay receipt
COMMIT

Both inserts occur in one transaction. If storing the receipt fails, the order insert rolls back too. One regression test forces exactly that failure with a SQLite trigger, then verifies that a later valid request can still create the order.

For concurrent deliveries, this example acquires the write transaction before reading the receipt. SQLite allows only one writer at a time. That makes the eight-request result straightforward: one request creates the order, and the other seven replay its result.

This choice also serializes unrelated writes. It is convenient for a small reproduction, but the test says nothing about its throughput at customer scale. A different database needs its own tested locking and conflict-handling path.

There are also boundaries the service must enforce when looking up a receipt. The key is scoped to the tenant and operation, so the same UUID in another tenant must not return the first tenant's order. The local test uses a header to supply tenant identity; a deployed service would have to obtain and authorize that identity from authenticated context. Possessing a key is not permission to see its result.

Within that scope, the request fingerprint prevents a key from being reused for different work. Changing the quantity returns 409 and creates no second order. Reordering the JSON fields remains a replay, because the fingerprint is computed from canonicalized input. Invalid quantities are rejected before the key is consumed.

These are explicit service semantics. Providers may make different choices about saved errors and retention. For example, Stripe documents its own replay and parameter-matching rules; copying a header name does not copy that contract.

A key did not fix the split transaction

The transaction around both writes may look like a small implementation detail. To test whether it matters, one comparison mode commits the order first and saves the receipt in a separate transaction.

The service then exits between those writes. After restarting, it has an order but no receipt. The caller retries with the original durable key, but the service finds nothing to replay and creates another order. The saved events show where the duplicate comes from:

order_committed_without_receipt  order A
process exits
request received with same key
committed                        order B
response_sent                    201

This excerpt shortens the UUIDs for readability. The complete events retain both IDs and timestamps.

All three repetitions produced two orders, despite the stable key. The missing guarantee was atomic storage of the effect and its replay record.

AWS's article on idempotent APIs makes the same requirement explicit: recording the request token and performing the mutations need to be an atomic operation.

That boundary becomes harder when the effect belongs to another system. A local database transaction cannot roll back a payment that an external provider has already accepted. The provider needs to recognize the same operation identity, or the integration needs a way to query and reconcile the outcome. Queuing the work through an outbox can make the local handoff durable, but the receiver still has to tolerate repeated delivery.

This experiment does not implement a payment provider, an outbox or cross-service recovery. Its guarantee ends at the order service's database.

Stopping retries does not establish failure

Even with both writes in one transaction, the workflow still has a problem if confirmation never arrives. Another scenario drops every response and stops after three attempts. The durable key keeps the final database at one order, but the caller has only three connection failures to work with. Its outcome remains unknown.

Reporting that operation as failed would be misleading. Automatically starting a new action with a fresh key could create another order. A workflow needs a distinct path for an unresolved outcome: retain the original identity, reconcile through an authorized lookup or repeat request when safe, and escalate if it cannot establish what happened.

For the support team, this means the workflow should not say either “replacement failed” or “replacement confirmed” based on those responses alone. An evaluation needs to capture the same distinction. A checker that sees only tool exceptions might count three failed operations; one that sees only the database might call the workflow successful. What actually happened is more specific: one order was created, duplicates were prevented, and the caller never received confirmation.

Retry limits, backoff and a total deadline still matter. The example uses fixed attempt counts to expose correctness; it does not test a production backoff policy or retry storms. Its socket timeout is not a complete workflow deadline.

How long does the protection last?

Keeping an unresolved action for later recovery raises another question: will the service still recognize it when the workflow resumes?

A final test deletes the replay receipt after a successful request, then sends the same key again. The service creates a second order. This models lost replay history rather than testing expiry against a clock, but it exposes the dependency: retaining the key on the caller is not enough if the service has forgotten it.

The retention window therefore needs to account for how long a workflow can remain paused, not just the few seconds an HTTP library spends retrying. Before enabling automatic recovery, the deployment needs an answer for what happens when an approved action resumes outside that window.

A durable business identifier with a uniqueness rule may provide longer protection than a temporary response cache. Where that is unavailable, a late resume may need reconciliation rather than another create request.

Run it and inspect the records

The source keeps these failure modes together so you can compare them against the same service. It runs on Linux with Python 3.11 or newer, uses only the standard library, and starts local processes listening on 127.0.0.1.

git clone https://github.com/deavgprime/iac-eval-bench.git
cd iac-eval-bench
git switch --detach 5de3e73a495878377f57324e9947f2e90ca89554
python3 docs/examples/safe_retries.py run \
  --output runs/safe-retries \
  --repetitions 3
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_safe_retries.py -v

Use a fresh output directory each time. The driver refuses to overwrite an existing run.

The saved evidence includes every client attempt, the server events and final order/receipt snapshots. The source includes the unsafe comparison modes, so the duplicate behavior can be reproduced as well as the protected path.

The recorded run used Python 3.12.3 and SQLite 3.45.1. It completed in 29.26 seconds, with 18.53 CPU seconds across child processes. The driver and largest child each reached a reported peak RSS of about 29.4 MiB. Those are per-process peaks, not total concurrent memory. Event logging flushes to disk and affects timing, so these measurements describe the test workload rather than service performance.

The crash tests terminate processes; they do not test a host outage, disk failure or regional failover. The fault headers are test controls, not an interface to expose in a deployment.

For a tool that creates orders, the first test worth borrowing is the one that started this article: commit the write, lose its response, then retry through the real workflow. Check how many orders exist, whether the workflow kept the same action identity, and what it tells the support team. A green status after the retry is not enough to answer any of those questions.

title: Best AI Design Tools/Agents For 2027
description:
‘AI design’ tools keep getting attention on X and in Reddit communities. With so many calling themselves AI design agents or canvases, it’s hard to tell what each one is actually useful for.

So I picked nine tools and grouped them by the kind of design work you might need to do.

I’ve skipped the usual “best tools” rankings and side-by-side comparisons. The idea is simple.

Which tool would you use, and when?

Tools by use case

  1. Google Stitch · Design app screens and try the flow
  2. Figma AI · Create and edit screens on the Figma canvas
  3. Paper · Design on a shared canvas with your coding agent
  4. pen.dev · Design and edit interfaces in your repo
  5. Kombai · Explore design directions for a website or product UI
  6. QuiverAI · Generate and edit SVG artwork
  7. Canva AI · Create branded slides and social posts
  8. Gamma · Build a presentation from a brief or outline
  9. OpenDesign · Build prototypes and decks with your own design instructions

Google Stitch for designing and prototyping app screens

Google Stitch gives you a browser canvas for designing app screens. Start with a sketch, screenshot, or brief. Once you have a few screens, link them into a prototype.

Say you’re designing signup. Workspace name or template first? Put both versions on the canvas and try each one.

Design canvas: Give Stitch a wireframe, some code, or a reference image. Describe what someone should be able to do on the screen.

Voice input: Speak to the Stitch Agent while it draws. Ask it to enlarge the template previews and watch the layout change.

To try the flow, link the screens and press Play. Stitch can also generate a next screen based on what you click.

For terminal work, the Gemini CLI extension connects to the same projects through MCP. Google also offers a JavaScript SDK.

Stitch canvas and integrations

Figma AI for creating and editing screens in Figma Design

The agent in Figma Design can create a layout, revise selected layers, or give feedback on a screen. In the web or desktop editor, it can also work with your team’s components.

Say a signup form needs an error state and the right field already exists in your library.

Libraries: Connect the library to the chat. Type @ to reference the email input or its error-color variable.

Component instances: Ask the agent to switch the field to its error variant and change the validation message.

Review the screen on your phone with the Figma mobile app. For work outside the editor, coding agents can connect through MCP. ChatGPT and Claude also support creating FigJam diagrams. The agent can also switch variable modes or flag colors and type sizes that fall outside the library.

To ask the agent to edit a shared file, you need a Full seat and edit access. View, Dev, and Collab seats can chat, and you can try agent edits in your own drafts.

Figma AI agent capabilities and access

Paper for designing with your coding agent on a shared canvas

Paper gives designers and coding agents a shared HTML/CSS canvas. You can design in the browser. To give Claude or Cursor access to the file through MCP, open Paper Desktop on Mac, Windows, or Linux.

Give a connected agent access to the CMS and ask it to populate six story cards. Five headlines might fit on one line. The sixth might take three. Do you widen every card for the sake of that one headline? You can try the layout by hand, edit the headline on the canvas, or ask the agent to carry a copy change back into the codebase.

The same desktop connection supports Claude Code and Codex, including the Codex tab in ChatGPT. Select a frame and the agent can work on that part of the feed, whether you need a mobile version or code for the layout.

If the site already has a type scale, ask the agent to create Paper tokens from the project’s CSS variables. You can also copy tokens from the Theme tab back into a CSS file.

How to connect an agent to Paper

pen.dev for designing interfaces alongside your code

pen.dev is a design editor you can open in VS Code or Cursor. Work on the canvas by hand or with an agent, then save the editable design alongside your code. A pull request for a new pricing card can include both pricing.pen and PricingCard.tsx.

You can start from a Figma file, paste Figma layers, or import a web page as editable layers in the desktop app. To implement the card, select its frame and tell the agent which source file and components to use. If the design changes again, ask for a corresponding code change. You can also export HTML with CSS or Tailwind. The web editor and desktop apps cover visual edits. For terminal work, pen.dev offers a headless CLI. Claude Code and Codex can edit through MCP.

One detail worth knowing before two people edit the same card: a .pen file needs its referenced images, fonts, and libraries. Commit those too. If Git reports a conflict, keep both copies. Open one in pen.dev, reapply the other changes there, and inspect the affected frames before committing.

pen.dev apps, extensions and agent setup

Kombai for exploring designs for websites and product UIs

Kombai is an AI design engineer for websites and product UIs. Its taste agent works out which layout, visual hierarchy, style, and motion fit the brief. It considers the design choices you’ve already made for your product.

Say you’re designing a project picker. A list makes names easy to scan. A grid gives each project a recognizable preview. Kombai can put both on its infinite canvas. The designs are live HTML and CSS, so you can try a hover state or compare how a transition feels.

Both versions can use the same colors, type, and spacing from a reusable design system. For a starting point, bring a Figma design or a website you like, or browse Kombai’s library of 20,000+ curated UI examples.

Use Kombai in its desktop app, in your IDE through its extension, or from a coding agent through the Kombai MCP Server.

QuiverAI for creating and editing vector graphics

QuiverAI generates, edits, and animates vector graphics. For an icon you’ll use in an app, start in the web editor. Describe the folder you need, add a reference image, or upload a sketch to turn into an editable SVG.

Try the folder beside a line of text. Can you still see the lid? Open the SVG on the canvas and select the shape, or ask for a simpler lid in chat. You can duplicate individual elements, too.

Once the icon is ready, the CLI can add it to your repo as a component. To generate it inside a coding agent, use the Cursor or Codex plugin, or connect Claude Code through MCP.

For motion, the animation API takes the SVG and an optional prompt. API calls draw on a separate prepaid balance from the credits in the app.

QuiverAI agent integrations

Canva AI for making branded graphics across formats

Canva AI turns a brief into an editable design, including a presentation, report, or social post. For a product launch, you might need the same announcement in two sizes. A slide has room for a screenshot and a few lines of explanation. A square post might need just the screenshot and a headline.

If the launch brief is already in ChatGPT or Claude, use the Canva connector there. Open the draft in Canva to move the headline or swap the screenshot. Canva runs in the browser, on Mac and Windows, and on iOS and Android. Connecting another app from inside Canva requires the web or desktop editor.

Brand Kits and Brand Templates: Use Apply Brand to select a shared kit and template. Check the generated deck against the original. Canva AI may skip pages that contain reusable components.

Editable layers: If the release moves to Friday, edit the date. The product shot is a separate object, so it can stay where it is.
Canva lists this feature for Pro, Teams, Business, Enterprise, Education, and Nonprofits users who have Brand Kit access. Canva says personal Brand Kits are outside the current rollout.

Connect Canva to ChatGPT or Claude

Gamma for turning ideas and source material into presentations

Gamma helps you create presentations, documents, websites, and social graphics. For a presentation, give its agent a topic or a brief. It drafts an outline you can edit before it lays out the slides.

For a design review, start with the decision you need. Should the team keep the current checkout or try the shorter version? Put the two designs up front and move the research notes to the end.

You can do this in the browser or in Gamma’s mobile app, where edits go through the agent. Export to PowerPoint if a teammate needs to edit the deck there, or PDF if they just need to read it.

How to create a presentation with Gamma’s agent

OpenDesign for designing with your own agent in an open-source workspace

OpenDesign is an open-source workspace where you can use your coding agent to make prototypes, websites, and slide decks. You can give the agent a design system to follow and save instructions you want it to use across projects.

Think about a comment that keeps coming up in form reviews. What happens if the payment fails?

You can put that question in a reusable skill. The next checkout brief can use the same review instructions.

Skills: Write the instructions in SKILL.md. Keep examples and reference material alongside the file. Edit it when your team’s review criteria change.

Design templates: Set the starting layout for a prototype or deck. Ask the agent to use your review skill on the resulting prototype.

Use the Mac or Windows app to work on the prototype, or run the browser interface from source. The same project is accessible from the od CLI and through local MCP integrations for Claude Code and Codex. In API mode, requests go to your configured provider.

That’s a wrap-up of nine AI design tools I found interesting and where each fits in your workflow.
