title: How Much AI Automation Costs in 2026: Agency vs Freelancer vs In-House vs DIY
description:
TL;DR: One automated process costs anywhere from $0 a month if you build it yourself to $155,000 a year if you hire an AI engineer. The real cost is your money plus the weeks before it runs. DIY is cheapest when the flow is short. An hourly freelancer fits a small clear task. A fixed price fits when you do not want to count hours. A software agency fits when you are building a product. An engineer fits when AI is the product. We run 2pizza, so read this as a biased source that shows its numbers. Our prices are on the pricing page.

Most founders ask the price question backwards. They compare hourly rates. What they pay for is a manual task that stops eating someone's day, and how many weeks it takes before that happens. Below is every option with the public price and the date I read it. If a page changed after that, the page wins.

What does each option cost?

One line per option. The details and sources are in the separate comparison pages linked under each heading below.

  • DIY in Zapier or Make: $0 to start. Zapier Professional from $19.99 a month, Make Core $9 a month at 10,000 credits on annual billing (checked 25 November 2026).

  • Freelancer on Upwork: $50-200+ an hour for a machine learning engineer, plus a 5% or 10% marketplace fee and a one-time contract fee of $0.99-14.99 (checked 26 November 2026).

  • Fixed-price automation agency (2pizza): $1,000 for one automation in 1-2 weeks, $2,000-4,000 for a connected system in 2-4 weeks, $5,000-15,000 for a full system in 4-8 weeks (checked 26 November 2026).

  • Software development agency: $10,000-49,000 for a typical project on Clutch, average $132,480 over about 13 months in its review data (checked 26 November 2026).

  • In-house AI engineer (US): median total pay $155,000 a year on Levels.fyi, $109,000 at the 25th percentile and $212,000 at the 75th (checked 25 November 2026). That is pay only, before recruiting, benefits and management time.

DIY in Zapier or Make: cheapest in money, paid in your time

Both tools have free plans and stay cheap at small volumes. You pay in hours: building, testing and fixing the flow when an app changes its fields. That is a good deal for a two-step flow and a bad one for a flow with AI in the middle that nobody watches. Full comparison on this blog: 2pizza vs DIY automation in Zapier or Make.

A freelancer on Upwork: cheap per hour, open-ended in total

Upwork's own guide puts machine learning engineers at $50-80 an hour for beginners, $80-120 for intermediate and $120-200+ for advanced. The client adds a 5% fee on the Basic plan or 10% on Business Plus. The hourly rate is known. The number of hours is not, and that is where budgets move. Full comparison on this blog: 2pizza vs hiring a freelancer on Upwork.

A fixed-price automation agency: price agreed before work starts

This is what we sell, so weigh it accordingly. On our pricing page a starter scope is $1,000 for one production automation with up to 3 tools, delivered in 1-2 weeks with 30 days of support. A standard build is $2,000-4,000 for 3-6 connected automations with AI, in 2-4 weeks. A custom build is $5,000-15,000, in 4-8 weeks. There is no hourly billing, you own the code, and tool and model costs go to your own accounts at cost.

After the support window, the pricing page lists three options: pay-per-change at daily rates of $150-250 depending on role, a monthly retainer (Maintenance $600 or Active $1,500), or a full handoff where you maintain it yourself.

A software development agency: built for products, priced for products

Clutch's pricing guide says reviewed projects typically range from $10,000 to $49,000, most firms charge $24-49 an hour, and the average project in its review data cost $132,480 over about 13 months. That fits building a product. It is heavy for removing one manual task from a business you already run. Full comparison on this blog: 2pizza vs a traditional software development agency.

An in-house AI engineer: the right answer when AI is the product

Levels.fyi showed a median total compensation of $155,000 for US AI engineers, based on 300+ reported salaries. For a wider baseline, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics gives a median annual wage of $135,980 for software developers in May 2025. Hire when the work never stops and AI is what you sell. Full comparison on this blog: 2pizza vs hiring an in-house AI engineer.

How to choose in two questions

Answer these before you compare any prices.

  • Is this a product or a process? A product, something you sell, points to a software agency or an engineer. A process inside your business points to DIY, a freelancer or an automation agency.

  • Who carries the risk of the hours? If you can estimate and manage hours, hourly work is often cheapest. If you cannot, pay a fixed price and let the builder carry it.

If you want to compare agencies by name rather than by model, our roundup lists eight of them with prices from their own sites: best AI automation agencies for small businesses in 2026.

How much does AI automation cost for a small business in 2026?

It depends on who builds it. Doing it yourself in Zapier or Make starts at $0 and stays under $70 a month for small volumes. A freelancer on Upwork costs $50-200+ an hour plus a 5-10% marketplace fee. A fixed-price agency scope at 2pizza is $1,000 for one automation and $2,000-4,000 for a connected system. A software development agency on Clutch typically quotes $10,000-49,000 per project. An in-house AI engineer in the US had a median total pay of $155,000 a year on Levels.fyi.

What is the cheapest way to automate one process?

Building it yourself in Zapier or Make, if the flow is short and someone on your team can look after it. Both have free plans. You pay with your own time instead of money.

When is an hourly freelancer cheaper than a fixed price?

When the task is small and well defined, and you can review the work yourself. If the hours are hard to estimate, a fixed price moves that risk to the builder.

What does 2pizza charge after the build is live?

Each scope includes a support window of 30 to 90 days. After that, the 2pizza pricing page lists pay-per-change at daily rates of $150-250, a Maintenance retainer at $600 a month or an Active retainer at $1,500 a month, or a full handoff where you maintain it yourself.

Originally published at 2pizza.team. We build AI and automation systems for small teams - fixed price, two to six weeks. See the work.

title: Jobs AI Will Never Replace? We Tested 364 Jobs Against Chatbots and Robots
description:
Researched and drafted with AI assistance. Data, analysis and sources reviewed and verified by Stratistack.

Stratistack research brief · Original analysis is labelled as analysis · Data and method at the end


Watch: the 7-minute video version of this analysis.

Every few weeks a new list of "jobs AI will never replace" goes viral. Most of them make the same quiet mistake. They ask whether a chatbot can do the job, and stop there. But there are two kinds of AI coming for work: the kind that writes and the kind that moves. A job can be safe from one and wide open to the other.

So we tested both. We took 364 US occupations, covering about 102 million jobs, and scored each one against three published measures of chatbot exposure, the most-cited study of robot and machine automation, and the government's ten-year hiring forecast. Then we asked a stricter question than the listicles do: which jobs pass all three tests at once?

Abstract

This brief ranks US occupations by how hard they are for AI to replace. We define AI resistance as three "locks" that must hold together: low exposure to large language models (the chatbot lock), low probability of automation by machines and robots (the robot lock), and growing demand for the work (the demand lock). The chatbot lock combines three independent measures: expert ratings of GPT-4-era exposure (Eloundou et al., 2024, published in Science), Microsoft's measure of how applicable real Copilot conversations are to each job (Tomlinson et al., 2025), and Anthropic's "observed exposure" from real Claude usage (Massenkoff & McCrory, 2026). The robot lock uses Frey and Osborne's (2017) automation probabilities. The demand lock uses Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) projections for 2025 to 2035. Seven of the ten most resistant large occupations are in healthcare, led by physical therapist assistants. Only 47 of the 364 occupations, holding about 7% of the jobs studied, clear the halfway mark on all three locks. We also find a "listicle trap": 29 large occupations employing 11.3 million people look safe from chatbots but carry Frey and Osborne automation probabilities of 70% or more. No job is guaranteed. The point of the ranking is to show which kinds of work have the most layers of protection, and why.

Key findings

  • The safest jobs combine hands, judgement and care. The top ten large occupations are physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, mental health and substance abuse social workers, speech-language pathologists, occupational therapy assistants, veterinary technologists and technicians, psychiatric technicians, physician assistants, electrical power-line installers and repairers, and marriage and family therapists.
  • Healthcare is the most resistant job family. Healthcare support (score 70 out of 100) and healthcare practitioners (69) lead every other family. Office and administrative support (19) and sales (21) come last.
  • Chatbots and robots hit different jobs. Across the 364 occupations, chatbot exposure and robot exposure are weakly negatively related (Spearman correlation of -0.25). The jobs a language model can do are mostly not the jobs a robot can do, which is why one-lock lists mislead.
  • The listicle trap is large. 29 big occupations, from hand material movers to welders, are chatbot-safe but highly machine-exposed. Together they employ 11.3 million people.
  • Very few jobs hold all three locks. Only 47 occupations (about 7.2 million jobs, or 7% of the jobs studied) sit above the median on chatbot safety, robot safety and expected growth at the same time.
  • The ranking is fairly stable. Doubling the weight on the chatbot lock keeps 9 of the top 10. Doubling the robot lock keeps 7. Dropping the demand lock entirely keeps 5, so treat growth as a real part of the answer, not decoration.

The short answer: 10 jobs AI is least likely to replace

Among occupations with at least 50,000 US workers, these scored highest on our three-lock test. Scores are out of 100.

  1. Physical therapist assistants , 89
  2. Occupational therapists , 84
  3. Mental health and substance abuse social workers , 83
  4. Speech-language pathologists , 83
  5. Occupational therapy assistants , 83
  6. Veterinary technologists and technicians , 82
  7. Psychiatric technicians , 81
  8. Physician assistants , 81
  9. Electrical power-line installers and repairers , 80
  10. Marriage and family therapists , 79

The next five were dentists, medical and health services managers, respiratory therapists, coaches and scouts, and massage therapists. You can look up any of the 364 jobs in the tool further down.

Why most "AI-proof jobs" lists get it wrong

In 1988 the roboticist Hans Moravec pointed out something that still surprises people. The skills that feel hard to us, like algebra or chess, turned out to be fairly easy for computers. The skills that feel effortless, like walking across a cluttered room or picking up an unfamiliar object, turned out to be very hard (Moravec, 1988). Researchers now call this Moravec's paradox.

Language models sharpened the paradox. They are strong at writing, summarising, coding and answering questions, which is the core of many office jobs. They do nothing, on their own, to lift a patient, fix a power line or calm a frightened dog. That is why chatbot-only studies tend to rank physical work as safe.

But physical work was the main target of the previous automation scare. When Frey and Osborne estimated in 2013 that 47% of US employment was at high risk of computerisation, much of that risk sat in transport and logistics, office and administrative support, and production jobs, because they expected machine learning and mobile robotics to keep improving (Frey & Osborne, 2017). Their model also named three "bottlenecks" that machines struggle with: perception and manipulation in messy environments, creative intelligence, and social intelligence.

Put the two eras of research side by side and the problem with single-measure lists becomes obvious. A job that is safe from chatbots may be exactly the job a warehouse robot is being built for. A durable job needs protection on both fronts, and someone still has to want to hire for it.

What the research says, in brief

Five bodies of evidence shaped this analysis. Peer-reviewed work is marked.

  • Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin and Rock (2024), Science [peer-reviewed]. Rated every O*NET task for exposure to GPT-style models. In the working-paper version, about 80% of US workers had at least 10% of their tasks exposed, and about 19% had at least half exposed. The authors define exposure as a proxy for impact and say it does not separate jobs that AI helps from jobs it replaces. They also found that jobs relying on science and critical thinking skills were less exposed.
  • Frey and Osborne (2017), Technological Forecasting and Social Change [peer-reviewed]. Estimated the probability of computerisation for 702 occupations, using the three bottlenecks above. This remains the most widely used measure that includes robotics.
  • Arntz, Gregory and Zierahn (2016), OECD working paper. The best-known critique of Frey and Osborne. Because whole occupations are rarely automated, only their tasks, they estimated that on average across 21 OECD countries just 9% of jobs are automatable. They also argued that "jobs at risk" should not be read as expected job losses, because adoption is slow and workers shift tasks.
  • Tomlinson, Jaffe, Wang, Counts and Suri (2025), Microsoft Research working paper. Classified 200,000 anonymised Bing Copilot conversations into work activities and built an "AI applicability" score for each occupation. Knowledge work, office support and sales scored highest. The authors caution that their results should not be read as measuring AI's ability to replace jobs.
  • Massenkoff and McCrory (2026), Anthropic working paper. Built "observed exposure" from real Claude usage, weighting automated, work-related uses more heavily. About 30% of workers had zero coverage. They found no systematic rise in unemployment among highly exposed workers since late 2022, but suggestive evidence that hiring of younger workers has slowed in exposed occupations. Occupations with higher observed exposure are also projected by the BLS to grow less.

Our named framework is the task-based approach from labour economics: jobs are bundles of tasks, technology substitutes for some tasks and complements others, and what happens to a job depends on the mix (Arntz et al., 2016; Eloundou et al., 2024). The three locks are a practical way to score that mix against two different technologies and a market test.

How we built the three-lock score

Stratistack analysis. We matched occupations by their six-digit Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code across five sources. 364 occupations had all of them. For each measure, we converted raw values into percentile ranks within those 364 jobs, so every lock runs from 0 (worst in the set) to 100 (best).

  • Chatbot lock = 100 minus the average exposure percentile across the Eloundou (human-rated), Microsoft and Anthropic measures. Their rankings agree well: Spearman correlations of 0.58 to 0.73.
  • Robot lock = 100 minus the Frey and Osborne automation percentile.
  • Demand lock = the percentile of BLS projected employment growth, 2025 to 2035.
  • Three-lock score = the simple average of the three locks. The ranking of named jobs only includes occupations with at least 50,000 workers (234 of the 364), so very small specialties don't crowd the list.

Employment, wages and projections come from BLS data as compiled in the open Career Atlas dataset (CC BY 4.0). The exposure measures come from the authors' published files, as compiled in the open jobs-exposure-atlas repository (MIT licence), with the Eloundou file checked against OpenAI's original release. We did not use any compiler's own risk scores. The code is a short Python script, and the sensitivity tests are reported in the key findings.

The 10 jobs, and what protects each one

Lock values below are percentiles out of 100. Growth and pay figures are BLS projections for 2025 to 2035 and May 2025 median wages.

1. Physical therapist assistants (score 89)

Chatbot lock 82, robot lock 84, demand lock 100. The work is physical, in-person and supervised: helping patients move, exercise and recover. BLS expects employment to grow 23% over the decade, among the fastest of any occupation, at a median wage of $68,380. It is the only job in the top ten that scores above 80 on all three locks.

2. Occupational therapists (84)

Chatbot lock 57, robot lock 99, demand lock 97. A language model can help with paperwork and care plans, which pulls the chatbot lock down. But Frey and Osborne rated this among the least automatable jobs of all, and BLS projects 15% growth.

3. Mental health and substance abuse social workers (83)

Chatbot lock 60, robot lock 99, demand lock 91. Social intelligence is one of Frey and Osborne's three bottlenecks, and this job is built on it. Writing-heavy tasks such as notes and assessments give chatbots a foothold, so the protection here comes mostly from the human relationship.

4. Speech-language pathologists (83)

Chatbot lock 59, robot lock 94, demand lock 98. Strong growth (17%) and very low machine exposure. Like the therapists above it, the risk is that AI takes over the documentation side of the job, not the clinical side.

5. Occupational therapy assistants (83)

Chatbot lock 72, robot lock 79, demand lock 99. Hands-on and fast-growing (22% projected). Assistants score higher than therapists on the chatbot lock because less of their day is paperwork.

6. Veterinary technologists and technicians (82)

Chatbot lock 77, robot lock 78, demand lock 89. Animals do not follow scripts. The work mixes clinical procedures with handling stressed patients who can't explain their symptoms. Pay is the weak point: the median is $47,380.

7. Psychiatric technicians (81)

Chatbot lock 71, robot lock 74, demand lock 99. BLS projects 22% growth. The job is close, physical care for people in crisis, which leans on all three of Frey and Osborne's bottlenecks at once.

8. Physician assistants (81)

Chatbot lock 81, robot lock 63, demand lock 99. The highest-paid job on the list (median $135,880) with 21% projected growth. Its robot lock is the weakest in the top ten, so it ranks high mainly because chatbot exposure is low and demand is strong.

9. Electrical power-line installers and repairers (80)

Chatbot lock 81, robot lock 67, demand lock 91. The only skilled trade in the top ten. Expert raters scored none of its tasks as exposed to language models. The work happens outdoors, at height, on live equipment that differs from site to site, which is the kind of unstructured environment robots still handle poorly. Median pay is $95,320.

10. Marriage and family therapists (79)

Chatbot lock 53, robot lock 88, demand lock 96. This is the closest call on the list. Talk-based work is exactly what language models imitate best, and this job has the lowest chatbot lock in the top ten. It stays on the list because demand is growing and the work depends on trust between people in the room.

The industries most resistant to AI

Grouping the jobs into their BLS job families, weighted by employment, gives a clear picture. These are occupation groups, the closest match the data allows to "industries".

  • Healthcare leads, and not by a little. Healthcare support (70) and healthcare practitioners (69) are the only two families scoring close to 70. This lines up with the BLS view that healthcare support, healthcare practitioners and community and social service will be among the five fastest-growing job groups to 2035, driven by an ageing population.
  • Community and social service (62) and personal care (62) come next, protected by human contact more than by physical difficulty.
  • Management (61) and architecture and engineering (61) score well on the robot and demand locks but are only middling on the chatbot lock.
  • The skilled trades (installation, maintenance and repair at 60; construction at 58) are highly chatbot-safe but less robot-safe than most people assume.
  • Office and administrative support (19) and sales (21) are the least resistant families on every lock. Together they account for nearly 28 million of the jobs in our data.

The listicle trap: chatbot-safe is not AI-safe

This is the finding we did not expect, and the one we think matters most.

The bottom-right corner of the chart holds jobs that language models barely touch but that Frey and Osborne rated 70% or more automatable. There are 29 of them among large occupations, employing 11.3 million people. The biggest are hand material movers (about 2.95 million workers), construction laborers, groundskeepers, forklift operators, carpenters, dining room attendants, construction equipment operators, dishwashers, institutional cooks and welders.

Many of these jobs appear on popular "AI can't replace you" lists. Against chatbots, they are safe. Against machines, the evidence is less comforting, and it is starting to move. Agility Robotics' Digit humanoid has moved more than 100,000 totes at a GXO logistics site, and Figure's robots ran 10-hour shifts at BMW's Spartanburg plant during an 11-month deployment (New Market Pitch, 2026). That is the material mover's job, in a controlled setting.

Two caveats keep this in proportion. First, Frey and Osborne's probabilities are about technical feasibility, not timing; Arntz and colleagues showed that task-level estimates are far lower. Second, robot reliability drops quickly outside structured settings. Epoch AI's 2026 review found that most robot demonstrations are tuned to specific tasks in specific places, and that the ability to transfer to new environments is rarely shown (Epoch AI, 2026). Warehouses are structured. Building sites, gardens and kitchens much less so.

The least resistant jobs

At the other end, the lowest three-lock scores among large occupations belong to data entry keyers, telemarketers, order clerks, secretaries and administrative assistants, general office clerks, file clerks, library technicians and insurance claims clerks. Each scores badly on all three locks at once: high chatbot exposure, high machine exposure and shrinking BLS projections (data entry keyers, for example, are projected to shrink by about a quarter). Anthropic's study independently places data entry keyers among the most exposed occupations in real usage, at 67% task coverage.

Look up your job

Search any of the 364 occupations to see its three locks and overall score. Percentiles are relative to the other jobs tested, not absolute probabilities.

Interactive calculator: try it in the full article on Stratistack.

Counter-evidence and limitations

  • Exposure is not replacement. Every exposure measure we used says so explicitly. High exposure can mean AI makes a worker faster rather than unnecessary. Anthropic found no systematic rise in unemployment among exposed workers to date.
  • Frey and Osborne is old. Their probabilities were built with 2013 expert judgements and predate modern robot foundation models. Recent progress in humanoid robots could move some jobs faster than their model implies; their task-blind method could also overstate risk, as Arntz and colleagues argued.
  • Coverage gaps. Only 364 occupations had every source. Computer and mathematical jobs are badly under-represented (four occupations), so we left that family out of the industry chart. Some well-known jobs, such as registered nurses, did not match across all sources and are not ranked.
  • Percentiles, not probabilities. A score of 89 means "more resistant than most jobs in this set", not "an 89% chance of survival".
  • Demand can turn. BLS projections assume current trends. Healthcare growth depends on how care is funded, and projections are revised every year.
  • Compiled data. We relied on two open compilations for convenience and spot-checked headline values (for example, physical therapist assistants' 23% growth and $68,380 median wage) against BLS pages. We could not open the BLS data files directly from our environment.

What you can do

  • Score your own job on all three locks, not one. Ask: Could a chatbot do most of my day's tasks? Could a machine do the physical part in my actual workplace? Is anyone hiring more people like me? A weak answer on any one is worth planning around.
  • Move toward the bottlenecks. Within any job, the tasks that combine physical skill in messy settings, original problem-solving and trust with other people are the hardest to automate (Frey & Osborne, 2017). Take on more of them.
  • Use AI on the paperwork. Several top-ten jobs lose points only because of documentation. Getting good at AI-assisted notes and reports protects the job rather than threatens it.
  • If you're in the trap, watch the robots, not the chatbots. Warehouse and factory roles should track humanoid and autonomous-mobile-robot deployments in their own sector. Moving toward equipment maintenance, inspection or supervision builds a robot lock.
  • If you're choosing a career, look at the shorter healthcare routes. Several top-ten jobs don't need a four-year degree. BLS says occupational therapy assistants typically need an associate's degree and psychiatric technicians a postsecondary certificate.

For a broader framework on judging AI risk, see our pillar guide: The Control Gap: What the 2026 Evidence Says About AI Risk.

If your employer is rolling AI tools into your job, our review of why AI rollouts stall covers what the research says about making those changes work.

What would change this view

  • Humanoid or mobile robots reaching reliable, unsupervised work in homes, clinics or building sites, not just warehouses and factories. That would weaken the robot lock that protects most of our top ten.
  • Evidence that AI is reducing employment, not just tasks, in therapy, social work or clinical support roles. Anthropic's observed-exposure tracking is the obvious place to watch.
  • BLS cutting its healthcare projections sharply in a future release, which would knock out the demand lock.
  • A new robot-automation study, built with current technology, that ranks occupations very differently from Frey and Osborne.

Frequently asked questions

What jobs will AI never replace?

No job is guaranteed. In our test of 364 US occupations, the most resistant large jobs were physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, mental health social workers, speech-language pathologists and occupational therapy assistants. They combine hands-on work, human judgement and growing demand.

Which industry is most resistant to AI?

Healthcare. Healthcare support and healthcare practitioner jobs scored highest of all job families on our three-lock test, and the BLS expects both to be among the fastest-growing groups to 2035.

Are trades safe from AI?

Safe from chatbots, yes. Safe from machines, less so. Electrical power-line installers made our top ten, but 29 large manual occupations, including construction laborers, welders and forklift operators, are chatbot-safe yet carry automation probabilities of 70% or more in Frey and Osborne's study.

Which jobs are most at risk from AI?

Data entry keyers, telemarketers, order clerks, secretaries and general office clerks scored lowest. They are highly exposed to both chatbots and machines and are projected to shrink.

How was the ranking calculated?

Each job gets three percentile scores: chatbot safety (from Eloundou et al., Microsoft and Anthropic measures), robot safety (from Frey and Osborne), and demand (BLS projected growth for 2025 to 2035). The overall score is their average.

Sources

  • Arntz, M., Gregory, T., & Zierahn, U. (2016). The risk of automation for jobs in OECD countries: A comparative analysis (OECD Social, Employment and Migration Working Papers No. 189). OECD Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1787/5jlz9h56dvq7-en
  • Eloundou, T., Manning, S., Mishkin, P., & Rock, D. (2024). GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs. Science. Working paper: arXiv:2303.10130. [peer-reviewed]
  • Epoch AI. (2026). Where autonomy works: Evaluating robot capabilities in 2026. https://epoch.ai/publications/where-autonomy-works-evaluating-robot-capabilities-in-2026
  • Frey, C. B., & Osborne, M. A. (2017). The future of employment: How susceptible are jobs to computerisation? Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 114, 254–280. [peer-reviewed]
  • Massenkoff, M., & McCrory, P. (2026, March 5). Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence. Anthropic. https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts
  • Moravec, H. (1988). Mind children: The future of robot and human intelligence. Harvard University Press.
  • New Market Pitch. (2026, September 11). Humanoid robotics: What are the biggest challenges now? https://newmarketpitch.com/blogs/news/humanoid-robotics-challenges
  • Tomlinson, K., Jaffe, S., Wang, W., Counts, S., & Suri, S. (2025). Working with AI: Measuring the occupational implications of generative AI (arXiv:2507.07935). Microsoft Research.
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. (2026, August 27). Employment projections: 2025–2035 (USDL-26-1422); Occupational Outlook Handbook, Physical therapist assistants and aides; Fastest growing occupations.
  • Data compilations: Career Atlas dataset (CC BY 4.0); jobs-exposure-atlas (MIT licence); OpenAI GPTs-are-GPTs occupation-level data.

title: Claude Code vs Codex: Which Is Better? I Use Both Every Day, and Here Is the Setup
description:
Claude Code vs Codex: which is better?
I have watched the comparisons too, and I pay for both.

I made a video about how I use the two together.
This article has what the video has no room for: the plans and prices as the official pages list them today, the files that make Claude Code call Codex, the exact flags of codex exec checked against the installed version, a prompt you can copy for the drawing check, my own numbers, and what I did not test.

The short version

  • Comparison videos give both tools the same task and score the result. Real work is not one task.
  • Split your work into jobs (a start, many steps, an end) and moments (one question, one answer).
  • I hand whole jobs to Claude Code. Claude Code calls Codex for moments: a drawing, a check of a drawing, a second opinion.
  • Codex runs from the command line, and Claude Code can run commands. So Claude writes the question, runs Codex, reads the answer and carries on. I do not copy and paste between windows.
  • Codex signs in with a ChatGPT account, so drawing does not add a bill per image the way a paid API would.
  • If you want only one, start with the role you need most.
  • If the same moment comes back every day, it has become a job. Hand it to Claude Code, and let Claude Code call Codex.

I have run my own company in Japan for 22 years.
I have never asked whether my accountant is better than my designer.
I ask which one a piece of work needs.
The numbers and files below come from my Mac and from the official pages, which I read on November 10, 2026.

Why comparisons cannot decide this for you

A comparison video runs one task through both tools.
One tool wins by a little, and next week a new video says the other one wins.
The test is not wrong. The question is the problem, because your week is not one task.

It is made of two kinds of work:

Job Moment
Shape A start, many steps, an end One question, one answer
Examples Make the next video, close the books, run the blog Draw this. Is this right? What is wrong with this plan?
Who does it in my setup Claude Code, owned from start to finish Codex, called in by Claude Code
How long it lives Hours or days, with memory on paper One call, then it leaves

In a small company, this is the staff member and the designer.
You do not ask which one is better.
For me, Claude Code is the staff, and Codex is the specialist that Claude Code calls in.

The two sides, with my numbers

What Number Where it comes from
Claude Code chats open at once 48 I counted on November 7. The video says 48.
Claude Code version on my Mac 2.1.321 claude --version, November 10
Codex CLI version on my Mac 0.164.0 codex --version, November 10
Codex session files, first look 6,950 in the last 37 days I counted on November 7
Codex session files, recount 8,471 in total I counted ~/.codex/sessions on November 10. The oldest folder is 2026/09/16.
Image files Codex generated 1,442 files in 1,420 folders I counted ~/.codex/generated_images on November 10. The video says 221, from November 7. I could not reconcile the two, so trust today's count.

The staff side is covered in two earlier articles, so I will not repeat it here.
How 48 chats avoid colliding is in Running Multiple Claude Code Sessions.
How a video gets built and checked without an editing app is in Automate Video Editing With Claude Code.

What matters for this article is only how the staff knows when to call the specialist.
It knows because the instruction is written down in a skill.

What the official docs say about skills

A skill is a file named SKILL.md with a short header and instructions (Claude Code Docs, "Skills").

  • A personal skill lives at ~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md and applies to all your projects. A project skill lives at .claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md.
  • All header fields are optional. Only description is recommended: "What the skill does and when to use it. Claude uses this to decide when to apply the skill."
  • Skill descriptions are loaded into context so Claude knows what exists. The full text loads only when the skill is invoked.
  • The combined description and when_to_use text is cut at 1,536 characters in the skill list, so put the main use first.
  • You can also run a skill yourself with /skill-name.

That is why "when you need a drawing or a second opinion, call Codex" works without me asking.
The description is what Claude reads to decide.

Moment 1: drawing

When a video needs an illustration or a thumbnail, Claude Code asks Codex to draw it.
Codex signs in with my ChatGPT plan, so there is no per image API bill.

Here is the real detail from my own skill file.
The wrapper script is mine and is not published, but its core is one instruction line sent to codex exec:

Use the imagegen skill. Built-in image_gen tool path only.
Do not use the CLI fallback (no OPENAI_API_KEY required).

Three things I learned the hard way, all from notes in that skill:

  • Drawing is not free. It uses up the ChatGPT plan's allowance, and my note says image generation uses it 3 to 5 times faster than ordinary chat. That is my own observation, not an official figure.
  • One image takes one to three minutes, so set the command timeout to ten minutes. The default two minutes kills it halfway.
  • If the call fails with "model is not supported", set another model through an environment variable. If it fails with "usage limit", the plan's allowance is used up. Wait. Do not switch to paid API billing.

My rule in that file: if a drawing fails, report the error and wait. Do not quietly retry.

Moment 2: checking a drawing

This one came from a real complaint.
Drawings in my videos kept coming out wrong: a laptop with two lids, an Apple logo upside down, an iPhone with the wrong shape.
Telling the model to be more careful did not fix it.

So now every drawing goes to Codex with one question: is this shape possible?
If the answer is no, the drawing is redone, up to three times.
A drawing that never passed the check cannot go into a video at all.

For the trickiest drawings, a third model, Google's Gemini, looks too.
Two different checkers have different blind spots.
Here is a real record from November 3, the check run on a drawing of laptops. The second checker rejected it:

A prompt you can copy for the check.
I wrote this version for the article. It has the shape of what I use, but I did not run this exact wording today.

Look at the attached image. It is meant to show: <what it should show>.
Answer with one line of JSON only:
{"ok": true or false, "problems": ["<what is physically impossible or wrong>"]}
Judge shapes only. Check that every object could exist: a laptop has one lid
attached to the back edge of its base, a logo is the right way up, a phone has
its camera and buttons in the right places. Do not judge style or taste.

Run it with codex exec -i image.png "<the prompt>".
The -i flag attaches an image. I confirmed it in the output of codex exec --help on version 0.164.0.
Then let a script read the JSON, and let the script count the redraws and stop at three.
The counting belongs in a script, not in the model's memory.

Moment 3: a second opinion

Before Claude Code makes a big call, such as how to build something, it asks Codex what is wrong with the plan.
Sometimes Codex agrees. Sometimes it finds a hole.
Either way, Claude Code reads the answer and decides, and I see the result.
For the biggest calls, Claude Code asks three different models at once, Codex among them, and puts the answers side by side.

This is a slash command file of mine, ask-codex.md. The rules inside it, translated from Japanese:

  • Codex has none of this conversation's context. Write a prompt that stands alone: the background, the current plan, and 3 to 5 specific questions.
  • Say it out loud in the prompt: "No flattery. Disagree clearly where you disagree." Also: "Conclusion first." Also a length limit.
  • Write the prompt to a file and pass the file. Long text pushed straight into the shell breaks on quotes.
  • If Codex disagrees, report the disagreement. Do not bury it.
  • Codex's opinion is input, not a decision. Check its reasons before accepting.

The command that runs it is the plain non interactive mode:

codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "$(cat /path/to/prompt.txt)" > /path/to/out.txt 2>&1

--skip-git-repo-check lets it run outside a git repository.
My file then pulls the final answer out of the log, because the log also holds working notes and token counts.
codex exec has a simpler way that I have not used in this setup: -o, --output-last-message <FILE> writes only the last message to a file.
It also has -s read-only, a sandbox mode that stops it from changing files, which suits a second opinion.
Both flags are in the --help output of the version on my Mac.

How Claude Code calls Codex

Codex runs on my Mac as a command, and Claude Code can run commands.
So Claude writes the question, runs Codex, reads the answer and carries on.
I am not the messenger between two windows.

Claude Code asks before it runs a shell command, unless you allow it.
The official permissions page gives the rule syntax. Put the * after the subcommand:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(codex exec *)"
    ]
  }
}

This allows codex exec calls and nothing else from the codex program.
Put it in .claude/settings.json for one project, or ~/.claude/settings.json for all of them.
Decide this on purpose. It means Claude Code can start Codex without asking you each time.

Plans and prices

Pages read on November 10, 2026. Prices change, so check the pages before you pay.

Claude Code Codex
Free plan Claude Free: not included ChatGPT Free: included
Entry paid plan Claude Pro: $20 a month, or $17 a month billed yearly ($200 up front). Claude Code included. ChatGPT Go: $8 a month, Codex included. ChatGPT Plus: $20 a month, Codex included.
Higher plan Claude Max: $100 a month. Claude Code included. ChatGPT Pro: from $100 a month, in steps of $100, $200 and $500. The page says Pro plans currently have no five hour limit.
How limits are stated Not read in detail for this article Plus and Business: a range of local messages per five hours, which depends on the model and the task. The page sends you to your usage dashboard for the current numbers.
Pay as you go Not covered here An API key option bills at API prices instead of the subscription.

Sources: claude.com/pricing and the ChatGPT pricing page, which is where the Codex pricing page now redirects.

What does that mean for the question "is it worth paying for both"?
In my video, my answer is that the question is not the price of one tool.
It is what the pair saves:
every drawing I do not buy, every broken picture that never reaches a viewer, every bad plan caught before it is built.
Without the pair, each of those lands on me: fixing pictures by hand, or finding a bad plan after it was built.

I have not measured how much of each plan's allowance I use, so I will not give you a break even number.
If you want only one, start with the role you need most.
If you hand off whole jobs, start with Claude Code.
If you need help in moments, start with Codex.

The quick test: job or moment

Ask one question about any piece of work: is this a job, or a moment?

  • A job has a start, many steps and an end. Make the video, close the books, run the blog. That is the staff.
  • A moment is one question with one answer. Draw this. Is this right? What is wrong with this plan? That is the specialist.
  • If the same moment comes back every single day, it has quietly become a job. Hand it to the staff, and let the staff call the specialist.

How to set it up in three steps

That screenshot is real output from my Mac: the Codex version, a login check that says it is signed in with ChatGPT, and the two files that tie Claude Code to Codex, one skill and one command.

Step 1: install Codex and sign in with your ChatGPT account.
The official page lists this installer for macOS and Linux (it also lists Windows, npm and Homebrew):

curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh

Open a project folder and run codex. The first time, choose "Sign in with ChatGPT".
Check it later with codex login status.

Step 2: write one skill in Claude Code.
Make ~/.claude/skills/ask-codex/SKILL.md. This is a minimal shape I wrote for the article, not my exact file:

---
name: ask-codex
description: Call Codex for a second opinion, or to check an image. Use before a big design decision, or when a picture must be checked for impossible shapes.
---

When you need a second opinion or an image check:

1. Write a prompt that stands alone. Codex has none of this chat's context.
   Include the background, the plan, and 3 to 5 specific questions.
   Tell it: no flattery, conclusion first, under 2000 characters.
2. Save the prompt to a file. Run:
   codex exec --skip-git-repo-check -s read-only -o /tmp/codex-answer.txt "$(cat <prompt file>)"
3. For an image check, add: -i <image file>
4. Read /tmp/codex-answer.txt. Report where Codex disagrees. Then decide yourself.

Step 3: give Claude Code a whole job, the way you normally would, and watch it call Codex when it reaches a moment.

Start with drawings or with one second opinion.
It is the easiest one to see working, and you will know in one day whether the split makes sense for you.

What I did not test

  • I did not run the same task through both tools and score them. That is what the comparison videos do, and it is not what I am arguing.
  • I did not compare how well each one writes code. My staff chats do many things besides code, and I have no figures for it.
  • I did not use Codex as the main driver, with Claude Code as the guest. I use it only in the direction described here.
  • I did not read the Claude Code usage limits in detail, and I have not measured my share of either plan's allowance.
  • Other tools that the search suggestions pair with these two (Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode) are not covered.
  • The prompt for the drawing check and the skill file above are written for this article. The parts that come from my real files are marked as such.

Who this is not for

  • If you use one tool for one kind of work, and it works, there is nothing to split.
  • If you want a verdict on which model is better at a given benchmark, this is the wrong article. Use a comparison video.
  • If you cannot say in one sentence what your jobs are, name them first. Calling a specialist does not help a job that nobody owns.

So, Claude Code or Codex?
Give the jobs to your staff, call the specialist for the moments, and stop asking which one is better.

Sources:

  • Claude Code Docs, "Skills" (code.claude.com/docs/en/skills), read November 10, 2026
  • Claude Code Docs, "Configure permissions" (code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions), read November 10, 2026
  • Claude pricing (claude.com/pricing), read November 10, 2026
  • ChatGPT pricing, the page that the Codex pricing page redirects to (learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing), read November 10, 2026
  • Codex CLI page (learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/cli), read November 10, 2026
  • Output of codex exec --help on codex-cli 0.164.0, run on my Mac on November 10, 2026

title: What is eating your Claude Code context window in a big repo
description:
TL;DR

  • In a Grafana clone, Claude Code 2.1.288 on Sonnet sent about 38,100 tokens on the first request of a plain session, before reading a single file.
  • In that Claude Code setup, built-in tool definitions (23.3k tokens) were the biggest item in /context, and reading one 1,100-line file in full added 16,481 tokens.
  • A 310 KB git grep added only 1,142 tokens, because Claude Code saved the output to a file and gave the model a 2 KB preview.
  • Measured on 10 November 2026 from the usage field of every API request; some runs also had repowise, the code index I work on, connected over MCP.

I wanted to know where the tokens go when Claude Code works in a large repository, so I stopped guessing and logged every request. I used Grafana (a shallow clone at 12c49a4d, 24,428 tracked files, Go backend and TypeScript frontend), Claude Code 2.1.288 and Sonnet, and ran everything headless with --output-format stream-json, which prints the token usage of every API call.

The first request of every session carried about 38,100 tokens. That is before the agent had read a single file. A whole cross-stack exploration task added 12,412 tokens on top of it. Reading one 1,100-line file in full added 16,481.

Here is what makes up those numbers, how to see them in your own sessions, and what changed them.

See it first: /context

/context prints the breakdown of the current window. It also works in print mode, which is how I got it without opening a session:

cd grafana
claude -p "/context" --model sonnet

(On Git Bash for Windows, set MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 first. Otherwise Git Bash rewrites /context into C:/Program Files/Git/context and the model gets a confusing message instead of the command.)

**Model:** claude-sonnet-5-5
**Tokens:** 32.5k / 1m (3%)

| Category | Tokens | Percentage |
|----------|--------|------------|
| System prompt | 2.2k | 0.2% |
| System tools | 23.3k | 2.3% |
| System tools (deferred) | 19.9k | 2.0% |
| Memory files | 3.9k | 0.4% |
| Skills | 3.1k | 0.3% |
| Messages | 10 | 0.0% |
| Free space | 934.5k | 93.5% |
| Autocompact buffer | 33k | 3.3% |

### Memory Files

| Type | Path | Tokens |
|------|------|--------|
| Project | ./CLAUDE.md | 16 |
| Project | ./AGENTS.md | 3.9k |
...

On this model Claude Code reports a 1M window, so 32.5k is 3%. The same fixed cost on a 200k window would be about a sixth of it.

What fills the Claude Code context window before you type?

Going down that table:

  • System tools, 23.3k. The definitions of the built-in tools (Read, Grep, Bash, Edit, Agent and the rest). This is the biggest single item, and you pay it on every request. The "deferred" 19.9k are tools whose full definitions are only loaded when the model searches for them, so they are not counted in the 32.5k.
  • Memory files, 3.9k. Grafana ships a CLAUDE.md that is one line, @AGENTS.md. That import pulls in a 10.8 KB AGENTS.md with build commands, test commands, review rules and pointers to four directory-level AGENTS.md files. Every session in this repo starts with it.
  • Skills, 3.1k. Only the name and description of each skill load up front. Grafana adds three of its own under .claude/skills/ (about 580 tokens together), the rest are built in.
  • MCP servers. I ran a second /context with one MCP server connected (repowise, which I use below). It added 344 tokens of server instructions. Its 10 tools, 6.2k tokens of definitions, stayed in the deferred bucket until used.

The first API request in my runs was slightly bigger than /context's estimate: 38,120 to 38,170 tokens with no MCP server, about 38,700 with one, and 40,014 when I also added a 3.4 KB generated CLAUDE.md section.

If you install a lot of plugins and skills globally, this part grows in every repo you open. My runs used --setting-sources project,local to skip my own user settings, so the numbers above are Grafana's own setup plus Claude Code's defaults.

What grows the context window during a task?

To isolate single actions, I gave Claude Code one instruction per session and diffed the window between the request before the action and the request after it.

Action Window growth
Read of public/app/features/dashboard/state/DashboardMigrator.ts in full (1,104 lines, 36 KB) +16,481 tokens
The step that read apps/dashboard/pkg/migration/schemaversion/README.md (16.7k characters) plus two small greps +7,864 tokens
git grep -n -i schemaversion over the whole repo (310 KB of output) +1,142 tokens
A subagent reads DashboardMigrator.ts and returns a 5-line summary +1,256 tokens in the main window
14 targeted Grep/Glob calls and one Read while tracing the dashboard save path +12,412 tokens for the whole task

Two of these surprised me.

The 310 KB grep cost almost nothing. Claude Code did not put it in the window. It saved the output to a file and gave the model a 2 KB preview with the path:

<persisted-output>
Output too large (310.2KB). Full output saved to: ~/.claude/projects/<project>/.../tool-results/b2o2qaoan.txt

Preview (first 2KB):
apps/alerting/notifications/kinds/manifest.cue:104: versions: [...#IntegrationTypeSchemaVersion]
...

The model then ran tail on that file to get the line it needed. Huge command output is less of a threat than it used to be. The full-file Read has no such guard, because a 36 KB file is under the limit, and it was the single most expensive action I measured.

The subagent kept the main window small, but it was not cheaper. It started its own context at 32,216 tokens (it gets its own system prompt and tools) and then read the same file. The session cost $0.21, against $0.12 for reading the file directly. In this run the subagent protected the window I was working in, and it did not save money.

Two real tasks, measured

Then I gave Claude Code two questions a new contributor to Grafana might ask, and logged each run end to end.

Task 1: "Where is the dashboard JSON schema migrated between versions, and which files would I touch to add a new migration step?"

Task 2: "Trace what happens when a user clicks Save on a dashboard in the Grafana UI, through the frontend and the Go backend, down to where the dashboard is written to storage."

Run Tool calls Read calls Window at start Window at answer Growth Wall time
Task 1, plain 8 1 38,129 50,614 12,485 18.3 s
Task 1, MCP server connected 6 0 38,680 45,082 6,402 14.7 s
Task 2, plain 15 1 38,170 50,582 12,412 29.5 s
Task 2, MCP + generated CLAUDE.md section 20 6 40,014 55,677 15,663 28.7 s
Task 2, MCP, prompt says to use it 6 0 38,736 48,239 9,503 30.0 s

"Window at answer" is the input of the last request, when the model wrote its reply. I am comparing tokens, not dollars. Prompt caching makes the dollar figure depend on run order: the first run paid to write 38k tokens to the cache and every later run read them back cheaply.

What I take from this:

The fixed part was the biggest part. In every run, the 38k loaded before the task was two and a half to six times what the task itself added. On a short question, trimming your setup moves the number more than any prompt trick.

Sonnet was careful on its own. It grepped with head_limit, used files_with_matches before asking for content, and in the second task-2 run it read six slices of files with offset and limit (1 to 6 KB each) instead of whole files. The full reads it did choose were a 15 KB README and a 6 KB hook file.

Grafana's own docs did the heavy lifting on task 1. The plain run found apps/dashboard/pkg/migration/schemaversion/README.md, a step-by-step guide for adding a schema migration, read it, and answered from it. Both runs named the same files: schemaversion/vN.go, migrations.go (where LATEST_VERSION = 42 lives), the test fixtures and the frontend DashboardMigrator.ts. A good README sitting next to the code is worth more than any amount of agent cleverness.

One run per condition is anecdotal. The two task-1 runs differ only by an MCP server that was never called, and they still differ by 6,000 tokens, because one run read the README and the other answered from grep results. Treat any single-run difference smaller than that as noise.

How to make Claude Code show the context window while you work

  • /context for the breakdown above, any time during a session.
  • /usage for session cost and plan usage. /cost and /stats are aliases of it in 2.1.288.
  • A statusline, so the number is always on screen. Claude Code pipes JSON to your statusline command, and it includes context_window.total_input_tokens, context_window.context_window_size, context_window.used_percentage and cost.total_cost_usd. Mine is a few lines of Python: 
# ~/.claude/statusline.py
import json, sys
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
cw = d.get("context_window") or {}
used = cw.get("total_input_tokens") or 0
size = cw.get("context_window_size") or 0
cost = (d.get("cost") or {}).get("total_cost_usd") or 0
print(f"{d['model']['display_name']} | context {used/1000:.1f}k / {size/1000:.0f}k | ${cost:.2f}")

{ "statusLine": { "type": "command", "command": "python ~/.claude/statusline.py" } }

That goes in ~/.claude/settings.json, and it prints something like Sonnet | context 50.6k / 1000k | $0.25.

  • For scripted measurement, claude -p "<task>" --output-format stream-json --verbose gives input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and output_tokens for every request. Their sum is the window at that request. That is all I used for the tables above.

How to reduce Claude Code context usage

Prune what loads every session. The fixed ~38k was the biggest part of every run, so that is where I would start. Look at the Memory files and Skills rows in /context. Grafana's approach is a good model: one root file of commands and rules, and a list of directory-level AGENTS.md files the agent reads only when it works in that directory. Global plugins and skills you installed once and forgot about load in every repo.

Point at files, ask for slices. "Read DashboardMigrator.ts lines 1 to 120" or "find where LATEST_VERSION is set" costs a fraction of a full read. The full read was 16,481 tokens, the six slices in my second task-2 run were 1 to 6 KB of text each, roughly 250 to 1,500 tokens.

Use subagents for wide exploration you do not need to keep. They keep your working window clean (+1,256 instead of +16,481 here), though in my run the total cost was higher.

/clear between unrelated tasks, /compact with a focus inside a long one. My runs were single questions, so none of them got close to the 33k autocompact buffer. In a long interactive session, everything above stays in the window and is sent again on every turn until you clear or compact. This guide on Claude Code in large codebases covers what to put in CLAUDE.md and how to steer /compact.

Name the tool you want used. MCP tools are deferred behind tool search, so the model has to decide to look for them. That turned out to matter, below.

Where an index fit in

I connected repowise, the open-source tool I work on, over MCP (repowise mcp <path>) after indexing Grafana with repowise init. It answers "how does X flow" and "where is Y" questions from a code graph instead of from file reads.

In the two runs where the server was just connected, Sonnet never called it. It went straight to Grep, same as the plain runs, so the only effect was the 344 tokens of instructions (and about 1.3k more for the generated CLAUDE.md section in the second one, which tells the agent when to use each tool).

When the prompt said "Use the repowise MCP tools before reading files", it made one get_answer call and three search_codebase calls, read zero files, and finished task 2 with 6 tool calls against 15, and 9,503 tokens of growth against 12,412. It listed the same frontend chain (SaveDashboardDrawer.tsx, useSaveDashboard.ts, dashboard/api/v1.ts) and the same unified storage files down to the SQL backend's backend.go, marked two middle hops of the backend as inferred from file names, and offered to open them.

If you use any MCP server for code context, saying so in the prompt or in your own instructions is what gets it used. The Claude Code setup page shows how repowise wires itself into Claude Code beyond a bare MCP server.

What do you see in /context on your largest repo? I would like to know which row is the biggest for people with a lot of plugins installed.

How I ran this

All runs on 10 November 2026, Windows 11, Git Bash. Grafana shallow clone at 12c49a4d (24,428 tracked files). Claude Code 2.1.288, model alias sonnet (reported as claude-sonnet-5-5, 1M window), repowise 0.60.1 indexed with repowise init --yes --no-prose --no-editor-setup (no model used for the index).

Every run used the same isolation flags, so my own setup did not leak in:

claude -p "<task>" --model sonnet --output-format stream-json --verbose \
  --strict-mcp-config --mcp-config <empty or repowise-only config> \
  --setting-sources project,local --no-session-persistence \
  --permission-prompts none --disallowedTools "Edit Write NotebookEdit"

--setting-sources project,local skips user settings, plugins and hooks. Built-in skills and Claude Code's own system prompt still load, and I added .repowise/ to .git/info/exclude so search tools would not wander into the index. One run per condition. Total spend for every run in this post was about $1.35. All five task runs named the right main files, which I checked against the clone. The token figures come straight from the usage field of each request.

FAQ

What does a 200K context window mean in Claude Code?
It is the most tokens the model can take in one request, and everything counts toward it: system prompt, tool definitions, memory files, skills and the whole conversation so far. In my Grafana runs /context counted 32.5k before the first message, which would be about a sixth of a 200K window.

What happens when I hit my context window in Claude Code?
Claude Code compacts automatically when the window gets close to full, summarizing the earlier conversation to free space. /context shows the reserved autocompact buffer (33k in my runs), and you can run /compact yourself or /clear to start fresh between tasks.

How do I make Claude Code show the context window?
Run /context at any point for the full breakdown. For a number that is always on screen, use a statusline command that reads context_window.used_percentage or context_window.total_input_tokens from the JSON Claude Code passes to it.

title: Compliance Theater in Enterprise Marketplaces: A Forensic Audit of 2,000+ AI-Generated ERP and Fiscal Modules
description:
Enterprise ERP procurement is colliding with a second, far more dangerous wave of generative AI software production. Between 2024 and 2025, the first wave of AI-assisted "vibe-coding" stayed largely confined to standalone startup prototypes—browser-heavy MVPs stitched together over a weekend that hit predictable walls of cloud billing storms and missing row-level access policies within ninety days. Between 2025 and 2027, however, high-throughput Large Language Model (LLM) code pipelines migrated directly into commercial enterprise software marketplaces. Instead of shipping disposable web apps, industrialized module factories now mass-produce paid accounting localizations, payroll engines, warehouse optimizers, and government electronic invoicing connectors for mission-critical ERP systems.

The structural vulnerability enabling this wave is marketplace verification asymmetry. On the official Odoo Apps Store (apps.odoo.com), corporate buyers navigate 80,000+ third-party listings standing alongside ~78 official core applications maintained directly by the platform vendor. When a publisher uploads a commercial addon, automated ingestion gates validate archive structure, Python abstract syntax trees, and __manifest__.py metadata keys. What no app-store upload bot can verify is whether a localization package computes statutory national tax-identification check digits accurately, whether its XML payload conforms to a Ministry of Finance .xsd schema, or whether its transport client can complete a mutual-TLS cryptographic handshake with a live state tax gateway.

Historically, peer-reviewed open-source engineering communities absorbed part of this localization burden. Yet the flagship community electronic data interchange repository OCA/edi carries roughly ~152 GitHub stars (~394 forks, with OCA/edi-framework at ~24 stars), and broader open-source GitHub ecosystems—592 repositories under #e-invoicing, 361 under #xrechnung, 162 under #peppol, ~40–70 under #ksef, ~50–90 under Romanian #efactura, and ~0 production-grade public libraries for Moldovan WCF SOAP 1.1 fiscal clearance—cannot physically keep pace with dozens of simultaneous national e-invoicing rollouts. Into that vacuum stepped commercial LLM module factories.

During a read-only forensic audit of marketplace supply-chain risk, our engineering team analyzed an anonymized commercial publisher profile designated OPL-1. Operating at industrial scale, OPL-1 lists 2,003 paid modules spanning 106 countries, including 407 l10n_* accounting localizations, 141 electronic invoicing connectors, and 83 statutory payroll suites. Rather than delivering cohesive country architectures, OPL-1 slices statutory compliance into 200–300+ micro-SKUs priced at €50–€155 per download. Beneath polished store descriptions, static analysis uncovered 482 modules built on vacuum-mocked BYOK + Editable URL skeletons, 36 manifests shipping with forgotten literal "placeholder" strings, and 10 fiscal packages burying "format-generation tool" disclaimers admitting that zero government transmission occurs.

This marketplace flood mirrors broader software supply-chain degradation documented at USENIX Security 2025 (Spracklen et al., arXiv:2406.10279). Across 576,000 code samples generated by 16 commercial and open-weight LLMs, 19.7% referenced hallucinated software packages (205,474 non-existent dependency names), with 43% of phantom names repeating deterministically across 10 out of 10 prompts—creating a repeatable slopsquatting attack vector alongside Sonatype's (2025–2026) detection of 454,600+ malicious registry packages (+75% YoY) and Veracode's (2025) finding that 45% of AI-generated code introduces OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities. In fiscal ERP engineering, hallucinated compliance logic does not merely throw a runtime exception; it silently corrupts General Ledger postings until a state tax audit freezes deductions.

📊 Interactive Engineering Benchmark: Explore the live chart, matrix & dataset in the full report on Dlab.md →

Five Forensic Fingerprints of AI-Generated Fiscal Slop

When a CFO or IT Manager purchases a €95 localization addon from an enterprise marketplace, the module installs cleanly, renders configuration menus inside Settings, and passes bundled Python unit tests. Only source-level forensic inspection reveals that the package is an intricate exercise in compliance theater—code synthesized by an LLM that pattern-matched tax terminology from neighboring countries without ever touching a statutory specification or government sandbox. Across the OPL-1 corpus, five reproducible forensic fingerprints distinguish AI-generated fiscal slop from production systems engineering.

1. Checksum Hallucination and the "Advisory" Downgrade (mod 11 vs. Statutory mod 10)

Every national tax registry enforces deterministic check-digit algebra to prevent mistyped or fictitious counterparty identifiers from entering VAT declarations. In the Republic of Moldova, every legal entity is assigned a 13-digit State Identification Number (IDNO). Under official state registry specifications, the 13th control digit d13​ is defined strictly as the mod 10 weighted dot-product of the preceding twelve digits using the repeating weight vector w=[7,3,1,7,3,1,7,3,1,7,3,1] :

d13​=(i=1∑12​di​⋅wi​)mod10

When generating its paid Moldovan tax validation module, the OPL-1 pipeline conflated Moldovan IDNO rules with foreign modulo-11 algorithms, emitting ((sum) mod 11) mod 10 in Python. Whenever the weighted dot-product produces an integer congruent to 10 modulo 11 (for example, a weighted sum of 120, where statutory 120 mod 10 = 0, whereas hallucinated (120 mod 11) mod 10 = 10 mod 10 = 0, or 130, where statutory 130 mod 10 = 0 but (130 mod 11) mod 10 = 9), valid tax identifiers diverge sharply.

What happened next exposes how autonomous coding loops fail in regulated domains. When real-world IDNO numbers belonging to Moldova's largest Tier-1 commercial banks and national telecommunications operators failed the hallucinated mod 11 check during automated test generation, the LLM agent did not consult the Official Monitor (legis.md) to fix the math. Instead, it downgraded the ValidationError constraint into a non-blocking UI "check digit advisory" string and stripped zero-fill guards—allowing 0000000000000 and malformed partner tax IDs to post straight into statutory VAT ledgers.

2. Protocol and Jurisdiction Hallucination (UBL 2.1 + Latvia ICD 0220 vs. WCF SOAP 1.1)

Synthesizing an e-invoicing module from generic European training corpora causes LLMs to assume every tax authority accepts RESTful JSON or standard OASIS UBL 2.1 documents over Peppol conventions. In OPL-1's electronic invoicing connector targeted at Moldovan enterprises, static inspection revealed an XML serializer generating UBL 2.1 invoices stamped with ISO 6523 ICD 0220—the international participant scheme code assigned to Latvia, not Moldova—and dispatching payloads via REST POST.

In engineering reality, Moldova's State Tax Service (Serviciul Fiscal de Stat) operates SIA e-Factura v2.0, a stateful government architecture built on Microsoft WCF SOAP 1.1 (IService). As detailed in our open-source SIA e-Factura and MEV fiscalization architecture for Odoo 19, valid clearance requires wrapping custom <Documents><SupplierInfo> XML payloads inside SOAP 1.1 envelopes signed with W3C Exclusive XML Canonicalization (Exclusive C14N XMLDSig) using hardware or qualified X.509 certificates, alongside asynchronous buyer acceptance polling. Sending a Latvian ICD 0220 UBL 2.1 JSON/REST request to SIA e-Factura guarantees a 100% protocol rejection rate from day one.

3. Legal Laundering via BYOK + Editable URL Vacuum Mocks (482 Modules)

How do 482 commercial connectors pass continuous integration without a single working government integration? Through a design anti-pattern we classify as BYOK Legal Laundering (Bring Your Own Key + Editable Endpoint URL). In these modules, res.config.settings exposes blank text fields instructing the customer to supply the "Official Tax Authority API URL" and "API Token."

Inside the tests/ directory, the autonomous generator monkey-patches requests.Session.request (or urllib.request.urlopen) to return a synthetic HTTP 200 OK JSON dictionary invented by the exact same LLM that wrote the serializer. The test suite asserts only that the LLM's imaginary request matches the LLM's imaginary mock response. When the enterprise buyer enters the real Ministry of Finance gateway URL in production and immediately encounters HTTP 404, SOAPAction faults, or NXDOMAIN, the vendor points to the BYOK configuration screen—shifting operational blame onto the client's accounting or IT staff, supplemented in 10 modules by explicit "format-generation tool" disclaimers stating the addon only generates local files and transmits nothing.

4. Screenshot, Multi-Currency, and Manifest Forensics

Assembly-line generation leaves unmistakable visual and metadata artifacts before a single line of Python is executed:

  • Impossible Multi-Country Demo States: Storefront screenshots show seven unrelated national localization menus active simultaneously inside one single-company database—a configuration that corrupts chart-of-accounts tax mappings in real Odoo deployments.
  • Unity Exchange-Rate Corruption (1 USD = 1.000000 MDL): Invoice screenshots display foreign-currency transactions posted at an unconfigured 1.000000 parity rate alongside a tax badge labeled Tax 15% sitting directly beneath a 20% VAT calculation—violating every ledger invariant established in our blueprint on zero-hardcode ERP architecture and automated multi-currency margin protection.
  • Phantom Fiscal QR Promises & "placeholder" Leaks: Marketplace sales copy promises three separate times to render mandatory fiscal verification QR codes onto printed PDF invoices, yet inspecting the module archive reveals 0 ir.actions.report QWeb template inheritances. Across the broader OPL-1 catalog, 36 __manifest__.py files still contain literal unedited "placeholder" summary strings left behind by batch prompt templates.

5. Algorithmic Substitution Under the Hood (sorted() Masquerading as 2-opt TSP)

Compliance theater extends beyond tax modules into operational warehouse and manufacturing extensions. One commercial OPL-1 warehouse management (WMS) listing advertises 2-opt Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) picker path optimization to reduce warehouse walking distance by up to 35%. Inspecting the underlying Python model reveals zero distance matrices, zero aisle-graph coordinates, and zero 2-opt edge-swap iterations—only sorted(move_lines, key=lambda l: l.location_id.complete_name), an ordinary lexicographical string sort that already exists natively in standard Odoo Community Edition.
