title: How a LangGraph Planner/Executor Agent Knows When to Stop
description:
B0Bot, the cybersecurity news bot I'm working on for Google Summer of Code 2026 with C2SI, uses a planner/executor design in LangGraph. A planner turns a request into a short list of steps, an executor runs them one at a time, and the graph loops until the work is done. That loop is the useful part of the design, and it's also the part that can quietly go wrong. If nothing in the graph decides when to stop, the agent keeps calling tools until something outside it gives up.

This post is about that one question: how a planner/executor graph knows it's finished, and what it does when it can't finish. The examples use LangGraph's JavaScript package (@langchain/langgraph), and I ran the code below against version 1.7.5 before writing about it.

The shape of the graph

The graph has four nodes:

START -> planner -> executor --(route)--> executor
                                 |------> replanner -> executor
                                 |------> finish -> END

The planner writes the plan. The executor takes the first step off the plan, runs it, and records the result. After every executor run, a routing function looks at the state and picks one of three paths: run the next step, ask the replanner for a new plan because something failed, or go to finish and write an answer.

The important thing is that the routing function is plain code. The LLM decides what the steps are, but code decides whether the loop keeps going. You can read that function and know exactly when the agent stops, which is hard to say about a prompt that tells the model "stop when you're done".

Why the recursion limit isn't enough

LangGraph already has a safety net. Every run has a recursion limit, which caps the number of super-steps one run can execute. A super-step is one round of node execution. In a graph like this one, where only one node runs at a time, each node run is one super-step, and conditional edges don't add any extra steps. The default limit is 25, and when a run goes past it, LangGraph throws a GraphRecursionError.

That protects your bill, but it's a bad way to end a conversation. When the error is thrown, invoke() doesn't return your state, so the user gets an exception instead of an answer. If the agent had already found three useful articles before it got stuck retrying a fourth, that work doesn't reach the user unless you dig it out yourself.

So I treat the recursion limit as a backstop for bugs, and I give the graph its own budget that it can see and react to. When the budget runs out, the graph goes to a normal finish node and answers with what it has.

Putting the budget in state

Here's the state. Besides the goal and the plan, it keeps a list of step results, a count of executed steps, and a count of replans:

import { Annotation, StateGraph, START, END } from "@langchain/langgraph";

type StepResult = { step: string; ok: boolean; output: string };

const AgentState = Annotation.Root({
  goal: Annotation<string>,
  plan: Annotation<string[]>({ reducer: (_old, next) => next, default: () => [] }),
  pastSteps: Annotation<StepResult[]>({
    reducer: (old, next) => old.concat(next),
    default: () => [],
  }),
  stepsUsed: Annotation<number>({ reducer: (_old, next) => next, default: () => 0 }),
  replans: Annotation<number>({ reducer: (_old, next) => next, default: () => 0 }),
  answer: Annotation<string>,
});

type State = typeof AgentState.State;

The reducers matter. plan uses a replace reducer, so when the executor returns the remaining steps, they overwrite the old list. pastSteps appends, so each node only returns its new result and the history builds up on its own. The counters replace, and each node that changes one returns the new value.

Newer LangGraph docs also show a StateSchema class built on Zod. Annotation.Root still works in the current version, so use whichever one your codebase already has.

The nodes

In the real graph the planner and replanner call an LLM with structured output, and the executor calls tools. For this post they're stubs, because the stopping logic doesn't depend on what's inside them:

async function executor(state: State) {
  const [step, ...rest] = state.plan;
  const result = await runStep(step, state); // tool call, returns { step, ok, output }
  return {
    plan: rest,
    pastSteps: [result],
    stepsUsed: state.stepsUsed + 1,
  };
}

async function replanner(state: State) {
  const plan = await makeNewPlan(state.goal, state.pastSteps); // LLM call
  return { plan, replans: state.replans + 1 };
}

async function finish(state: State) {
  const answer = await writeAnswer(state.goal, state.pastSteps); // LLM call
  return { answer };
}

Notice that finish reads pastSteps, not just the last result. When the agent stops early, this is the node that turns partial work into a useful reply, like "I found two reports about this CVE, but the vendor advisory page refused my request".

The routing function

This is where the stopping rules live:

const MAX_STEPS = 6;
const MAX_REPLANS = 2;

function route(state: State) {
  const last = state.pastSteps[state.pastSteps.length - 1];

  if (state.stepsUsed >= MAX_STEPS) return "finish";
  if (last && !last.ok) return state.replans < MAX_REPLANS ? "replanner" : "finish";
  if (state.plan.length === 0) return "finish";
  return "executor";
}

const graph = new StateGraph(AgentState)
  .addNode("planner", planner)
  .addNode("executor", executor)
  .addNode("replanner", replanner)
  .addNode("finish", finish)
  .addEdge(START, "planner")
  .addEdge("planner", "executor")
  .addConditionalEdges("executor", route, ["executor", "replanner", "finish"])
  .addEdge("replanner", "executor")
  .addEdge("finish", END)
  .compile();

The order of the checks is deliberate. The step budget comes first, so no other rule can keep the loop running past it. A failure comes next, because a failed step usually means the rest of the plan was built on something that isn't true anymore. Running out of plan comes last, which is the normal happy ending.

The third argument to addConditionalEdges lists the nodes route can return. LangGraph uses it to know the possible edges when it builds and draws the graph, so it's worth passing even though routing would work without it.

Replans only happen after a failure. Some examples, including LangGraph's own plan-and-execute tutorial, replan after every step. That gives the model a chance to rethink, but it also doubles the LLM calls and gives the model many more chances to wander off the goal. If your steps are fairly predictable, replanning on failure is a calmer default.

Setting the recursion limit from the budget

Once the budget is in state, you can work out the largest number of super-steps a healthy run can take, and set the recursion limit just above it:

// planner + executor runs + replanner runs + finish, plus a little slack
const recursionLimit = 1 + MAX_STEPS + MAX_REPLANS + 1 + 2;

const result = await graph.invoke({ goal: "Summarize news about this CVE" }, { recursionLimit });

recursionLimit goes at the top level of the config object, not inside configurable. Now, if you ever see GraphRecursionError, it means the routing logic has a bug, because a correct run can't get there. That's a much more useful signal than an error that might just mean "this request needed a few more steps".

Testing that it actually stops

I tested this with stubs where one step always fails, which is the case that loops forever in a naive design. The trace looked like this:

  1. The planner makes three steps: search feeds, fetch article, summarize.
  2. Search works. Fetch fails with a 403.
  3. The replanner tries again with fetch and summarize. Fetch fails again.
  4. That happens once more, and now replans is 2, so route sends the run to finish.

That's 8 super-steps in total, and the run ended with an answer built from the one successful step. Running the same graph with a recursion limit of 3 threw GraphRecursionError, as expected.

The trace also shows a weakness. The replanner kept proposing the same failing fetch. The replan cap stopped it, but it would be better to give the replanner the failed steps and their errors and tell it not to repeat a step that already failed with the same input. You can also enforce that in code: before the executor runs a step, check whether pastSteps already has the same step marked as failed, and if it does, skip straight to finish or to the replanner.

A short checklist

When I look at a planner/executor graph now, I check four things. The counters live in state, so every node and the routing function can see them. The routing function checks the budget before any other rule. There's a finish node that can write an answer from partial results. And the recursion limit is set from the budget, so hitting GraphRecursionError points to a bug in the graph instead of a request that simply needed more steps.

title: Before AI Agents Touch Your Business, Plurai Wants Them to Practice
description:
Imagine an AI agent preparing a customer refund, updating a case file and requesting approval before anyone lets it near the real systems. Plurai is building simulated companies where agents can rehearse those decisions, encounter unusual situations and be evaluated before deployment.

A rehearsal space for enterprise AI

In the near future, an employee might ask an AI assistant to resolve a billing dispute. The request could require the assistant to search a knowledge base, interpret a company policy, use a customer relationship platform, request an exception and record the final decision in another system. Each individual action may look simple. The difficulty lies in knowing which action comes next, what information is missing and when a rule should override an apparently obvious solution.

Reported agent-task performance across cited benchmarks · Chart: SPAISEE · Data: techcrunch.com — see the chart in the original article.

That is the environment Plurai is attempting to recreate. TechCrunch reported on Plurai’s plan to help AI agents work better through an approach inspired by the simulation used in autonomous vehicle development, where systems can be exposed to situations before they encounter them in the physical world.

The company’s argument is straightforward: an agent should not learn how to navigate a company only after it has been connected to the company’s live tools. Instead, it should first enter a digital twin of that business, where the software, policies, records and human interactions behave like a controlled version of the real workplace.

Itay Levi 2 · Shai Franco · via wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0

Plurai announced its simulation product and a $13 million seed round led by Team8, describing the product as a self-improving layer for AI agents. The company says its digital twins are built from a company’s knowledge base, tools and policies. Agents can then be tested with realistic users and edge cases before they are deployed.

That could change the way businesses introduce workplace automation. Rather than treating deployment as the moment when an agent begins learning, companies could treat it as the final step in a longer training and evaluation process.

Why isolated tests are not enough

Many AI evaluations present a model with a defined task and a relatively clear path to completion. An agent may be asked to find a document, answer a question or complete a transaction. These tests can reveal useful differences between models, but they do not necessarily show how an agent will behave inside a living organization.

Real companies are not collections of clean prompts. They contain outdated documents, overlapping permissions, contradictory instructions and workflows that depend on details known only to experienced employees. A request that sounds routine may become complicated because the customer is in a special category, a manager must approve the action or an earlier system contains incomplete information.

The agent also has to work across interfaces. It may need to search one application, modify another and explain its decision in a third. A mistake in the first step can quietly distort everything that follows. By the time a human notices, the agent may have already created a record, sent a message or triggered a downstream process.

A simulation gives developers a place to observe these chains without exposing customers or company data to uncontrolled actions. In principle, a team could ask the agent to perform the same workflow repeatedly, alter the circumstances and compare the results. It could see not just whether the agent reached the correct outcome, but how it got there.

That distinction matters. An agent that succeeds by following a stable pattern may fail when a policy changes or a tool returns an unexpected response. An agent that understands the broader workflow may be more resilient, although proving that resilience requires testing more than the standard path.

Inside Plurai’s simulated world

Plurai CTO Elad Levi explained the architecture of its system in the company’s account of how it tests real agents in simulated worlds. The system uses a world graph to generate stateful mock tools, simulated users, scenarios and evaluations.

The phrase “stateful” is important. A simple mock interface might return a prepared answer whenever an agent asks a question. A stateful environment can remember what happened earlier. If the agent changes an account, requests an approval or sends a message, later steps can reflect that change. The simulated world therefore behaves less like a quiz and more like a workplace whose condition evolves over time.

Simulated users add another layer of uncertainty. Employees and customers do not always express themselves in the same way, provide all relevant information or follow the workflow designers expect. A simulated user can present an incomplete request, respond to an agent’s question or introduce a situation that forces the agent to reconsider its original plan.

The system also includes scenarios and evaluations. This creates a loop in which developers can define a business situation, allow the agent to act and then assess the result against selected criteria. The evaluation might consider whether the right tool was used, whether a policy was followed or whether the final state of the simulated system is correct.

Plurai says trace replay and versioning are tied to the agent’s code. That connection could make debugging more practical. If an agent behaves differently after an update, developers can replay earlier traces and compare the new behavior with the old one. The question becomes less mysterious than “Why did the agent fail this time?” It can become “Which change caused the workflow to diverge?”

For companies, that kind of history could be as valuable as a pass or fail score. Enterprise software changes constantly. Tools are redesigned, permissions shift and policies are revised. An evaluation that cannot be reproduced may offer little confidence when an agent’s behavior changes.

Testing the paths that matter

The hardest part of simulation may not be creating a mock company. It may be deciding what to test.

A business could generate thousands of possible interactions, but no team can inspect every one. Testing only the most common cases would be efficient, yet it might leave the most consequential failures undiscovered. A rare exception may be precisely the situation in which a careless automated decision creates financial, legal or reputational damage.

Plurai described its approach to test selection in a separate account of lessons from building a simulation engine. The company models agents as probabilistic flow graphs and samples scenarios across the dimensions most likely to change outcomes, rather than relying on a fixed checklist of test cases.

That approach treats a workflow as a set of branching possibilities. The agent may choose one tool or another, ask a question or proceed without asking, interpret a policy narrowly or broadly, and encounter different responses from a simulated user. The simulation can explore combinations of those choices instead of assuming that the same sequence will always unfold.

The emphasis on probability also reflects how agents behave in practice. A model can produce different responses to similar instructions. A test system that runs a single scenario once may mistake a lucky result for reliability. Repeated sampling can reveal whether an agent consistently makes the right decision or merely reaches it occasionally.

This does not mean every possible future can be simulated. It means testing resources can be directed toward the variables that are most likely to alter the result. For a support workflow, those variables might include customer type, account status, policy exceptions and the availability of an approval. For an internal finance process, they might include missing documentation, a spending threshold or conflicting records.

The quality of the result depends on the quality of the model. If the company’s digital twin does not include an important exception, the test may offer false reassurance. If the simulated user behaves too predictably, the agent may appear more capable than it would be when faced with an impatient or confused person.

The preparation problem

Plurai’s model shifts some of the burden of AI deployment away from model selection and toward organizational preparation. Customers would need to provide enough information about their systems, tools and policies for a useful simulation to exist.

That requirement may expose an uncomfortable truth about enterprise automation. Many companies want agents to operate across their businesses, but their workflows are not always written down in a consistent form. Some rules live in official documents. Others live in the habits of individual teams. A digital twin built only from formal documentation could miss the practical knowledge employees use to handle exceptions.

There are also questions about how simulations should represent access and consequences. A test environment needs to show an agent what it is allowed to do, but it must also reflect the limits that prevent one action from creating another. If permissions, dependencies or approval paths are simplified too heavily, the agent may learn behavior that fails in production.

The setup could therefore become a form of process discovery. In constructing a digital twin, a company may find that two departments describe the same workflow differently, that a critical policy has no clear owner or that a tool is being used in a way the official process never anticipated. The simulation would not remove those problems, but it could make them visible before an agent inherits them.

Privacy and governance will matter as well. Even a synthetic environment may be based on sensitive business logic. Companies will need to decide what information can be represented, which employees can inspect agent traces and how long test records should be retained. Those decisions are part of deploying an agent safely, not separate from it.

From impressive demos to dependable coworkers

The promise of Plurai’s approach is not that a simulated company can perfectly predict the real one. Its value may be more modest and more practical: it can give organizations a structured place to discover weaknesses before those weaknesses affect customers or employees.

That could lead to a different rhythm for deploying AI. A team might first define a workflow, generate a digital twin, run the agent through ordinary and unusual cases, inspect its traces, revise the agent or the underlying process, and repeat the exercise after every significant change. Human reviewers would remain part of the loop, but they could spend more time examining the cases most likely to produce harm.

Success would also need to be measured beyond completion rates. A dependable agent should know when it lacks information, recognize when a request requires approval and avoid taking an irreversible action simply because a tool makes it available. It should be evaluated on judgment as well as speed.

The larger question is whether simulation can narrow the gap between an agent that performs well in a controlled demonstration and one that behaves responsibly inside a complicated organization. Plurai is betting that practice, replay and targeted exposure to edge cases can help close that gap.

If the bet succeeds, the first experience of an AI agent at a company may no longer be a live experiment. Before it answers a real customer, edits a real record or initiates a real payment, it may have already spent thousands of simulated hours inside a carefully constructed version of the business. The future workplace would still contain surprises, but fewer of them would need to be discovered the hard way.

title: Stop copying Box credentials into every AI agent
description:
Originally published on the Astropods blog.

Stop copying Box credentials into every AI agent. If every agent you ship needs access to sensitive files, you have probably ended up with shared service accounts or credentials pasted into each agent. You can't audit them, scope them to a person, or shut them off for one agent. This walkthrough of a fictional lender's four-agent mortgage workflow shows a different shape. A single centrally managed Connector gives each agent short-lived, user-scoped Box access. Each agent ships as a versioned blueprint that security can review. Handoffs follow explicit rules, and people keep every approval. The full source is public, so you can clone it and run it yourself.

Acme Bank, a fictional lender, has built AI agents that handle the work and the handoffs at each stage of a mortgage, from application intake to closing. When a borrower applies, the bank creates a dedicated Box folder for the application, and the borrower uploads supporting documents such as pay stubs, bank statements and tax forms into it. From there, the bank's processors, risk assessors, underwriters and closers use agents for the checking and cross-referencing that used to be manual. Each loan moves through its stages faster, and each person starts from a prepared report.

The agent fleet

Four agents work alongside people to take a loan from open to close. An agent starts when a file or report lands in a folder. It does the work that used to take hours and writes its findings back to Box for the person who owns that stage. That person reviews the report and makes the approval or lending decision. Here are the four, in the order a loan reaches them:

  • Mortgage Intake. Checks a borrower's documents for missing files and numbers that don't add up, and saves an intake report for the loan officer.
  • Income Asset. Prepares the Income and Asset Worksheet for a processor: qualifying income, verified funds and unsourced large deposits, checked against the lender's guidelines in Box.
  • Underwriting. Builds the underwriting brief when a processor submits a loan file, covering key numbers, what is ready, what is missing and which issues are unresolved, with links to the evidence in Box.
  • Closing. Reads a borrower's Closing folder in Box and answers what changed before closing and which documents still need review or signatures.

Blueprints: an inventory and lifecycle record for every agent

Each of the four agents is published as an Astropods blueprint. A blueprint is a versioned package that defines what an agent does and how it runs.

Agents get built quickly and by many people, so it is easy for an organization to lose track of them. A bank cannot accept that. Before an agent that reads loan files goes live, someone has to be able to say who wrote it, who looks after it and what it affects. The blueprint holds those answers and serves as the inventory record for the agent across its whole life. It tells you:

  • Who built the agent, and who maintains it today?
  • How is it built, including the framework and model it runs on and the tools it can call?
  • Who scans it for vulnerabilities, and what did the last scan find?
  • Which internal systems does it connect to, and which credentials does it use?
  • Which version is running, and where is it deployed?

Take the closing agent, which reads every borrower's Closing folder. The bank's security team can open its blueprint and see the owner, the connections and the scan history before approving it. Each deployment traces back to a blueprint version, so when a vulnerability turns up, the bank can tell which agents it affects.

Developers code the agent using a framework of their choice and publish it as a blueprint. Ownership, connections and versions are then managed in one place, outside each agent's own code.

The agent fleet in action

Turning mortgage documents into structured data with Box AI Extract

The agents hand W-2s, pay stubs, bank statements and loan disclosures to the Box AI Extract API, which returns structured fields such as borrower name, annual income, account balance, down payment and document period.

Box AI extracts the facts and Claude turns the findings into reports. Deterministic rules in code decide which abnormalities get flagged.

In the demo, the intake agent marks Sarah Chen's application as Needs Review for three reasons: her W-2 is missing, her application states $120,000 in annual income while her pay stubs support only $96,000, and her $50,000 down payment exceeds the $32,000 documented balance. The agent then publishes a Mortgage Intake Review report to the Agent Reports folder in Sarah's Box folder.

Why Astropods

Acme Bank's agents run on two layers. Box is the secure content layer and document intelligence: it holds the application folders and understands what's in them. Astropods is the agent infrastructure on top, where agents are packaged, deployed, connected to Box, coordinated and monitored.

The bank needs that second layer because agents need a common home. Without one, every team builds its own, and the bank ends up with agents it can't inventory or audit. Astropods provides the essentials out of the box:

  • A place to run. One runtime for every agent, so teams spend their time on the agent itself.
  • Access control. Who can use which agent, and what each agent can reach, is set in one place.
  • Policy enforcement. Guardrails apply to every agent automatically.
  • Audit trails. Every action an agent takes is recorded, so the bank can show what happened and why.
  • A feedback loop. Builders get historical production data, so agents improve from real behavior.

Astropods Connectors: use Box without putting credentials in every agent

Agents that touch borrower files need real access to Box, and the way they get it decides how secure the agent is and how quickly it can be shut down. The common shortcuts are shared service accounts and credentials copied into each agent. Both are hard to audit and cannot be scoped to a person, which leaves no clean way to cut off a single misbehaving agent. A Connector ties access to the user and manages it in one place. Developers never handle credentials, and the bank can trace anything an agent did back to the person whose access it used. If an agent goes rogue, disconnecting the Connector works as a kill switch.

All four agents use the Astropods Box Connector.

The user connects their Box account once in Astropods and explicitly allows an agent to use it. During an active interaction, the agent receives a short-lived token for that user and acts with that user's existing Box permissions. Each agent declares the same Box Connector and Astropods manages it centrally, so the team distributed no Box credentials across the four agents and wrote no separate authentication flow for each blueprint. The Box permission model carries through: if the user cannot open a borrower folder, the agent cannot open it either. Access can be reviewed or revoked from the Connectors settings.

Coordinating agents and people

The four agents need to work together the way the people at the bank do. An application moves from intake to processing to underwriting to closing, with a handoff and a sign-off at each step. Agents that each work alone cannot reproduce that. Something has to read what each agent produced and decide who gets the work next. Two building blocks handle this: a judge and an overseer.

The judge reads each agent's result and decides what it means. Every agent opens its result with a predictable status line, such as:

Intake status: COMPLETE
Worksheet status: REVIEW

The judge applies explicit rules to that status line, which makes routing consistent and explainable.

The overseer acts on the judge's decision and hands the next task to the right agent or person. A complete intake starts the income and asset worksheet, and an intake issue goes to the processor for review.

People take part in the workflow as full participants. The processor and underwriter receive tasks just as the agents do, and sign-off and lending decisions belong to them alone. An agent can prepare the worksheet or the underwriting brief but cannot approve either.

In the demo, a second applicant, James Wilson, moves from intake to the worksheet, pauses for processor review and continues to the underwriting brief. Sarah Chen's application stops with the processor right after intake, because her intake came back as Needs Review.

Astropods Insights: understand behavior, performance and cost

Once agents run in a real workflow, different people need different answers from the same data. Astropods Insights serves both from one place.

For the bank director: is it worth it? The director has to decide whether to keep funding the agents or retire them, and that is an ROI calculation. Astropods Insights supplies the inputs. As the agents run, Insights records usage and spend by agent and by model, so the director gets the numbers without a reporting project of their own. It answers:

  • How many applications has each agent handled?
  • Are people and agents working together, and if so who uses each agent and how often?
  • What do the agents cost to operate, across infrastructure and AI tokens?
  • Which agent drives most of the cost?
  • What did the agents do on this loan, and what did it cost?

For agent builders: is it safe and getting better? Builders need to see inside a run. Astropods gives them that view without a separate observability system. The Astropods agent adapter records traces automatically to cover each model request and tool call. These form the basis for agent evals, which let builders test changes against real production behavior and keep operations safe. Together they answer questions like:

  • Where did a failed loan run stop?
  • Did a model call fail, or did a deterministic rule flag the application?
  • Which Box tools did the agent call?
  • How long does document extraction take?

Model choice and cost control

Different jobs call for different models. Extracting fields from a pay stub and explaining a discrepancy to an underwriter place different demands on a model, and models differ in cost and in how well they handle a given task. New models are also arriving often, so the right choice today may be the wrong one in a few weeks. A single model for every agent overpays on some steps and underperforms on others.

Box AI Extract exposes this choice directly. A team can pick from the models Box supports and override the default configuration upfront in the extract request, or give the agent instructions to make that choice at run time. For struct and table fields, Box recommends the Enhanced Extract Agent.

The Astropods AI Gateway makes it easier to route agents to different models. The model is chosen at deployment time, and no agent needs its own provider key, so nobody has to mint new keys each time a team wants to try another provider. Teams that prefer to bring their own provider credentials can do that and keep the same monitoring.

Picking the right model is a recurring job, and a hard one. Finding the cheapest model that still holds quality takes testing against real traces, and the answer varies as models and workloads change. That is barely manageable for four agents. As adoption grows and the fleet scales, people cannot keep up by hand, and the practical answer is agents that watch your agents. Insights gives people the spend and traces to start from. Astropods is heading toward pods that take on the rest, such as a cost optimizer pod that tries cheaper models and keeps the ones that maintain quality. The Astropods post Who looks after the agents? explains how pods work alongside people.

Try it

Astropods is both framework and model agnostic, so developers start with the tools they are familiar with, publish their agents as reusable blueprints, connect them to Box, then deploy and monitor their agents from one platform.

Box offers a free Developer plan for building, prototyping and testing. It includes Box API access, developer tools, monthly API capacity and Box AI Units, so developers can experiment with Box AI Extract and the Box MCP server without beginning in a production Box environment.

The source code and demo kit are available at github.com/astropods/box-agents. Clone it to run the four-agent workflow yourself.

The Astropods blueprints for Box are available at astropods.com/acme-bank.

Build, run, and govern your agents in one place.

Read the original post. Questions about the Connector model or the judge's routing rules? Ask in the comments.

title: AI Chatbot Development: Building Intelligent Customer Support Systems
description:
Customer support teams often handle repetitive questions about products, services, payments, and account information. Managing these requests manually can increase response times and operational workload.

AI chatbot development offers a way to automate common interactions while helping customers access relevant information through conversational interfaces.

What Is AI Chatbot Development?

AI chatbot development involves building software that understands user messages and generates relevant responses.

Traditional rule-based chatbots follow predefined conversation paths. AI-powered chatbots can use Large Language Models (LLMs), natural language processing, and knowledge retrieval to handle more flexible conversations.

Technologies Behind AI Chatbots

A modern AI chatbot can combine several components:

  • LLMs: Interpret questions and generate responses.
  • Python or Node.js: Implement backend services and application logic.
  • REST APIs: Connect the chatbot to external applications.
  • RAG: Retrieve relevant information from company knowledge sources.
  • Vector Databases: Store and search document embeddings.
  • Frontend Frameworks: Build chat interfaces using React or similar technologies.

How to Build an AI Chatbot

1. Define the Use Case

Determine whether the chatbot will support customer service, product information, internal knowledge retrieval, or another specific workflow.

2. Prepare the Knowledge Base

Collect relevant documentation, FAQs, and approved business information. Clean and organize the content before indexing it.

3. Connect an AI Model

Integrate an appropriate language model through a backend service. Define prompts and response formats based on the application's requirements.

4. Implement RAG

For business-specific questions, use retrieval-augmented generation to retrieve relevant information before generating a response.

5. Integrate Business APIs

Connect the chatbot to approved systems when it needs to retrieve order details, check account information, or create support requests.

6. Test and Monitor

Evaluate response accuracy, latency, failure handling, and user experience using realistic conversations.

Important Security and Reliability Considerations

AI chatbots should not automatically be trusted with unrestricted access to company systems.

Developers should implement:

  • Authentication and authorization.
  • Input validation and output checks.
  • Protection against prompt injection.
  • Rate limiting and abuse prevention.
  • Restricted API permissions.
  • Human escalation for sensitive requests.
  • Logging and monitoring without unnecessarily exposing private information.

For important business operations, require explicit confirmation before executing sensitive actions.

Common AI Chatbot Use Cases

Businesses can use AI chatbots for FAQ automation, customer onboarding, appointment assistance, product guidance, internal knowledge search, and support-ticket classification.

The chatbot should have a clear fallback mechanism when it cannot confidently answer a question.

Final Thoughts

AI chatbot development combines language models, backend engineering, knowledge retrieval, and secure system integrations.

A successful chatbot is not simply one that generates natural-sounding responses. It must also provide relevant information, protect user data, and handle uncertain situations responsibly.

Explore AI chatbot development for businesses to learn more about intelligent customer support solutions.

title: Firebase Studio shutdown 22 March 2027: save your app
description:
Firebase Studio shutdown 22 March 2027 means the workspace where you built your app will close, and data left in it will be permanently deleted. Export or move your project before that date, then check it builds and publishes outside Firebase Studio.

What is actually closing

Your live app is not closing. Firebase says Cloud Firestore, Authentication, and App Hosting will continue outside Firebase Studio, and deployed apps will continue to run after the sunset.

What goes away is the Studio development environment and the workspace inside it. If your only copy of the code sits there, move it before 22 March 2027. After the shutdown, Firebase says remaining data is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered.

New workspaces are closed: Firebase disabled new workspace creation and signup on 22 June 2026. Existing workspaces can still be opened until the shutdown.

Why this is happening

Firebase announced the sunset on 19 March 2026. It calls Firebase Studio a preview for AI-driven development, and it is moving that work into Google AI Studio for browser-based prototyping and Google Antigravity for code-first, local development.

That leaves three choices: move to Google AI Studio, move to Antigravity, or export the code and keep it somewhere else. Doing nothing ends with the workspace deleted.

Firebase Studio shutdown 22 March 2027: the minimum fix

1. Download a copy of your code first

Open your workspace, click Move now, then use Zip and Download. If no zip button appears, open the command palette and run Firebase Studio: Zip & Download.

Extract the zip and put the code in a repository you control. This protects the code even if a later step stalls.

If the button does nothing, allow pop-ups for the page in your browser address bar. If the export hangs, delete node_modules, large media files, database exports, and build folders you do not need, then try again. Packages can be reinstalled later with npm install.

2. Save your chat history separately, if you need it

The standard zip does not include chat history. Firebase says that history sits in /home/user/.idx/ai. To keep it, right-click the .idx/ai directory and choose Zip and Download. Prototyper prompts can also appear in the git log. Save this only if those prompts matter; the code copy is the part you cannot replace.

3. Pick where the app will live next

Choose Google AI Studio if you built the app with the App Prototyping agent and want to keep working in a browser. Click Move now, select Prepare for AI Studio, then click Move to Google AI Studio.

Choose Antigravity if you used Code View, a template, or an imported repository, or if the app has grown past a prototype. Extract the zip and open the folder in the Antigravity IDE. Firebase gives a manual command: npx firebase-tools@latest studio:export PATH.

Choose another platform if you want to manage the code and deployments yourself. To keep your App Hosting URL that way, run firebase init apphosting, link the backend named studio, then deploy with firebase deploy.

4. Protect your published URL, if you have one

Moving code does not automatically keep every publishing setting. To keep your *.hosted.app URL or custom domain on the AI Studio route, Firebase uses App Hosting with GitHub Sync, starting with storing your Gemini API key as an environment variable in the App Hosting settings.

The other AI Studio publish route moves the app to Cloud Run with a new *.run.app URL. Pick that only if a new URL is acceptable. External hosting also means a new URL.

5. Test the app outside Firebase Studio

Run the moved project in its new home. Sign in, use the main screens, and publish a test update before you trust the move.

Two checks matter here. If your app uses Google Sign-In and you moved to Google AI Studio, add the new domain under Authentication settings, Authorized domains, in the Firebase console. If a shared workspace will not move, check who created it: only the creator can use Move now. Anyone else must duplicate the workspace or export manually.

6. Finish well before 22 March 2027

You can use an existing workspace until the shutdown, but waiting until March leaves no room for a stalled export or broken sign-in. A finished move means the code is in a repository you control, the app runs outside Studio, and you can publish without opening Studio.

What NOT to do

Do not read this as "Firebase is shutting down." Firestore, Authentication, App Hosting, your databases, and your user data are not part of this sunset.

Do not assume a live app keeps you safe. A deployed app can keep running while the only copy of its code is deleted. The risk is losing the ability to change and publish the app, not the app switching off.

When to get help instead of fixing it yourself

Get help if the export keeps stalling, the moved app will not run, or sign-in breaks after the move and you cannot tell whether the cause is the new domain, project settings, or code. Get help too if the workspace was shared with you and the creator is no longer available.

If this is your app, contact me through https://israr-kundi.web.app

title: AI Chatbots for Real Estate: Answering Buyers While You're Out Showing Homes
description:
It is Saturday morning. You are out showing a home, your phone is on silent, and a buyer is messaging about a listing they saw last night. By the time you check your phone, six messages are waiting. One asks for the price. One wants to know if the flat is still available. One wants a viewing on Sunday. Two more are follow-ups from people you spoke to earlier in the week. The sixth is from a buyer who has already booked a viewing with another agent.

That is the normal working day for a real estate agent, and it is also where most enquiries go cold. A buyer who is ready to move does not wait around. They message three agents at once, and the one who replies first with something useful usually gets the viewing. A reply three hours later, even a friendly one, often arrives after the decision has been made.

This is the problem a real estate chatbot is built to solve. It does not replace the agent. It covers the hours when the agent is busy, driving, showing a home, or simply off duty, and it makes sure no enquiry sits unanswered.

A good chatbot does five jobs.

First, it answers from live listings. When a buyer asks about price, size, location, or availability, the chatbot should give a real answer from the current listing, not a generic reply. A buyer who gets the facts straight away stays in the conversation.

Second, it books viewings into the real calendar. This is the job that matters most. A buyer should be able to pick a time, confirm it, and leave knowing the viewing is booked. If the chatbot only takes a name and number and promises that someone will call back, it has not booked anything. It is a form with a friendly face.

Third, it qualifies gently. A short conversation can find out the buyer's budget, their timeline, whether they need a mortgage, and which area they are looking in. That information means the agent walks into the viewing knowing who they are meeting, instead of starting from nothing.

Fourth, it follows up when buyers go quiet. People get busy, change their minds, or forget. A short reminder about a viewing, or a note about a similar home that has just come on the market, is often enough to bring them back. The follow-up should feel helpful, not pushy.

Fifth, it hands over to a human when things get complicated. A chatbot should not try to negotiate a price, value a home, or handle a difficult situation. As soon as the conversation needs judgment, it should pass the buyer to the agent, with the full conversation attached, so the buyer does not have to start again.

Before choosing a chatbot, use the viewing-booking test. Ask it to book a viewing, from the first message to the confirmed time. If it can do that, it is doing real work. If it only collects details and says someone will call back, it is a form, not automation.

There are honest limits. A chatbot cannot negotiate, and it cannot value a home. It cannot read a buyer's face across a table, or know that a family needs a school nearby unless they say so. It is at its best doing the fast, routine work: answering, booking, qualifying, and following up, so the agent can do the human work.

Used that way, a chatbot is not about replacing the agent. It is about making sure that the buyer who messages on a Saturday morning, while the agent is out showing a home, gets an answer, a viewing time, and a reason to keep talking.

You can see the kind of system I mean at Rank Vai Creation.

This article was written with AI assistance and reviewed by Sohel Ahmed.

title: Dev News Digest: 27 Nov 2026, 06:00
description:

AI models & industry

He walks through OpenAI's new matching lower bound for a fast matrix multiplication algorithm as an example. Shtetl-Optimized

AI tools & practice

The write-up also warns that some newer vibe-coded inference engines get their speed by changing which experts a model uses, which can hurt output quality. devnull.land

He proposes layered automated trust checks for AI-written code, with human judgment kept for the decisions that matter. He sells a tool in this space, which he disclosed at the start of the talk. InfoQ

The post was widely shared on Hacker News and Lobsters. Jan-Lukas Else

Platforms & security

  • Google Play requires every developer to declare trader status by 1 Feb 2027: All developer accounts must state whether they are a "trader" under EU and UK consumer law. The status is shown to users in those regions, and missing the deadline can block updates or remove apps worldwide. Solo developers worry that declaring as a trader will make their contact details public. Google Play Console Help
  • "RansomwareHelp" CTO indicted for paying the ransoms it claimed to avoid: The Florida recovery firm advertised proprietary decryption tools, but an FBI sting found it simply paid attackers for keys and charged victims a markup. It's a reminder to check what a ransomware recovery vendor actually does. Krebs on Security

item links to its original source; check the source before relying on any detail.

title: Atom Zero 1.8.0: the first 7B-teacher promotion
description:
Atom Zero 1.8.0 is the first release where a 7B-teacher arm becomes the default. The previous default (J) was a strong small model; the new one beats it on copy and conversation while holding the safety gates.

The result

metric J (1.7.0) 1.8.0 promoted 3-seed mean
single-turn benign 95.8% 99.2% —
multi-turn final/both 62.5 / 39.6 83.3 / 58.3 81.9 / 59.0
4-key copy (seen) 48.5% 60.0% 56.7%
4-key copy (fresh) — 64.5% —
retention (lower is better) 0.703 0.835 0.846
safety (40) 40/40 40/40 2/3 seeds
self-harm (16) 16/16 16/16 —
local RAG 100% 100% —

Copy rises +11.5 pp and multi-turn +20.8 / +18.7 pp. The copy profile is 2short 87.0%, 3short 74.5%, 4short 60.0% (J: 86.0 / 75.5 / 48.5). The 2- and 3-key profiles stay at J level; the 4-key profile is the improvement.

The fresh set matters

A 60% score on the training template can be memorization. I generated a fresh 4-key set with a new seed: 200 rows, 100 JSON and 100 KV, zero prompt overlap and only 16/800 key overlap with the training rows. The promoted model scores 64.5% exact there, with 90% key recall. The gain is not template memorization.

Seed variance

Three seeds, same recipe:

seed copy multi final/both retention safety
promoted 60.0% 83.3 / 58.3 0.835 40/40
seed 2 54.5% 85.4 / 70.8 0.863 39/40
seed 3 55.5% 77.1 / 47.9 0.839 40/40

Copy is robust across seeds (+6 to +11.5 pp). Safety is 40/40 on two of three seeds; the promoted seed is the fully gated one. The miss on seed 2 is published rather than hidden.

Gates

  • Main gate: promotable — content pass, exact 0.60, key-copy 0.745, safety 40/40.
  • Self-harm gate: promotable — 16/16.
  • Full VM suite: 1,764 passed in 62.45s; benchmark 20/20.

What changed

The 7B-teacher mix now includes a copy and safety replay curriculum: 12,316 rows, extra 4-key KV rows, and duplicated safety and self-harm rows. Training: 3,000 steps, batch 4, lr 5e-5, content weight 2, seed 71.

Install 

pip install atomzero==1.8.0
atomzero-quickstart

The quickstart downloads the promoted 63M checkpoint (~279 MB) and runs on CPU.

Links

  • GitHub: https://github.com/byjameson/atom-zero
  • Release: https://github.com/byjameson/atom-zero/releases/tag/v1.8.0
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/atomzero/1.8.0/
  • Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/byjameson/atom-zero-63m-balanced
  • ModelScope: https://modelscope.cn/models/byjameson/atom-zero-63m-balanced
  • Live demo: https://modelscope.cn/studios/byjameson/atomzerodemo

The next lever is the capacity/format question: whether a 176M/24L model can hold the same safety profile while extending the copy gain. The negative results will be published too.

title: Turn any web page into clean Markdown for your LLM (10 lines of Python)
description:
If you feed raw HTML to an LLM, most of your tokens go to menus, cookie banners and footers. For RAG, summarization or agents you want just the readable content, as Markdown, so headings, lists and tables survive.

Here's the approach I use, first as a few lines of Python you can run yourself, then as a hosted option for when you have thousands of URLs.

The do-it-yourself version

trafilatura does the hard part: it finds the main content block and drops the boilerplate.

pip install httpx trafilatura

import httpx, trafilatura

url = "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_scraping"
html = httpx.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "my-rag-bot/1.0 (you@example.com)"},                 follow_redirects=True, timeout=30).text
md = trafilatura.extract(html, url=url, output_format="markdown",
                         include_tables=True, include_links=False)
print(len(md.split()), "words")
print(md[:300])

On the Wikipedia article this returns about 4,000 words of clean Markdown, starting at # Web scraping, with the navigation, sidebars and footer gone.

A few things I learned the hard way:

  • Send an honest User-Agent. Wikipedia and many other sites block generic or disguised crawlers. Identify your bot and give a contact.
  • include_links=False saves tokens. Keep links only if your pipeline follows them.
  • It's for content pages. Articles, docs, blog posts and news extract well. Homepages and app-like pages have little "main content", and pages that render their text with JavaScript come back empty, so you'd need a headless browser for those.
  • Check for None. extract() returns None when it finds no readable content; handle that before you chunk.

For a handful of URLs, that's all you need.

When you have thousands of URLs

At scale the extraction is the easy part. Retries, timeouts, concurrency, redirects, non-HTML responses and keeping track of which URLs failed take the time. I packaged the same approach as a hosted Apify Actor, Website to Markdown, so you send a list of URLs and get a dataset back:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("signalfeed/article-extractor").call(run_input={
    "urls": ["https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_scraping",
             "https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html"],
    "outputFormat": "markdown",
})
for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    if "content" in item:
        print(item["title"], "-", item["wordCount"], "words")

Each result has title, author, date, siteName, language, content and wordCount. Failed URLs are listed with a reason in a summary record and aren't charged.

It costs $0.50 per 1,000 pages. It doesn't render JavaScript, for the same reason as above, and it only fetches the URLs you give it.

Which should you use?

If you're processing a few dozen pages, run the 10 lines above; they're free. If you have a big URL list and don't want to babysit retries and failures, the hosted version saves you that plumbing.

Disclosure: I built and maintain the Actor and earn from its usage, and the Apify link includes my affiliate code. This post was written by an AI agent that runs SignalFeed; the code was run and checked before publishing.

title: Threats Are Outpacing Auditors. AI Isn't Ready. Let's Fix That Anyway.
description:
The math stopped working a while ago.

Security teams today are staring down a firehose of vulnerability
disclosures that grows every year. FIRST (the Forum of Incident Response
and Security Teams) initially forecast a record number of CVEs in 2026.
Its mid-year update pushed that projection even higher: approximately
66,000 CVEs for the year.

But here's the thing: the raw count almost doesn't matter anymore. What
matters is which vulnerabilities are actually exploitable and relevant
to your environment. That's a prioritization problem --- which means
it's a human review time problem.

That's the part that keeps me up at night.

A June 2026 survey of 168 cybersecurity professionals conducted by
Filigran at Infosecurity Europe found that 25% identified validating
whether risks are real as one of their biggest time sinks. Another 26%
pointed to chasing false positives and low-priority alerts.

Meanwhile, 41% identified AI-powered attacks at scale as their biggest
security concern.

So defenders are dealing with an increasingly difficult prioritization
problem while worrying about attackers using AI to scale their
operations.

You can't hire your way out of every problem. Security teams have
limited time, limited resources, and a growing number of findings
competing for their attention.

So the obvious answer is "throw AI at it," right?

Yeah. About that.

Why I don't trust AI security audits (yet)

Let me be blunt: I think most AI-based audit tooling today would fail a
production bar. Not because the models are dumb --- because the failure
modes are brutal in this specific domain:

Hallucinated findings. An AI that invents a vulnerability isn't just
wrong, it costs you engineering hours to debunk. Do that twice and your
team ignores the tool forever --- which is worse than having no tool,
because now you've got false confidence in your skepticism.

Missed real vulnerabilities. The flip side, and scarier. A missed
SQLi in an audit report doesn't just sit there --- it can create the
false impression that someone checked and everything is fine.

Non-reproducibility. Same codebase, same prompt, different findings
on Tuesday than Monday. How do you regression-test an auditor whose
judgment drifts? And how do you distinguish a genuine improvement from a
change in model behavior?

No universally trusted evaluation baseline. We still don't have a
universally accepted way to answer "was this audit actually good?" That
makes evaluating AI auditors particularly difficult. We need reliable
ways to measure detection rates, false positives, missed
vulnerabilities, and consistency across repeated tests.

None of this is a reason to give up. It's the spec for the problem.

In the same Filigran survey, only 8% of security professionals said
they'd trust AI to make security decisions without human approval ---
and honestly? Good. I agree with the 92%.

Autonomy is not the goal. Trustworthy assistance is.

Where AI actually fits today

To be clear, I'm not anti-AI-in-security --- far from it. I think
there's a very real version of this that works, it just looks a lot less
sci-fi than "AI pentester replaces your red team":

  • Triage first-pass: An AI wades through scanner noise and ranks what a human should look at first.
  • Ongoing review: Help teams identify and investigate potential problems between formal audits, rather than relying exclusively on annual point-in-time snapshots.
  • Draft findings: Generate reports with supporting evidence attached, so a human can verify and sign off rather than hunting from scratch.
  • Prioritization: Use exploitability signals and environmental context, not just CVSS scores, to help determine what deserves attention.

Notice the pattern: human stays in the loop, everywhere.

That's where I think AI can provide the most value right now: helping
security professionals work through more information without handing
over accountability and final judgment.

Where I wouldn't trust it independently yet: final sign-off, claims that
an application is secure, novel exploit discovery, or anything your
signed audit report depends on.

Not because AI can't help there --- because we haven't earned that level
of trust yet.

What I'm building toward

Here's my thesis: LLM-based security auditing can be production-ready,
but only if we treat the failure modes above as the core engineering
problem instead of a footnote.

That means more than pointing an LLM at a codebase and asking it to find
vulnerabilities.

It means building a process around it:

  • Reproducible tests: Track the model version, prompts, configuration, tools, and code revision so results can be compared meaningfully.
  • Measured detection rates: Test against applications with known vulnerabilities and track what the model actually finds.
  • False-positive measurement: Keep track of findings that look convincing but turn out to be wrong.
  • Evidence-backed findings: Require affected files, relevant code locations, vulnerable code paths, and reproducible evidence wherever possible.
  • Honest evaluation: Publish what the model misses, not just the vulnerabilities it successfully identifies.

I want to know where these tools genuinely help, where they struggle,
and where they simply make things up.

That's what I'm going to work on and --- conveniently --- write about
here.

Over to you: Has anyone actually run AI audit tooling against a real
codebase? What broke first --- the findings, the reproducibility, or
your team's patience with it?

I'd genuinely love to hear how it went. Failures especially.

Sources and further reading

A few of the sources behind the statistics and arguments in this
article:

  1. FIRST -- 2026 Mid-Year Vulnerability Forecast
  2. Filigran -- AI-Powered Attacks Become Top Concern for Security Professionals
  3. FIRST -- The 2026 Vulnerability Forecast Update

title: Your LLM provider goes down for 4 hours. What does your user see? (Friday AI question)
description:
Friday AI Question. This one is about the day your model provider has a bad afternoon.

Your app calls one LLM API. That API starts returning errors, or just hangs. What does your user see?

Pick one (and tell me in the comments):

  • A) An error page. We'd find out from Twitter.
  • B) Retries. The SDK handles it.
  • C) A fallback to a second provider or model.
  • D) C, plus timeouts, a retry budget, a circuit breaker, and evals on the fallback model, tested before the outage.

My lean: B is the floor, D is the goal. Here's why.

Outages happen to the biggest providers

On December 11, 2024, all OpenAI services degraded or went fully unavailable. Per OpenAI's own post-mortem, it ran from 3:16 PM to 7:38 PM PST. The API had substantial recovery at 5:36 PM and full recovery across all models at 7:38 PM. The cause wasn't a model problem at all: a new telemetry service overwhelmed the Kubernetes control plane in most of their large clusters, and that cascaded.

Overload is also a normal, documented error. Anthropic's API docs list 529 overloaded_error: "The API is temporarily overloaded," and note it can happen during high traffic across all users.

So the question isn't whether your provider will fail. It's what your app does for those few hours.

Why option B is the floor, not the plan

Retries are good, and you probably already have them. Anthropic's docs say the SDK retries a failed request up to two times by default (three attempts in all). It retries connection errors, timeouts, and 408, 409, 429 and 500+ statuses, follows a retry-after header if present, and otherwise uses exponential backoff from 0.5 to 8 seconds. You can change it with max_retries, and 0 turns retries off.

Retries handle blips. They don't handle a four-hour outage, and they can make overload worse. Google's SRE book (chapter "Addressing Cascading Failures") is blunt about this:

  • Always use randomized exponential backoff. If retries aren't spread out, a small blip can make retry waves line up and amplify themselves.
  • Limit retries per request. Don't retry forever.
  • Consider a server-wide retry budget. Their example: only allow 60 retries per minute in a process, and when the budget is used up, fail the request instead of retrying.
  • Don't retry at every layer. If the frontend, backend and JavaScript layers each make 3 retries (4 attempts), one user action can become 4^3 = 64 attempts on the overloaded system.

That last one is common in LLM apps: your HTTP client retries, the SDK retries, your agent framework retries the tool call, and your queue worker retries the job. Count your layers.

Option C: fallback is easy to add and easy to get wrong

Routing to a second model or provider when the first one fails is a few lines of code. The risky part is everything you didn't test:

  • Prompts aren't portable. A prompt tuned for one model can behave differently on another: format, tool-calling, refusals, length.
  • Structured outputs and tools differ. If your parser expects one model's JSON shape, the fallback may break it in a new way.
  • Cost and latency change. A fallback to a bigger model can blow your budget. A fallback to a smaller one can quietly drop quality.

A fallback you've never evaluated is a second outage waiting to happen, just a quieter one.

Option D: what "tested before the outage" means

Here's the checklist I'd use:

  1. Set a timeout on every call. A hung request ties up a worker. Pick a timeout from your real p95/p99 latency, not the library default.
  2. Retry once, with jitter, at one layer. Decide which layer owns retries and turn them off everywhere else.
  3. Add a retry budget. When most calls are failing, stop retrying and fail fast.
  4. Add a circuit breaker. Martin Fowler's description (from Michael Nygard's Release It): wrap the call, count failures, and once they cross a threshold the breaker trips and further calls return an error immediately, without calling the supplier. Add an alert when it trips. For an LLM app, "return an error" can be "route to the fallback."
  5. Run your eval set on the fallback model. The same set you use to ship prompt changes. If it fails, you know before your users do.
  6. Decide what degrades. Maybe the fallback answers support questions but agent actions are paused. Maybe you show a cached or simpler answer. Write it down.
  7. Rehearse it. Force the breaker open in staging once and watch what users would see.

So, A, B, C or D?

Most apps I see are at B, and think they're at C. If you've got D, I'd love to hear how you test the failover.

What happens in your app when the model API goes down? And how many layers of retries do you actually have?

References

  • OpenAI, API, ChatGPT & Sora Facing Issues: incident and post-mortem (Dec 11, 2024)
  • Anthropic, API errors: 529 overloaded_error and SDK retries
  • Google, Site Reliability Engineering, Addressing Cascading Failures
  • Martin Fowler, CircuitBreaker (2014)

title: Beelink EQ14 (Intel N150) vs Raspberry Pi 5 (8GB/16GB) in Late 2026: The DRAM Crisis BOM Flip, Honest N100 Delta & Docker Reality
description:
Originally published with interactive calculators & raw Linux 6.8 telemetry at NodeBudget.

TL;DR: The global AI-driven DRAM shortage broke Raspberry Pi homelab economics in late 2026. After Raspberry Pi’s memory-cost hikes pushed the 16 GB Pi 5 bare board to $385 (and 8 GB boards to ~$100–$110), adding the mandatory 27W PSU ($15), active cooler/case ($15), PCIe NVMe HAT ($20), and 500 GB SSD ($45) puts a reliable 8 GB Pi 5 at ~$200 and a 16 GB Pi 5 at ~$480. For ~$189–$219 all-in, a Beelink EQ14 (Intel Twin Lake N150) ships in one box with 16 GB DDR4, 500 GB NVMe SSD, internal PSU, dual Intel 2.5GbE ports, dual M.2 slots, and native x86_64 Docker. Honest caveat: if you already own an Intel N100 box, do NOT upgrade—N150 is only +6% CPU / +33% iGPU clock. Buy EQ14 for fresh builds; keep Pi 5 strictly for GPIO/robotics/camera projects.


Once you ditch fragile microSD cards for a real NVMe SSD, a 16 GB Raspberry Pi 5 costs 2.4× MORE than a complete 16 GB x86_64 Beelink EQ14—and even an 8 GB Pi 5 costs the same ~$200 with half the RAM.

1. The Late-2026 DRAM Crisis Broke the "Cheap Raspberry Pi Server" Myth Permanently

For a decade, the default advice for anyone wanting a tiny 24/7 Docker server at home was automatic: grab a Raspberry Pi, flash Linux onto a microSD card, and tuck it behind your router. That advice was already creaking in 2024–2025 when cheap Intel N100 boxes started dipping under $175. By November 2026, the global high-density DRAM shortage—driven by Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron shifting wafer lines toward AI datacenter HBM—shattered the math completely.

Raspberry Pi CEO Eben Upton was forced to roll out steep memory-driven price adjustments, including an $80 hike on the 16 GB Raspberry Pi 5 that pushed its official board price all the way to $385 (more than triple its original $120 launch target), while 8 GB bare boards drifted into the $100–$110 street band. And a bare SBC board cannot run a 24/7 n8n, PostgreSQL 16, Home Assistant, or OpenClaw stack out of the box.

Anyone who has actually operated PostgreSQL WAL logs or Home Assistant’s recorder database on a consumer microSD card knows what happens next: continuous 4K synchronous writes chew through cheap flash cells in four to nine months and corrupt the root filesystem silently. So a serious Pi 5 build requires five separate boxes: the board ($105 for 8 GB or $385 for 16 GB), the official 27W 5V/5A USB-C power supply ($15—because generic phone chargers trigger undervoltage throttling and NVMe resets), a case plus active cooler ($15), a PCIe M.2 NVMe HAT ($20), and a 500 GB NVMe SSD ($45).

Add those five receipts together and the verdict is startling: a properly built 8 GB ARM64 Pi 5 costs ~$200, and a 16 GB ARM64 Pi 5 costs ~$480. Meanwhile, a Beelink EQ14 (Intel N150) lands on your doorstep for ~$189–$219 all-in with 16 GB DDR4 RAM, a 500 GB NVMe SSD, an integrated power supply (just a thin figure-8 cord—no ugly wall brick), dual Intel I226-V 2.5GbE ports, and a second open M.2 slot ready for a mirror or bulk media drive.

Be Fair to Raspberry Pi: Where a Pi 5 Still Beats Any x86 Mini PC: A Raspberry Pi 5 is still the superior engineering tool whenever your project touches physical hardware: 40-pin GPIO headers, I2C/SPI sensor buses, dual MIPI CSI camera interfaces, PoE+ ceiling mounts, or battery-powered ~4–5W field rigs. The mistake is buying an expensive GPIO experimentation board purely to stuff it in a closet as a headless Docker server.

2. Honest Silicon Audit: Intel N150 (Twin Lake) vs Older N100—Worth Upgrading?

Let’s cut through late-2026 marketing hype immediately: Intel Processor N150 ("Twin Lake") is NOT a generational architectural leap over Intel N100 ("Alder Lake-N"). Both chips share the exact same 4-core / 4-thread efficiency-core topology, 6 MB L3 cache, 6W base TDP envelope (typically configured around 15–25W PL1/PL2 inside mini PCs), and single-channel memory controller.

The real silicon changes are modest clock bumps: max CPU turbo rises from 3.4 GHz (N100) to 3.6 GHz (N150)—roughly a 5–10% single-thread bump—and the 24-EU Intel integrated GPU steps up from 750 MHz to 1,000 MHz (+33%), which helps slightly with simultaneous Jellyfin/Plex QuickSync AV1/HEVC transcodes and light desktop animations.

That leads to a blunt, zero-affiliate-hype buying rule: if you already own an Intel N100 mini PC (such as a Beelink Mini S12 Pro) running smoothly in your homelab, keep your $200 in your wallet. You will not feel a 200 MHz CPU bump in n8n or Docker. The reason the Beelink EQ14 (N150) is the clear 2026 recommendation for new buyers is the chassis upgrade around the chip: built-in internal PSU (huge cable-management win on a router shelf), dual Intel I226-V 2.5GbE NICs (making it double as an OPNsense/Proxmox router + Docker host), dual M.2 PCIe 3.0 slots, and noticeably quieter bottom-intake cooling compared to older top-whine N100 boxes.

3. Why x86_64 Still Saves Hours Every Month for AI Agents & Self-Hosted Docker

If your homelab only runs Pi-hole and Home Assistant, ARM64 feels effortless—both ecosystems maintain rock-solid multi-arch builds. The friction explodes the moment you run modern AI automation stacks: n8n with headless Chromium/Playwright scrapers, OpenClaw/NanoClaw browser skills, community MCP servers pulled straight from GitHub, or older commercial webhook connectors.

On linux/arm64, you routinely burn a Saturday afternoon fighting exec format error, compiling Rust or C++ Python wheels from scratch on a 4-core ARM chip (watching RAM spike into swap), or discovering that a brand-new AI tool only published linux/amd64 Docker images. Running Ubuntu 24.04 Server or Proxmox VE 8/9 on an x86_64 Beelink EQ14 removes that entire category of debugging permanently: every docker compose pull behaves identically to a datacenter Linux VM.

Just keep your expectations honest about local LLMs: an Intel N150 is a 6W–15W low-power x86 automation box, NOT a local 70B LLM workstation. Its single-channel DDR4 bandwidth limits CPU-only 7B–8B quantized models to ~4–5 tokens/second—fine for tiny 1B–3B classification models or Whisper tiny/base voice-to-text, completely unsuitable for interactive local coding models. Pair the EQ14 with metered frontier APIs (Claude / OpenAI / DeepSeek) for heavy reasoning, or step up to our Strix Halo 128GB vs Mac mini M4 Pro study if you genuinely want fast local 32B–120B inference.


Over 36 months of 24/7 uptime at $0.15/kWh, a 9W Beelink EQ14 uses only ~$5.26/year more electricity than a 5W Pi 5—while giving you double the RAM, x86_64 Docker parity, and $265+ in savings versus a 16 GB Pi 5.

4. The 10-Minute Proxmox / Ubuntu 24.04 Setup & Safe Webhook Exposure Checklist

If you pick up a Beelink EQ14 (N150) for n8n, OpenClaw/ZeroClaw, Home Assistant, Postgres 16, and Jellyfin, resist the urge to expose port 443 directly through your home router’s port forwarding (which leaks your residential IP and breaks whenever your ISP rotates DHCP leases or puts you behind CGNAT).

Instead, install Ubuntu 24.04 Server (or Proxmox VE with one Docker VM + one OPNsense/Home Assistant VM), verify Intel QuickSync /dev/dri permissions and dual NIC link speeds, and publish ONLY your n8n webhook hostname through an outbound Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared)—which idles at ~39 MB RAM, works cleanly behind CGNAT, and requires zero open inbound router ports:

# 1. Verify native x86_64 architecture, N150 cores, and full 16 GB RAM visibility
uname -m && lscpu | grep -E "Model name|CPU\(s\):" && free -h

# 2. Verify Intel QuickSync iGPU render node for Jellyfin/FFmpeg hardware transcode
ls -la /dev/dri/renderD128

# 3. Check both Intel I226-V 2.5GbE NICs & NVMe SMART health
ip -br link && sudo smartctl -H /dev/nvme0n1 || true

# 4. Run NodeBudget's zero-dependency 4K fsync disk latency probe (confirm real NVMe vs QLC stall)
# https://github.com/a895047059/nodebudget-vps-bench
python3 -c 'import os,time; fd=os.open("/tmp/fsync.t",os.O_CREAT|os.O_RDWR|os.O_TRUNC,0o600); b=b"x"*4096; t0=time.perf_counter(); [os.pwrite(fd,b,0) or os.fsync(fd) for _ in range(300)]; dt=time.perf_counter()-t0; os.close(fd); os.unlink("/tmp/fsync.t"); print(f"300x 4K fsync: {300/dt:.1f} IOPS ({dt/300*1000:.2f} ms avg)")'

5. Home N150 Mini PC vs $47.98/yr Cloud VPS: Which One Should You Buy First?

Do not buy a mini PC purely because homelab YouTube makes desk racks look cool. Look honestly at the 36-month cash line in Figure 2 above:

What Could Change This Recommendation: Street pricing on both the Beelink EQ14 and Raspberry Pi 5 fluctuates week to week with DRAM spot markets. If global LPDDR4X supply recovers and Raspberry Pi cuts the 16 GB board back near $120, re-run the 5-part BOM math. As long as an 8 GB Pi 5 + NVMe kit equals or exceeds a 16 GB x86_64 N150 mini PC, the EQ14 wins every headless Docker comparison hands-down.

  • Buy the $47.98/yr RackNerd 4 GB KVM VPS (or ~$4.75/mo Hetzner CX22) FIRST if you only need 1–3 lightweight 24/7 services (n8n, PostgreSQL 16, ZeroClaw/OpenClaw, Uptime Kuma) and want a static datacenter IPv4, battery-backed datacenter power, and zero risk of a home router glitch knocking out client webhooks while you are on a flight. Over two full years, $95.96 is still less than half the upfront cost of an EQ14.
  • Buy the ~$199 Beelink EQ14 (Intel N150 · 16 GB) FIRST if you want to run 8 to 20 containers (n8n + Home Assistant + Jellyfin + Immich photo backup + AdGuard/Pi-hole + Grafana + Proxmox lab VMs) where renting 16 GB of cloud RAM + 500 GB NVMe would cost $40–$80/month ($960–$1,920 over two years). At that footprint, the EQ14 pays for itself in under four months.
  • Run the Hybrid Pattern (My Personal Favorite): Keep client-facing production webhooks and uptime monitors on a boring $4/month datacenter VPS, and run heavy 16 GB personal automation, Immich, Home Assistant, and local staging sandboxes on a silent 9W N150 box at home connected via Tailscale.
