title: Open Ontologies 2.0: plan ontology changes before production
description:
Open Ontologies 2.0

Approving a vocabulary mapping because the labels look right is not enough. Downstream, exactMatch means two terms are interchangeable, and a wrong match quietly changes what your data means. Open Ontologies plans ontology changes before they reach production. It reasons over each vocabulary separately and downgrades an exactMatch the evidence does not support, with the reason given. It also reports terms the mapping does not carry. It cannot confirm a match, and a wrong sibling under the right parent can still pass, so treat it as a check, not proof. As of 27 November 2026 it has 2,971 stars on GitHub, is MIT licensed, and the latest release is v2.1.0 from 23 October 2026.

Repo: https://github.com/fabio-rovai/open-ontologies

What you get

  • A plan for ontology changes before they reach production, with a blast radius report and a proof an auditor can re-check
  • Reasoning over each vocabulary separately, instead of trusting labels that look right
  • Unsupported exactMatch matches downgraded, with the reason given
  • A report of the terms a mapping does not carry

Treat it as a check, not proof: it can flag a bad match, but it cannot confirm a good one.

Quick poll

What would you use Open Ontologies 2.0 for first?

  • Planning an ontology change before production
  • Checking a vocabulary mapping for bad exactMatch
  • Reviewing terms a mapping does not carry
  • Reading the docs first

Vote in the comments.

If you found Open Ontologies 2.0 interesting, I write about tools like this every week in The AI-Native Engineering Leader, what actually works for engineering leaders building with AI agents, and what to skip.

title: How to collect health answers and photos from a new enquiry safely
description:
You collect health answers and photos safely by asking for them through a private link that belongs to your clinic, not through social direct messages or email attachments, and by asking the health questions and taking consent before anything is booked. That keeps sensitive information in one place and under your control.

I will describe the flow as we built it, say where the limits are, and give you a checklist. This is not legal advice, and I point to our security page for what we do and do not say about patient data.

Why not collect photos in direct messages?

Because they scatter sensitive information across personal accounts, phones and platforms you do not control. A photo sent in a social message lives in someone's app, and your clinic has no clean way to find it later, restrict who sees it or delete it when asked.

Our product line is plain about it: photos by private link, never Instagram DMs. Our security page says the same thing in other words: patients send photos and health answers by private link, not by direct messages or email attachments.

What does a safer enquiry flow look like?

  1. 1The enquiry arrives by form, chat or message.
  2. 2The first reply answers it and asks the health questions your practitioner needs.
  3. 3Consent is taken before the consultation is confirmed.
  4. 4The patient uploads photos through a private link in your clinic's name.
  5. 5Everything lands on one record that your team can see before the consultation.

The order matters. Health questions and consent come first, then photos, then the booking. A booking made before the history is in leaves your practitioner meeting a patient they know nothing about.

Which health questions should you ask?

The ones your practitioner asks for. I am not a clinician and I will not write a clinical questionnaire. In Conduit the system collects the history and photos your practitioner asks for, and your clinical team sets the content. That keeps clinical decisions with clinicians.

What I can say as a builder is to keep the first form short, because a long form at the first touch can put people off, and to make the rest part of the consultation. Ask what you need to book safely, and ask the rest in the room.

Where does the data go and who owns it?

You own it. Our security page says patient and clinic data is held in Sydney, Australia (Supabase on Amazon Web Services), that the website runs on Vercel, and that only your clinic's users and our team, to set up and support your account, can see it. We do not sell patient data or use it for advertising.

On the law, the page says health information is sensitive information under the Privacy Act 1988, and that we handle personal information in line with the Australian Privacy Principles. It is a plain summary, not a contract, and your service agreement sets the final terms. Read it before you rely on it, and ask your own adviser about your obligations.

What happens if a patient asks you to delete their data?

You need a way to do it. Our page says: ask and we delete your clinic's data or hand it back, at any time, not only when you leave. Whatever tool you use, check that you can answer a deletion request without hunting through three inboxes and a phone camera roll.

This is another reason to keep photos out of direct messages. A single record with a clear owner is far easier to correct or delete than copies scattered across personal accounts.

What should the reply say about privacy?

Keep it short and plain: what you are collecting, why, and who will see it. Avoid reassurance that overpromises, such as saying the data can never be accessed by anyone. Say what you actually do.

The reply is also advertising-adjacent text, so it follows the same wording rules as your website: no offers, no medicine names, no promises about results. A privacy line that is honest and short fits those rules naturally.

What are the limits of a private link?

A private link is safer than a direct message, but it is not magic. A link can be forwarded, a phone can be shared, and a patient can still send a photo some other way if they prefer. The flow reduces the problem and makes the preferred route obvious. It does not remove human behaviour.

So say plainly, in the first reply, where to send things and why. How quickly that first reply arrives is its own question, covered in how fast a clinic should reply. Most patients are glad to be told. And have a rule for what staff do when a photo arrives in the wrong place: move it into the record, delete the original and tell the patient where to send things next time.

What is a checklist you can use today?

  • Stop asking for photos in social direct messages
  • Use a private link or an upload form owned by your clinic
  • Ask health questions and take consent before confirming the booking
  • Keep the first form short and ask the rest at the consultation
  • Know where the data sits and who can see it
  • Have a documented way to delete a patient's data on request

If you want to see this flow on your own clinic, book a demo. We run a test enquiry through the system so you can see each step, and you decide if it fits. The Grow plan, priced on a call after we see your clinic, includes the health form, photos, booking and deposit link, and you can read the rest on the pricing page.

Originally published at conduitclinics.com.

Conduit helps aesthetic clinics win back patients and capture every enquiry. conduitclinics.com

title: A Guide to AI Agent Memory, Cases, and Reusable Skills
description:
Why AI Agent Experience Should Be Reusable

An AI agent can complete a task successfully without knowing how to repeat the same process later. When its session ends, useful steps, decisions, and findings may not remain available for another run. This can lead to repeated work, especially when agents handle similar tasks regularly.

We can address this problem by preserving useful execution experiences. Instead of keeping only the final output, we can record how the agent reached that result. This includes the original goal, the actions taken, important decisions, and the outcome.

However, storing every completed task does not automatically create a reusable workflow. We need a way to distinguish individual experiences from procedures that can help with future work.

Cases and skills provide a way to organize this information. Cases preserve individual agent experiences, while skills capture useful procedures that can be applied to similar tasks.

In this article, cases and skills refer to two ways of organizing agent experience. Their implementation may differ across AI agent frameworks, but the underlying idea is to preserve useful execution history and turn reliable patterns into reusable procedures.

Understanding the Difference Between Cases and Skills

Cases and skills are related, but they serve different purposes. Understanding this difference helps us organize agent experience without treating every completed task as a reusable instruction.

What Is a Case in AI Agent Memory?

A case is a record of an agent's execution history. It captures the task, the steps taken, important decisions, and the final outcome. This gives us a way to review how an agent completed a task instead of looking only at its final answer.

For example, imagine an agent responsible for checking a website for technical problems. During one run, it checks page availability, reviews broken links, identifies loading issues, and prepares a report.

A useful case can preserve important parts of that process, including the following information:

  • The task objective, relevant conditions, actions, and decisions made during execution.

  • The outcome, including successful steps, failed attempts, and useful observations.

This record helps us understand why a particular approach worked or failed. It also gives future workflows useful information that may help them handle similar situations.

Not every agent run needs to become a meaningful case. A short interaction with no lasting value may not provide enough information for future use. The most useful records contain a clear task, meaningful actions, and an outcome worth reviewing.

What Is a Skill in AI Agent Memory?

A skill is a reusable procedure or pattern that an agent can apply to similar tasks. While a case describes an individual experience, a skill captures an approach that has proven useful across repeated experiences.

For example, one website review may show how to identify broken links. After several similar reviews, the agent may recognize a consistent sequence of checks that works across different websites.

When the same approach produces reliable results across comparable tasks, we can turn that pattern into a reusable skill. Before doing so, we should check whether the steps are useful beyond the original examples.

A skill should explain the general process without depending too heavily on the details of one particular task. It should also make clear when the procedure applies and when another approach may be needed.

Cases vs. Skills: A Simple Comparison

The following table shows how both memory types contribute to a reusable agent workflow and why keeping their roles separate makes previous experience easier to manage.

Aspect Cases Skills
Main purpose Preserve individual execution experiences Store reusable procedures
Information Actions, decisions, and outcomes Repeated methods and patterns
Scope A particular task or run Similar tasks across multiple runs
Main value Provides evidence from previous work Guides future execution
Relationship Supplies experience for learning Captures useful patterns from experience

Both memory types work together. Cases provide the experiences, while skills make recurring successful approaches easier to reuse.

How to Identify Repeated Successful Workflows

Not every repeated action deserves to become a skill. Some tasks may look similar but have different requirements, while others may produce different results because the working conditions have changed.

We should review multiple cases to find patterns that appear across comparable tasks. A single successful run can provide a useful example, but repeated results give us stronger reasons to consider a procedure reusable.

For instance, an AI agent that prepares weekly reports may follow a similar process each time. It collects information, checks the source material, organizes the findings, and prepares a summary.

If these steps consistently produce accurate results, they may represent a useful pattern worth reviewing.

Look Beyond the Final Result

A successful output does not always mean the process was successful. An agent may reach the correct answer after several unnecessary attempts or rely on information that was only available for one particular task.

We should examine the execution process before treating it as a reusable method. To decide whether a pattern is worth keeping, we can review previous cases and look for evidence across comparable task runs.

  1. Did the agent follow a similar sequence of actions across successful runs?

  2. Did the same decisions help produce accurate results under comparable conditions?

  3. Were there any unnecessary steps, errors, or external conditions that affected the outcome?

These questions help us distinguish a repeatable procedure from an isolated success. They also help us avoid turning an unreliable approach into a general instruction.

Group Cases by Task Type

Organizing cases by task type makes recurring patterns easier to identify. For example, website reviews, data extraction, and report preparation should not automatically become one general skill.

Each task category has different goals and requirements. Keeping related experiences together helps us identify procedures that are relevant to a specific type of work.

Turning Agent Experience Into Reusable Skills With EverOS

Once we identify useful patterns, the next step is to organize that experience so future tasks can benefit from it.

EverOS supports this approach through shared memory for AI agents. Its memory system organizes agent execution trajectories as cases and consolidates recurring patterns into reusable skills.

This distinction is important when several agents work within the same environment. One agent may handle research, while another handles writing or technical checks. They may need access to useful working procedures without treating every previous interaction as an instruction.

With a shared memory foundation, relevant agent experience can be made available to connected workflows. This helps agents reuse knowledge across tasks while keeping individual execution records and reusable procedures organized according to their purpose.

How the Case-to-Skill Process Works

We can understand the relationship between cases and skills through three main stages, from recording individual experiences to making useful procedures available for future work.

1. Record the execution

The agent completes a task and records its execution trajectory. The resulting case preserves useful information about the task, the actions taken, and how the agent handled different situations.

2. Consolidate repeated experience

Related cases provide the experience needed to identify recurring approaches. Useful patterns can then be organized into skills that describe how to handle similar tasks.

This step requires more than finding repeated actions. We should consider whether the approach produces reliable results and whether it applies beyond the original examples.

3. Make reusable skills available

Once a useful pattern becomes a skill, it can serve as a reference for future tasks. An agent can retrieve relevant experience when handling similar work and use it alongside current instructions.

This process does not mean that every new task must follow exactly the same steps. It provides a useful starting point while leaving room for task-specific decisions.

Retrieving the Right Skill for a New Task

Creating reusable skills is only part of the process. We also need to select the right procedure when an agent receives a new request.

A skill that worked well for one task may not be suitable for another. For example, a procedure for checking a small website may not cover the requirements of a large online store.

The retrieval process should consider the task's objective, conditions, and required outcome. This helps us avoid applying a familiar procedure simply because it contains similar keywords.

Match the Current Task With Relevant Experience

We should use clear task descriptions when searching for previous experience. A request such as "review this website" may be too broad to identify the correct procedure.

A more specific request, such as "check page availability and identify broken internal links," provides better information about the required work.

Retrieval should also consider the actual requirements of the task. A skill for checking internal links may be useful for a website review, but it may not cover page speed, security checks, or content quality.

Combine Previous Knowledge With Current Instructions

A retrieved skill should guide the process rather than replace current instructions. The agent still needs to check the latest requirements, available tools, and task-specific restrictions before applying it.

This is important because previous experience may come from different working conditions. Using a skill as a reference allows the agent to benefit from past results without assuming that every task is identical.

Measuring Improvement Across Similar Tasks

We need a practical way to determine whether reusable skills actually improve agent performance. Without measurement, repeated execution may look like progress even when the results remain inconsistent.

We can compare similar tasks before and after introducing a reusable skill. The comparison should focus on measurable outcomes rather than assumptions about how well the agent remembers previous work.

The following measurements can help us evaluate whether a reusable procedure makes a meaningful difference across comparable tasks.

Measurement What We Should Check Expected Improvement
Completion time Time required to finish similar tasks Less unnecessary repetition
Accuracy Errors and incorrect results More consistent outputs
Tool usage Number of unnecessary actions More focused execution
Task completion Whether the required steps were completed Fewer missed requirements
Consistency Differences between repeated results More predictable outcomes

These measurements do not need to be complicated. Even a simple record of task time, errors, and completion status can help us understand whether a skill is useful.

We should also compare tasks with similar levels of difficulty. Otherwise, a more complex task may make a useful skill appear less effective than it actually is.

Guardrails for Managing Reusable Agent Skills

Reusable knowledge needs regular review. A procedure that worked under previous conditions may become unsuitable when tools, task requirements, or available information change.

We should treat skills as working procedures that require validation rather than permanent instructions that never need updating. Three areas deserve particular attention: validation, versioning, and outdated information.

Validate Skills Before Wider Use

A skill should be tested against new examples before we depend on it for important tasks. We can check whether its steps still produce the expected results and whether its conditions match the current environment.

We should also preserve failed attempts when they explain why a particular approach did not work. These experiences can help us understand which conditions affect a procedure and avoid repeating known mistakes.

Use Versioning to Track Changes

Versioning helps us understand how a skill changes over time. When we update a procedure, we should keep track of what changed and why.

For example, a report-generation skill may need an additional verification step after the source format changes. Recording that update helps us understand which version applies to the current workflow.

Handle Outdated Skills Carefully

An outdated skill should not continue influencing new tasks without review. We can mark it for revision, replace it with a tested procedure, or retire it when it no longer applies.

This is particularly important when several agents share experience. A procedure that is no longer suitable for one project should not automatically become a general instruction for every connected workflow.

Improving AI Agent Performance Through Reusable Skills

Turning agent runs into reusable skills gives us a practical way to make completed work useful beyond its original task. Cases preserve individual execution experiences, while skills capture recurring procedures that can guide similar work in the future.

The process works best when we identify reliable patterns, organize relevant experience, and retrieve procedures based on current task requirements. We should also measure results and review stored skills as working conditions change.

With this approach, we can build AI agent workflows that benefit from organized experience instead of repeating the same work without learning from previous results. The goal is not to make every run identical, but to help each new run start with useful knowledge from work that has already been completed.

title: Your local coding agent spends its first 8 minutes reading the harness
description:
Claude Code sent a 2-bit Inkling 2 Mini 13,331 tokens before it was allowed to open a single file. System prompt, twelve tool definitions, an environment block. On an 8-core CPU with 15 GB of RAM and no GPU, just reading that took 7 minutes and 51 seconds.

On a CPU, the agent harness is the workload. Every tool schema you ship is paid for in wall clock time before any reasoning starts.

The part that decided the run came later. The model tried to write its fix with a shell redirect, the permission check refused, and it replied to itself: "The sandbox blocks shell file writes. Use the Write tool instead." It switched tools and passed a hidden test suite 5 of 5 in 14 minutes 33 seconds.

Reading a refusal and changing tactics mattered more than raw benchmark smarts. If you're evaluating local agents, time the first request and watch what the model does after its first denied tool call.

I ran Qwen3.8 and Gemma 4 through the same bug fixes. Only one of the three finished. Full write-up (free friend link): https://pub.towardsai.net/i-tested-3-open-models-as-local-coding-agents-only-one-finished-bad117703175?sk=71c2ae30456743b11a6bff58e8b2174b

title: How We Ran a 306B Frontier MoE (GLM-5.3-Flash) on a Single 15 GB T4 & 24 GB GPU — Even With RAM Capped Below Model Size"
description:
Running a 306-billion-parameter frontier model normally implies an 8xH100 or 4xA100 server cluster.

What happens if all you have is a single 15 GB NVIDIA Tesla T4 or a single 24 GB PCIe GPU—or worse, a cloud container where even Host RAM is hard-capped at 112 GiB, 74 GiB smaller than the quantized model itself?

We put deimos-stream to a live cloud stress test on zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash (305.78 GiB across 62 FP8 shards, 45 hybrid layers, 12,096 routed experts), head-to-head against upstream llama.cpp (UD-Q4_K_XL, 185.99 GiB).

Here is the complete step-by-step engineering breakdown: every hardware wall we hit, how we solved it from first principles, verbatim live reasoning traces from the 306B model running on a single GPU, and the raw benchmark numbers.

TL;DR — Live Cloud Results (tau = 1.0, Zero Expert Skipping)

  • Single 15 GB NVIDIA Tesla T4: DeimosStream ran 306B GLM-5.3-Flash inside 10.71 GiB PyTorch VRAM (11.3 GiB nvidia-smi peak), generating clean structured Markdown. llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe 42 crashed immediately trying to allocate a 20.88 GiB CUDA buffer.
  • Single 24 GB GPU (NVIDIA A10, 224 GiB Host RAM):
    • 4-Bit Backbone (--backbone q4 --slots auto): Hit 3.44 tok/s decode and 23.0s TTFT (164.8 GiB RSS)—beating llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe 45 (2.92 tok/s, 81.7s TTFT, 187.7 GiB RSS) by +17.8% on decode and 3.55x on TTFT, while llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe 42 crashed with CUDA OOM even on 24 GB VRAM.
    • Full Unquantized 16-Bit Backbone (--backbone fp16 --slots 8): Kept all 45 layers of non-expert KDA/DSA attention, mHC streams, routers, and shared experts in 16-bit FP16 inside 19.55 GiB PyTorch VRAM at 3.31 tok/s—still faster than llama.cpp!
  • Out-of-Core 112 GiB Hard-Capped Host RAM (< 61% of the 186 GiB Q4 Model Size!):
    • DeimosStream ran cleanly inside 112.86 GiB peak RSS at 2.14 tok/s and 46.2s TTFT—2.10x faster decode, 3.17x faster TTFT, and 74.8 GiB lower RSS than llama.cpp (1.02 tok/s, 146.5s TTFT, 187.66 GiB RSS).

Step 1: Anatomy of a 2026 306B Hybrid MoE (And Why Whole-Layer Offloading Breaks)

Modern 2026 frontier models are no longer uniform Transformer stacks. Inspecting zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash (Glm5NextForConditionalGeneration) reveals four distinct architectural mechanisms operating simultaneously:

  1. 45 Decoder Layers (hidden_size = 4096): Layers 0..2 are dense (intermediate_size = 12288); layers 3..44 (42 layers) are sparse Mixture-of-Experts with 288 routed experts + 1 shared expert per layer (12,096 routed experts total, top_k = 8, moe_intermediate_size = 2048).
  2. Hybrid Token Mixing (34 KDA + 11 DSA Layers): 34 layers use Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) gated linear recurrence (fla-core Triton kernels); 11 layers use DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) with compressed MLA latents (kv_lora_rank = 512, NoPE) and cross-layer full/shared k-pool indexers.
  3. Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC): Tokens propagate along hc_mult parallel residual streams mixed via Sinkhorn-Knopp doubly-stochastic matrices (attn_hc, ffn_hc).
  4. Clamped SwiGLU (swiglu_limit = 10.0): Expert gates clamp gate <= 10.0 and up in [-10.0, 10.0] before SiLU(gate) * up to prevent FP8/FP16 outlier explosions.

Why llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe Hits a Granularity Wall

llama.cpp offloads MoE experts one entire layer at a time:

# Why whole-layer offloading hits a brick wall on 288-expert MoEs:
experts_per_layer = 288
bytes_per_expert  = 13.5 * 1024 * 1024       # 13.5 MiB in 4-bit precision
layer_moe_gib     = (288 * 13.5) / 1024      # ~3.80 GiB for ONE single MoE layer!

# Layers 0, 1, 2 are dense -> `--n-cpu-moe 42` leaves MoE layers 42, 43, 44 on GPU:
# 3 MoE layers (~11.4 GiB) + ~9.5 GiB non-expert backbone = 20.88 GiB CUDA0 buffer!
# Result: CUDA OOM on BOTH 15 GB T4 and 23 GB A10.

Because even 3 MoE layers overflow a 24 GB budget alongside KV/compute buffers, llama.cpp is forced all the way to --n-cpu-moe 45 (zero MoE experts on GPU, leaving ~11 GiB of a 24 GB GPU completely idle during MoE compute!).

Step 2: Carving 305.8 GiB Into a Permanent Backbone + 12,096 Page-Aligned Leaves

Instead of downloading 306 GiB to disk up front, DeimosStream's reference-counted converter prefetches 3 safetensors shards ahead in background threads, dequantizes [128, 128] block-scaled FP8 tensors on GPU in 32-expert chunks (< 1.5 GiB VRAM), deletes each shard the moment its reference count hits zero, and emits a decoupled DEIMIDX2 store:

glm53_flash_deimos_q4/       (175.6 GiB total from 305.78 GiB FP8 source)
├── embed_tokens.bin          1.20 GiB   # CPU mmap FP16 lookup table (0 MiB GPU VRAM!)
├── hf_backbone.safetensors  14.30 GiB   # 34 KDA + 11 DSA + 3 dense MLPs + 42 shared experts + mHC
├── lm_head_int8.bin        605.30 MiB   # Symmetric INT8 output head (no 1.2 GiB logit spikes)
├── cas_experts_q4.bin      159.42 GiB   # 12,096 experts x exact 14,155,776 B (13.500 MiB, 16 KB aligned)
└── merkle_tree.idx           1.80 MiB   # DEIMIDX2 header + 12,096 SHA-256 leaf hashes + Tier-1 XOR root

Two subtle implementation details proved critical here:

# 1. Zero-RAM meta instantiation with strict FP16/FP32 split (model_adapters.py)
with torch.device("meta"):
    # Explicit dtype=torch.float16 prevents 2x float32 VRAM bloat and mHC matmul mismatch,
    # while transformers preserves _keep_in_fp32_modules_strict (A_log, dt_bias, conv1d,
    # router gate.weight, e_score_correction_bias, and mHC base/scale) in exact FP32!
    model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_config(
        full_cfg, dtype=torch.float16, trust_remote_code=True
    )
    model.model.visual = None  # Drop vision tower for text inference (0 bytes allocated)

And every single expert leaf (gate_up_proj + down_proj + Group-64 FP16 scales & mins) packs into exact 14,155,776 bytes (864 x 16,384 B)—an exact OS 16 KB page multiple with zero padding waste.

Step 3: Sub-Layer TinyLFU GPU Slot Arena + Clamped __dp4a CUDA Kernels

Instead of pinning 288 experts in 3 layers and 0 in the other 39, TorchPagedExpertArena allocates S physical expert slots inside every single one of the 42 MoE layers:

  • On a 24 GB GPU (--slots auto), the memory planner budgets 19–21 slots/layer (~840 hot experts resident in VRAM simultaneously).
  • Real natural-language routing is heavily skewed: caching just 20 / 288 (6.9%) of experts per layer via TinyLFU frequency admission yielded a 27.6% – 31.2% live cache hit rate (4.3x higher than uniform random)!
  • Hit slots execute directly on GPU through custom nvcc __dp4a (sm_75 / sm_86 / sm_89) Q4 GEMV kernels with fused swiglu_limit = 10.0 clamping: 
// Fused clamped SwiGLU inside deimos_cuda_q4.cu & deimos_simd_q4.h
// Matches GLM-5.3-Flash & DeepSeek-V4 outlier clipping without extra HBM passes
float gate = fminf(gate_raw, swiglu_limit);                     // clamp(max=10.0)
float up   = fminf(fmaxf(up_raw, -swiglu_limit), swiglu_limit); // clamp(min=-10.0, max=10.0)
float act  = (gate / (1.0f + expf(-swiglu_alpha * gate))) * (up + swiglu_up_offset);

Step 4: The Core Breakthrough — Zero-PCIe Hybrid Execution (16 KB vs 4.75 GB)

Here is the trap that kills naive "stream weights from RAM to GPU on demand" engines:

The PCIe Math: At top_k = 8 across 42 layers, GLM-5.3-Flash touches 336 x 13.5 MiB = 4.43 GiB of expert weights per token. Even at a 30% GPU cache hit rate, copying 3.1 GiB of missed expert weights over PCIe Gen4 (~12–16 GB/s effective) stalls every single token by 200–260 ms before a single FLOP executes!

So DeimosStream never copies missed expert weights over PCIe during token decode. Instead, it moves the tiny activation vector to the weights:

                 GPU Stream (CUDA)                         Host CPU (22 AVX2 Workers)
        +----------------------------------+          +----------------------------------+
        | 1. KDA / DSA Attn + mHC + Router |          |                                  |
        | 2. Burst D2H: x_f16 (8 KB) + IDs +--------->| 3. TinyLFU Split (Hits vs Misses)|
        | 4. Shared Expert + Hit Q4 SwiGLU |  8 KB!   | 4. Parallel Q8_1 x Q4 AVX2 GEMV  |
        |    (__dp4a on resident slots)    |          |    in-place over zero-copy mmap  |
        | 5. Residual Add <----------------+----------+    -> Pinned H2D y_cpu (8 KB)    |
        +----------------------------------+  8 KB!   +----------------------------------+
        Background _dma_stream: asynchronously promotes <= 1 hot TinyLFU expert via ring buffer
  1. Burst D2H (~8.1 KB): Only the 4096 x FP16 hidden state and 8 routed expert IDs/weights cross PCIe into pinned host memory.
  2. True CPU + GPU Overlap: While the GPU computes the shared expert + all TinyLFU hit experts in parallel, C++17 worker threads quantize x once to Q8_1 and run AVX2 fused clamped-SwiGLU dot products directly over cas_mmap for the missed experts—sending back a single 8 KB FP16 residual.
  3. Non-Blocking Promotion: An asynchronous CUDA _dma_stream promotes at most 1 newly hot expert per layer into the TinyLFU ring buffer in the background without stalling decode.

Step 5: Breaking the Host RAM Ceiling (112 GiB Capped RAM for a 186 GiB Model!)

What happens when Host RAM (112 GiB) is 47.5 GiB smaller than cas_experts_q4.bin (159.5 GiB)?

Normally, staging 11.6 GiB of hot experts into GPU VRAM leaves those exact same 11.6 GiB duplicated in the Linux OS page cache—starving CPU-miss experts of RAM and triggering violent NVMe thrashing. Worse, we discovered a subtle Linux glibc trap along the way:

// TRAP: On Linux glibc, posix_madvise(..., POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED) is a SILENT NO-OP!
// FIX (deimos_merkle.mm): Invoke raw Linux madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) the instant an
// expert is staged to GPU VRAM, enforcing strictly disjoint RAM vs VRAM residency:
#if defined(__linux__)
    madvise(leaf_addr, expert_stride_bytes, MADV_DONTNEED); // Immediately frees 13.5 MiB host RAM!
#endif

Combined with POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED on hf_backbone.safetensors (14.3 GiB) right after GPU upload, DeimosStream held peak RSS to 112.86 GiB while running the full 306B model!

(What about the DEIMIDX2 SHA-256 + XOR Merkle tree? For pure local/cloud speed we pass --no-verify for **zero* runtime overhead; when streaming from untrusted cold storage with verification enabled, the engine cryptographically verified 10,146 SHA-256 expert leaves + 22,242 XOR proofs on the fly with zero corrupted pages.)*

Live Human Verification: Watching the 306B Model Think & Solve Its Own VRAM Math

Benchmarks are meaningless if quantization or paging corrupts reasoning. Below are two unedited live outputs generated by 306B zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash (tau = 1.0, greedy temp = 0) running on a single 24 GB NVIDIA A10 GPU (17.8–18.3 GiB PyTorch VRAM).

Live Test 1 — Cryptographic Streaming Architecture (960 tokens, 3.27 tok/s, 27.84% Hit Rate)

Prompt:

"Explain how a two-tier SHA-256 + XOR Merkle tree can cryptographically verify 4-bit Mixture-of-Experts weights streamed on demand into a single 16 GB GPU without stalling token generation, and include a concise Python pseudocode snippet."

Verbatim 306B GLM-5.3-Flash Reasoning + Output:

<think>User asks a technical design question. Provide explanation + pseudocode. Keep reasonably concise.</think>

Two-Tier SHA-256 + XOR Merkle Tree for On-Demand MoE Weight Verification

Tier 1 — Chunk hashes (SHA-256): Each expert shard (say 32 MB of 4-bit weights) is split into 64 KB chunks. Each chunk gets a SHA-256 digest. This lets you verify one chunk at a time as it streams — you never wait for a whole expert.

Tier 2 — XOR aggregation (compact commitment): All Tier-1 digests of an expert are XOR-folded into a single 32-byte "expert commitment." All expert commitments are XOR-folded into one root commitment published when the model is signed... (Note: XOR alone is malleable, so Tier-1 SHA-256 digests are the collision-resistant layer; XOR is only an aggregation convenience over already-cryptographic digests.)

# Verbatim Python pseudocode generated live by 306B GLM-5.3-Flash on 1x 24GB GPU:

# ---- Offline (publisher) ----
def build_commitments(shards):                 # shards: list of expert weight blobs
    expert_commits = []
    for shard in shards:
        chunk_roots = merkle_root([sha256(shard[i:i+65536])
                                   for i in range(0, len(shard), 65536)])
        expert_commits.append(chunk_roots)
    root = xor_fold(expert_commits)            # 32-byte root commitment
    return sign(root, publisher_key)           # Ed25519 signature over root

# ---- Online (inference loader, overlapped with generation) ----
class VerifiedLoader:
    def __init__(self, root, sig):
        self.root = verify_sig(root, sig)      # trust anchor
        self.pending = {}                      # expert_id -> xor accumulator

    def stream_chunk(self, eid, chunk, digest, proof):
        assert merkle_verify(sha256(chunk), digest, proof)   # Tier 1 SHA-256 check
        self.pending.setdefault(eid, b'\0'*32)
        self.pending[eid] = xor(self.pending[eid], digest)   # Tier 2 XOR fold

(Notice the 306B model independently highlighted the exact cryptographic nuance that XOR is malleable on raw data and derives its security strictly from the underlying collision-resistant SHA-256 digests!)

Live Test 2 — Asking the 306B Model to Derive Its Own Engine's Exact VRAM Slot Budget (3.31 tok/s, 31.20% Hit Rate)

Prompt:

"A cloud server has 22.5 GiB of usable GPU VRAM. A 306B-parameter MoE model has a 5.4 GiB quantized non-expert backbone and 42 MoE layers, where each expert takes 13.5 MiB in 4-bit precision. Leaving 1.5 GiB for KV cache and activations, calculate the exact maximum integer number of expert slots per layer that can reside in GPU VRAM simultaneously (note: 1 GiB = 1024 MiB), show every step, and explain how a CPU SIMD cache-miss engine avoids PCIe weight stalls."

Verbatim 306B GLM-5.3-Flash Reasoning Trace:

<think>
...Available for experts = 22.5 - 5.4 - 1.5 = 15.6 GiB.
Convert to MiB: 15.6 * 1024 = 15974.4 MiB. Each expert = 13.5 MiB.
Total expert slots across all layers = floor(15974.4 / 13.5) = 1183.288888... -> floor 1183.
Then per layer = floor(1183 / 42) = 28.166... -> floor 28.

Check memory used: If all 42 layers have 28 expert slots resident:
42 * 28 * 13.5 MiB = 15876 MiB = 15.50390625 GiB (leaves 98.4 MiB spare!).
If 29 per layer: 42 * 29 * 13.5 = 16443 MiB = 16.0576171875 GiB > 15.6 GiB by 468.6 MiB!

Since GPU can hold limited experts, remaining experts stay on CPU. A CPU engine performs
matrix-vector multiplication for "cache misses" (experts not in GPU VRAM) using SIMD/AVX...
</think>

Every single number—15,974.4 MiB budget, 28 slots/layer (15,876 MiB used, 98.4 MiB spare), and why 29 overflows by 468.6 MiB—was solved live without a single arithmetic slip.

Full Cloud Head-to-Head Benchmarks (306B GLM-5.3-Flash, 64 Greedy Tokens, tau = 1.0)

All runs used identical prompts, greedy decoding (temp = 0), 24 vCPUs (-t 22), and unsloth/GLM-5.3-Flash-GGUF (UD-Q4_K_XL, 185.99 GiB) on upstream llama.cpp (master, CUDA 12.8.1).

Suite 1: Single 24 GB GPU (NVIDIA A10, 23,028 MiB) + 224 GiB Host RAM

Engineering Honesty Note on the Uncapped T4 Row: Why did llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe 45 reach 4.02 tok/s vs 2.27 tok/s on T4 when 224 GiB Host RAM was uncapped? At slots = 8 / 288 (10.3% GPU hit rate), 90% of expert compute is strictly host-DRAM bandwidth bound (~4.3 GB/token). Unsloth's dynamic UD-Q4_K_XL quantizes less-sensitive routed experts down to Q2_K/Q3_K (~3.4 bits/weight on cold experts), reading ~25–30% fewer DRAM bytes per miss than DeimosStream's uniform 4.5 bits/weight Group-64 affine Q4 across all 12,096 experts. Adding optional Q3_K cold CAS leaves to DEIMIDX2 directly closes that pure-CPU bandwidth gap while keeping our 24 GB and 112 GiB Capped-RAM leads!

title: Stop LLM Hallucinations & Passive-Voice Bluffs with a Deterministic Semantic Role Filter (MCP + Prompts)
description:
Large Language Models are remarkably fluent—especially when they have no factual ground to stand on.

When an LLM lacks concrete data, or when a vendor drafts a slippery contract clause, both rely on the exact same linguistic camouflage:

  1. Passive voice without an agent ("The Empty Seat"): "Deadlines were shifted", "The service is deemed accepted", "Errors occurred." Nobody is in the Nominative case; nobody is accountable.
  2. Unanchored percentages: "Efficiency improved by 240%"—with no baseline (before -> after), no sample size N, and no time window.
  3. Rubber deadlines: "In a reasonable timeframe" or "soon" instead of a closed verification window [t₁, t₂].
  4. Intent disguised as action: "We plan to optimize" presented as a completed deliverable.

To catch these structural failures deterministically—before an AI agent sends an email, approves a contract clause, or hallucinates a report—I built The Dated Record Method ("Case Filter" v1.3) and the MACRO-OS prompt suite.

The Core Idea: Semantic Role Auditing (E = Ω(T) ⟿ σ(O))

Instead of asking an LLM "Does this sound true?" (which invites more hallucination), the filter checks whether a statement is properly assembled across 5 mandatory semantic roles:

title: Simple Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Pipeline
description:
Large Language Models are highly capable but encounter several issues like creating inaccurate or irrelevant content, using outdated information, and operating in ways that are not transparent. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique to solve these problems by augmenting LLM knowledge with additional domain specific data. A key use of LLMs is in advanced question-answering(Q&A) chatbots. To create a chatbot that can understand and respond to queries about private or specific topics, it's necessary to expand the knowledge of LLMs with the particualr data needed.This is what the RAG can help.

Basic RAG Pipeline
This is how a basic RAG pipeline looks like -
1.Data Indexing
2.Retrieval & Genration

Data Indexing Processing:

  1. Data Loading: This involves importing all the documents or information to be utilized
  2. Data Splitting: Large documents are divided into smaller peices, for instance, sections of no more than 500 characters each.
  3. Data Embedding: The data is converted into vvector form using an embedding model, making it understandable for computers.
  4. Data Storing: These vector embeddings are saved in a vector database, allowing them to easily searched.

Retirieval and Generation process

  1. Retrieval: When a user asks a question:
  • The user's input is first transformed into a vector using the same embedding model from the Data Indexing phase.
  • This query vector is then matched against all vectors in the vector database to find the modt similar ones that might contain the answer to the user's question. This step is about identifying relevant knowledge chunks.
  1. Generation: The LLM model takes the user's question and the relevant from the vector databse to create a response. This process combines the question with the identified data to generate an answer.

title: Tesla, good enough and well packaged: the numbers agree
description:
He showed his son a Tesla and said: this is how Americans do it - make something reasonably reliable, then great branding and packaging. Quality, in his words, is not the point; it just has to not break, and comfort can be sacrificed. Checked on 27 November against his own Tesla research from 30 October: the numbers show exactly that picture, "reasonably" reliable and strong where it shows in the window

1. ⭐⭐⭐ New cars hold up. In Consumer Reports' 2026 brand rankings Tesla entered the top 10 for reliability for the first time, ninth, over a survey of about 380,000 vehicles. Only the Cybertruck is below average.

2. ⭐⭐⭐ Reliability drops with age. In Germany's TÜV Report 2026, among cars aged two to three years, the group average is 6.5% significant defects; Model 3 is at 13.1% and Model Y at 17.3%, the worst in the group. Brake discs and suspension lead. In Consumer Reports' 2025 used-car study Tesla was last of 26 brands.

3. ⭐⭐ The strong side is the visible one. Crash tests give Tesla top marks: Model Y 2025 IIHS Top Safety Pick+, Model 3 five stars in Euro NCAP 2025. What can be shown is done well.

4. ⭐ What follows. His formula "don't break, keep running, comfort is not the point" matches the measurements almost word for word: a new car is reliable, mileage eats into it, and the window is strong. On comfort these measurements have no data; that part is his observation.

5. ⚠️ Limits. The numbers come from our Tesla safety research of 30 October and the post of 4 November. German data does not transfer automatically to US cars or to newer versions.
