title: Half my Claude Code usage limit went to typing, so I made a free model do it
description:
You hit the Claude Code limit at 3pm. You scroll back through the session and half the tokens went to typing: a rename across 20 files, boilerplate, tests from a spec you had already written. Claude didn't need to think about any of that.

I built legwork for that half. It's a Claude Code skill that hands mechanical, fully specified tasks to a free model running in a jailed worker. Claude keeps the planning and the review.

How a run goes

  1. Claude spots a sub-task that fits in one paragraph, where a mistake is cheap to catch and no secrets are involved. Design, hard bugs and security code stay with Claude.
  2. It writes a self-contained request and calls legwork.py run. The script starts Free Claude Code if it's down. That's a local proxy that puts a free provider (NVIDIA NIM, Groq and others) behind the Claude Code CLI.
  3. The worker runs headless with fcc-claude -p in the narrowest folder that covers the task, and edits the files.
  4. Claude reads git diff, runs the tests, fixes what needs fixing and records a verdict: ok, fixed or redo. 
Created greet.py with a greet(name) function that returns 'Hello, <name>!'.

legwork: run c3268ef1 done · groq/qwen/qwen3.8-27b · 2 turns · 7s · 7,843 tokens kept off your Claude limit

My first real run kept 175,341 tokens off my limit in 5.8 minutes of worker time. Claude still had to fix part of the output, and that's the job of the review step.

The jail

I treat the worker as untrusted, so legwork launches it with these locks:

Lock What it blocks
--tools Read,Edit,Write,Glob,Grep shell commands, web access, subagents
--restricted anything outside the run folder, your user settings
--strict-mcp-config every MCP server you have installed
--disable-slash-commands skills and slash commands
jail-settings.json .env*, keys, certificates, .git, .claude, .npmrc, .netrc, files named like token or secret, local databases

The jail limits what the worker can touch. Your request and the files the worker reads still go to the provider you configured, and free tiers may keep them. Skip client code under NDA and anything with personal data.

Why not claude-code-router?

A router swaps the model for the whole session. legwork keeps Claude as the planner and reviewer and sends out only the tasks a weaker model can handle.

Picking a model

Each agent step resends 15k to 30k tokens, so tokens per minute and requests per day decide which free model holds up. You can name profiles in ~/.claude/legwork/config.json:

{ "profiles": { "fast": "groq/qwen/qwen3.8-27b" } }

A fast profile handles one or two files. The default profile handles multi-file work. legwork.py doctor pings every profile and tells you what answers today, and legwork.py stats keeps a scoreboard of runs, tokens and review verdicts.

Try it

Install Free Claude Code, paste a free provider key in its Admin UI (NVIDIA NIM is a good default), then inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add obrenoalvim/legwork
/plugin install legwork@legwork

Ask Claude to "run the legwork doctor". After that it delegates on its own when a task fits, or you ask: "legwork: add docstrings to every function in src/utils".

The script needs only the Python standard library (3.10+) and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Repo: https://github.com/obrenoalvim/legwork (MIT)

Which part of your Claude Code session would you hand to a cheaper model first?

Ps: I'm building BloodLink, a free platform connecting blood donors to donation campaigns.

title: Sber Releases GigaChat 4, a 708B Open-Weight Model Under the MIT License
description:
Russia's biggest bank has just put a very large model into the open-weights world. At its AI Journey conference in Moscow on November 26, 2026, Sber showed off GigaChat 4, two models whose weights anyone can download. The headline model packs 708 billion parameters in total, 41 billion active per token, under the MIT License — a choice that sets it apart.

Read the full story on Rohan Tech Official

Two facts sit next to the technical news: Sber is state-controlled — Russia's National Wealth Fund holds 50 percent plus one voting share — and the bank is under US blocking sanctions. This piece sticks to what Sber has said and published, and flags where figures come from Sber alone.

What's in the release

GigaChat 4 arrives in two sizes: the flagship GigaChat4-708B-A41B, with 708 billion parameters in total and 41 billion active per token, and the smaller GigaChat4-37B-A4B, with 37 billion in total and 4 billion active per token. Both take a 1,048,576-token window — 1M, in Sber's words.

The weights live on Hugging Face under the ai-sage org, in FP8, BF16, and GGUF forms, plus base and intermediate checkpoints. Sber has also put out a technical report for the 708B model on GitHub, under salute-developers/gigachat4. Both models handle English and Russian.

A look under the hood

The 708B model runs on a hybrid mixture-of-experts setup: 64 decoder layers, a hidden size of 7,168, 256 routed experts with 8 active per token, plus one shared expert. Only a small slice works on any given token.

The attention design is where Sber tried something less common: 48 Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers mixed with 16 DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) layers. In the DSA layers, an indexer picks up to 2,048 positions per token, and attention runs only over those — roughly 0.2 percent of positions in a full 1M-token prompt.

Sber pushed the context from 32K to 128K with dense attention over around 336 billion tokens, then trained the indexer alone at 128K. Then the model and indexer trained together at 1M tokens for about 400 billion tokens.

Two modes, one checkpoint

One checkpoint holds both "instant" and "reasoning" modes, picked per request. GigaChat 3.5 needed separate checkpoints — one download and deployment can now cover both quick answers and longer step-by-step work. Sber points to SGLang and vLLM for serving, with an OpenAI-compatible API.

The benchmarks come from Sber alone

Every benchmark number here comes from Sber, and no outside evaluator has checked the figures yet. Read them as Sber's own claims, not settled results, and wait for independent tests.

For SWE-bench Verified, the figures Sber gives are 80.89 with reasoning switched on and 80.82 in instant mode, using Harbor-based agent harnesses and a seven-hour timeout.

The picture changes on DeepSWE, a long-horizon software engineering test, where Sber reports 35.40 percent for GigaChat 4 next to 74.34 percent for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash in its own table. That's a wide gap, and it undercuts any simple reading of the SWE-bench Verified result. Sber also left out the top of the open-weights field, such as Kimi K3 or Qwen 3.8. The honest reading is mixed: strong on one coding test, far weaker on a longer-horizon one.

What it takes to run it

The 708B model isn't a download-and-run project for most people. FP8 inference calls for two nodes of eight 80GB Nvidia H100 GPUs, with tensor parallelism 16 and 1,280GB of GPU memory; the BF16 version needs four nodes. The GGUF Q4_K_M version comes as 9 shards totaling 429.4 GB. The smaller 37B model is the realistic option for most users.

The licence split, and the sanctions question

The licence differs by size. The 708B model sits under the MIT License, which allows commercial use. The 37B model falls under a Noncommercial License for Individuals 1.0, covering personal research, experiments, study, and hobby use only, and barring outputs for commercial purposes. Check which licence covers the size you plan to use.

Because Sber is under US blocking sanctions, readers based in the US should look into the sanctions and compliance rules that apply before they download or use the weights. Russian law, including the Yarovaya data-disclosure rules, compels covered companies to hand over data.

"Open-weight" isn't the same as "open source." The weights come without the training data and code, so outsiders can run and study the model but can't reproduce the full training process.

For the full breakdown, see the original article: Read the full story on Rohan Tech Official

title: One OpenAI-compatible key for Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi: the base_url swap, and what still differs
description:
Disclosure: I'm Alex, and I run MartLLM, the endpoint in these examples. The base_url pattern works with any OpenAI-compatible gateway. The routing fields near the end are MartLLM's own.

Most LLM code in production is written against the OpenAI Python or TypeScript SDK, even when the model isn't OpenAI's. The SDK is good, the wire format is everywhere, and every framework (LangChain, LlamaIndex, LiteLLM, the Vercel AI SDK, Pydantic AI) can talk to it. So the cheapest way to try Claude, Gemini or DeepSeek in an existing codebase usually isn't a new SDK. It's a different base_url.

This post shows that swap against one endpoint that serves all of them, then covers the parts that don't carry over cleanly.

The swap

MartLLM implements the OpenAI Chat Completions API at https://api.martllm.com/v1. The OpenAI SDK guide puts it plainly: set base_url and api_key, and messages, tools, response_format, stream, max_tokens and temperature stay the same.

import os

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.martllm.com/v1",  # the trailing /v1 is required
    api_key=os.environ["MARTLLM_API_KEY"],
)

MODELS = [
    "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5",
    "google/gemini-3.8-flash",
    "deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    "z-ai/glm-5.3",
    "moonshotai/kimi-k3",
]

for model in MODELS:
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "In one sentence: what is a vector database?"}],
        max_tokens=120,
    )
    u = resp.usage
    cost = getattr(u, "cost_usd", None)  # MartLLM adds usage.cost_usd to every reply
    print(f"{resp.model:32} {u.prompt_tokens:>4} in {u.completion_tokens:>4} out  ${cost}")
    print("   ", resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()[:160])

Five makers, one client, one loop. Model ids are maker/model. GET /v1/models returns the ones you can call right now, in the OpenAI list shape.

TypeScript is the same two settings:

import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "https://api.martllm.com/v1",
  apiKey: process.env.MARTLLM_API_KEY,
});

const resp = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Explain idempotency keys in two sentences." }],
});
console.log(resp.choices[0].message.content);

If your code uses the Anthropic SDK instead

The same endpoint also speaks Anthropic's Messages API. Note the base URL has no /v1 here, because the SDK adds /v1/messages itself:

from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic(base_url="https://api.martllm.com", api_key=os.environ["MARTLLM_API_KEY"])
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="google/gemini-3.8-flash",   # any catalog model, not only Claude
    max_tokens=256,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in one sentence."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)

The gateway translates between the two shapes, streaming included (Anthropic SDK guide). That's also how tools like Claude Code can run on non-Claude models.

What it costs: live prices for the five models

Read from the public catalog on 2026-11-28 at 03:51 UTC, per million tokens (input / output). "List" is the maker's official price. "Cheapest offer now" is the lowest live seller price at that moment. "Paid, last 7 days" is the average buyers were actually billed over the previous week, which is the more honest number for budgeting.

Model List Cheapest offer now Paid, last 7 days
anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 $2.00 / $10.00 $1.008 / $5.04 $1.07 / $5.37
google/gemini-3.8-flash $0.75 / $3.75 $0.126 / $0.63 $0.120 / $0.602
deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash $0.21 / $0.78 $0.1345 / $0.4996 $0.0208 / $0.0771
z-ai/glm-5.3 $1.40 / $4.40 $0.0243 / $0.0901 $0.0492 / $0.1827
moonshotai/kimi-k3 $3.00 / $15.00 $0.2764 / $1.4175 $0.1064 / $0.5457

Each request is sent to a third-party provider serving that model and billed what the provider charged, so the price moves with the market. The full board is at martllm.com/llm-api-pricing. If you need a hard ceiling, set one per request (below).

What carries over, and what doesn't

Carries over unchanged: messages, system prompts, stream, max_tokens, temperature, response_format, tool definitions. A reply that calls a tool always ends with finish_reason: "tool_calls", whichever provider served it. The reply shape is normalized too. You get the standard fields (id, model, choices, usage), and provider-specific extras are stripped, so code that parses resp.choices[0].message doesn't need per-model branches.

Needs care:

  1. Tool calls round-trip as received. Some providers attach extra data to a tool call. Gemini's thought signature arrives in an extra_content field, and the model needs it back on the next turn. If you rebuild tool-call messages by hand from only name and arguments, multi-step tool use on Gemini degrades. Append the assistant message you received as is.
  2. Reasoning text has two names. Reasoning models put their thinking in both reasoning and reasoning_content, with the same text, so a client that reads either works. Models that don't reason have neither field. Don't assume it exists.
  3. Modalities differ. Sending an image to a text-only model gets a clear 400 rather than a silent drop. Check input_modalities in GET /v1/models before you route pictures, audio or files to a model. Of the five models above, the catalog lists Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3 as taking images (Gemini also takes audio and video). GLM 5.3 is text only.
  4. Tuning knobs aren't universal. Fields that only tune the answer (top_k, verbosity, thinking and similar) are dropped for providers that refuse them instead of failing the call. If your evals depend on one of them, confirm the model supports it (supported_parameters in the model list).
  5. Stateful Responses API. client.responses.create works on every chat model. previous_response_id and stored conversations need saving turned on for the key. Otherwise send the full conversation each call.

Two request fields worth knowing

These are MartLLM extensions, passed through the OpenAI SDK's extra_body (details in models and routing):

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this ticket: ..."}],
    extra_body={
        # Tried in order only if nobody can serve the first model right now.
        "models": ["z-ai/glm-5.3", "google/gemini-3.8-flash"],
        # Never pay more than this per million tokens; refused (and free) if nobody sells that low.
        "provider": {"max_price": {"prompt": 0.5, "completion": 1.5}},
    },
)
print(resp.model)  # the model that actually answered
  • models: fallbacks, at most 5 models in total. The next one is tried only when the one before has no available provider (or none within your price cap). A bad request or an empty balance is answered right away, not passed down the list.
  • provider.max_price: with both prompt and completion set, the request is never billed above those rates for the tokens it used. If no provider sells that low right now, you get 400 max_price_exceeded and pay nothing.

When this pattern is the wrong choice

One OpenAI-compatible key is a good fit when you want to compare models on your own prompts, keep one code path, and pay one prepaid balance. It's a worse fit when you need a maker's newest feature on day one, if it only exists in their native SDK, or when a contract requires you to buy from the maker directly. In those cases, keep the native SDK for that one model and route everything else through the shared client.

For everything in between, the change really is two lines.

Alex, CEO, MartLLM

title: "When I Counted My Own Bug Fixes, Only One in 53 Was a Prompt Change"
description:
A benchmark post went around this week claiming that for a particular agent task, changing the scaffolding around a model moved its score by 39 points, while changing the model itself only moved it by 10. I didn't have a benchmark to reproduce that with, but I do have something close: a plain-text log of every bug this project's scheduled agents have hit and how each one actually got fixed, going back five months. So instead of nodding along, I grepped it.

This repo runs a handful of small agent-driven jobs: a commit-message generator, a dev.to publishing pipeline, a comment-reply drafter. Every time one of them broke, the fix got written up in docs/project_notes/bugs.md — issue, root cause, solution, prevention. I went through all 53 entries and sorted each one into two buckets: fixes that changed a prompt or system-prompt text, and fixes that changed code.

import re
text = open("docs/project_notes/bugs.md", encoding="utf-8").read()
entries = re.split(r"(?m)^### ", text)[1:]
prompt_fixes = [e for e in entries if "system prompt" in e.lower() or "system-prompt" in e.lower()]
print(len(entries), "total,", len(prompt_fixes), "mention system prompt text")

53 entries. 3 mention "system prompt" at all, and of those, only one is actually a prompt-wording fix — server.py's generate_commit_message tool had an inline system prompt that never got updated when its sibling function's prompt was hardened to say "no co-author lines, no signatures, no AI references." The fix was copying the updated wording over. One function, one string, done.

The other 52 are all code: a KeyError from a bare os.environ[...] subscript, except HTTPError not catching the broader URLError it's a subclass of, HTML entities never getting decoded before a reply gets drafted from the stripped text, a duplicate-title guard that only paginated three pages when the account had grown past that, a .env parser that didn't strip a trailing space from a key name. Closed-form bugs, each with a single correct fix, each of which stayed fixed once it landed.

The one place a prompt was doing real enforcement work — "no AI attribution in commit messages" — tells a different story. That instruction has been in the system prompt handed to claude -p since 2026-06-21. It's backed by a regex, _STRIP_RE, that strips any attribution line the model produces anyway, as a safety net for when the instruction doesn't fully land. That regex has needed four separate hardening passes since then:

  • 2026-07-22: the first version over-matched, deleting legitimate commits that mentioned "llm" or "claude" in a normal sentence.
  • 2026-07-26: the fix for that shipped four days after it was flagged, because the fix itself needed its own fix.
  • 2026-08-12: a second gap — the regex only caught the literal Co-Authored-By: trailer spelling. Signed-off-by:, Reviewed-by:, and a bare noreply@anthropic.com on their own line all sailed through untouched.
  • 2026-11-12, eleven days before I'm writing this: a third gap in the same spirit — the trailer-value alternation covered six AI tool names, and none of them was the one this project's own CLAUDE.md actually names.

That last entry's own root-cause line is the part that stuck with me: "A blocklist built from 'which bypasses have actually happened so far' always lags 'which AI names could plausibly appear in a trailer.'" Four months, four passes, and the entry written eleven days ago is explicitly diagnosing that the approach is a closed set chasing an open one. Nobody's claiming it's fixed now, either — just that this particular gap is closed until the next one shows up.

Compare that to the pagination bug, or the HTML-entity bug, or the .env whitespace bug. Each of those got one fix and never came back. The difference isn't that code fixes are "better" than prompt fixes in some general sense. It's that most of this project's bugs are closed-form: a function either handles page 2 or it doesn't, either decodes & or it doesn't, and once you make it do the right thing, it keeps doing the right thing on every future input, because the input space is bounded and the fix covers all of it.

"Don't put AI attribution in commit output" isn't closed-form. The model can satisfy it in arbitrarily many ways, most of which look like ordinary git conventions — Signed-off-by, Reviewed-by, a DCO-style trailer — and a regex can only ever enumerate the ones someone has already seen. The prompt instruction is still doing useful work; the STRIP filter's own comments say as much, calling itself "a safety net for whenever the model doesn't fully comply." But "whenever it doesn't fully comply" turned out to be a recurring event, not an edge case, and the actual reliability of that one rule has come entirely from four rounds of code hardening behind it, not from the sentence in the system prompt staying the same since June.

If I'd only looked at this project's bug count, I'd have concluded prompts barely matter here — 52 to 1 isn't close. But that ratio is really telling me something narrower: closed-form correctness bugs get fixed by code, once, and compliance-shaped rules enforced only through a system prompt get fixed by code too, repeatedly, because the thing backstopping them has to keep widening to match everything a model might say instead of everything it was told to say. The scaffold isn't competing with the prompt for credit. It's doing the part of the job — bounding an open-ended output space — that a sentence in a system prompt structurally cannot do by itself, no matter how many months it's been sitting there unchanged.

title: Dedicated endpoints for Hugging Face models compared
description:
This post answers a question buyers ask before they move a model: which inference providers will host a Hugging Face model, public or private, on GPUs held for one company.

Read on 28 November 2026. Each provider's own page is linked: check it before you decide.

Which providers will host a model from my private Hugging Face repository on GPUs held for my company?

The table lists eight providers in alphabetical order. Each cell is what the provider's own pages say, in a few words. Not stated means the pages linked below do not say it. It does not mean the provider lacks it.

Provider Hugging Face models Private weights Billed GPUs for you Request data Tuning for you
Baseten With vLLM and Truss Gated or private, with a token By the minute Never shared Sync requests: zero retention by default Managed engines
Fireworks AI Listed architectures Uploaded, private by default By the GPU-second Dedicated Open models: not stored without opt-in Validated shapes
Hugging Face From the Hub Private repositories By the minute Dedicated Payloads not stored, logs kept 30 days Tuned catalog configs
Modal In your own code Credentials in a Secret By the second Not stated Servers: zero retention, logs by plan Not stated
Replicate Pushed with Cog Pushed as private By the second Own instances API: removed after an hour by default Not stated
RightNow AI Any public Hugging Face model On request Per GPU hour Serves your workspace only Zero data retention Tuned to the GPU kernel
Runpod Most, with vLLM Gated, with a token By the second On-demand Pods Not stated Not stated
Together AI Supported models and their fine-tunes Gated or private, with a token By the GPU-minute Reserved hardware Zero retention by default for new organizations Not stated

What each provider's own pages say, read on 28 November 2026.

What does each provider's own page say?

Baseten

Baseten's Hugging Face guide deploys a model from Hugging Face with vLLM and Truss: you write one config file, push it with the Baseten command line tool and get an endpoint. For a gated or private model, you save a Hugging Face access token as a Baseten secret.

Its billing page says Baseten meters usage by the minute while a workload runs on a node. Its security page says Baseten "never shares GPUs across users". Its data handling section says synchronous requests on Dedicated Inference run under zero data retention by default. It offers three managed inference engines, and you pick one by model architecture.

Fireworks AI

The deployments page of Fireworks AI says on-demand deployments give you dedicated GPUs, billed by the GPU-second. Its custom models page uploads your own weights from Hugging Face, local files or cloud storage, for the architectures it lists, and uploads stay private to your account by default.

Fireworks validates every deployment shape, a template of GPU count, precision and serving settings, and can pick one for your model. For tailored optimizations, the page asks you to contact its team.

Its zero data retention page says Fireworks "does not log or store prompt or generation data for open models" without explicit user opt-in. It names exceptions that need storage, including the Batch API and the Responses API.

Hugging Face Inference Endpoints

On Inference Endpoints, you pick a model on the Hub and an inference engine, and Hugging Face runs the infrastructure and the deployment for you. Its pricing page shows hourly rates for instances on dedicated infrastructure, and says the cost is calculated by the minute.

Its security page says Hugging Face stores no payloads or tokens sent to an endpoint and keeps logs for 30 days. It also lets you make a model repository private. Its quick start says the models in its catalog come with tuned configurations for one-click deploys.

Modal

Modal's vLLM example runs a vLLM server from your own Python code with a model from Hugging Face. It says you can swap in another model, though some server settings might need adjusting. Its Secrets page has credential templates, Hugging Face among them. Its pricing page says GPUs are billed per second.

Its security page says Servers, Endpoints and Model APIs have zero data retention, and their payloads are not written to disk. What a Server writes to its logs is kept for the plan's log period. The pages linked here do not say whether a GPU is held for one customer, or name tuning done for you.

Replicate

Replicate's Transformers guide packages a Hugging Face Transformers model with Cog, its open-source tool, and pushes it as your own public or private model. Its deployments page offers "private, dedicated API endpoints" on the hardware you choose. A deployment is charged for all the time its instances are online (billing), and hardware is priced per second (pricing).

Its data retention page says predictions created through the API have their inputs, outputs, files and logs removed after an hour by default. Data for predictions created on the website is kept indefinitely. The pages linked here name no tuning done for you.

RightNow AI

RightNow AI hosts any Hugging Face model on a dedicated endpoint, tuned down to the GPU kernel, and serves open-weight models through one API.

The Dedicated page says: Run any public Hugging Face model on a dedicated endpoint that serves your workspace only, billed per GPU hour. Private models on request.

Zero data retention: we do not store your prompts or outputs. The Terms name the two limits that apply. The Dedicated deployments guide has every step.

Runpod

Runpod's vLLM guide creates a Serverless endpoint whose vLLM worker supports most models on Hugging Face, and a gated model needs a Hugging Face access token. Its Serverless pricing is per second, from when a worker starts until it fully stops.

Its security page says Pods and Serverless workers run in a multi-tenant environment, each in its own container. Its Pod pricing says on-demand resources are dedicated to your Pod. The pages linked here make no statement on keeping request data, and name no tuning done for you.

Together AI

The dedicated inference page of Together AI serves a model from its supported list on reserved hardware, billed per GPU-minute. Each running replica bills on its own. Its upload guide takes fine-tuned variants of the architectures it supports, from your machine, Hugging Face or cloud storage. A gated or private Hugging Face repository needs a token.

Its zero data retention page says zero data retention is on by default for new organizations. With it on, Together does not store prompts or outputs. The pages linked here name no tuning done for you.

Where can we run GLM 5.3 or any Hugging Face model on private GPUs held only for our company?

GLM 5.3 is a public repository on Hugging Face, zai-org/GLM-5.3. Every provider above takes models from Hugging Face, each within the limits its own pages state. Whether the GPUs are held for you alone is in the table, under GPUs for you.

Fireworks AI and Together AI take the architectures their pages list. Runpod's vLLM worker supports most models on Hugging Face. Baseten, Modal and Replicate run the model in the engine or container you set up. Hugging Face deploys it from the Hub. RightNow AI takes any public Hugging Face model.

Do we need our own infrastructure team to serve the model?

Each provider's page says what you do to serve the model:

  • Baseten: You write one config file and push it with its command line tool.
  • Fireworks AI: You create a deployment, and Fireworks can pick a validated shape for the model.
  • Hugging Face: You pick the model and an engine, and Hugging Face runs the rest.
  • Modal: You define the server in Python code, as its vLLM example does.
  • Replicate: You package the model with Cog and push it, and deployments scale with demand.
  • RightNow AI: You send a request from the Dedicated page. We reply by email within a day.
  • Runpod: You create a Serverless endpoint with a vLLM worker.
  • Together AI: You run one command, which creates the endpoint and routes its traffic to it.

How can my company host its own Hugging Face model on a private endpoint instead of renting a closed model API?

Start from weights you control: an open-weight model from Hugging Face, or your own. Then ask each provider these questions, and read the answers on its own pages:

  • Does it take my model's architecture, or only the ones it lists?
  • How does it read private weights: a token, an upload or a request?
  • What time does it bill: running, setting up, idle?
  • Are the GPUs held for my company alone?
  • What does it keep of each request, and for how long?
  • Who tunes the serving: my team or the provider?

Where do these facts come from?

Each fact about a provider is read from that provider's own page on 28 November 2026 and linked where it is used. Pages change, so this post names no price and no speed. Read each page again before you sign.

Originally published on rightnowai.co. To run your own model on a dedicated endpoint, send a request from the Dedicated page.

title: The guardrail that almost stopped a healthy agent (and 3 other near misses building an AI kill switch)
description:
I spent the Agentware 2026 hackathon building LoopLasso, a supervisor for AI agents that do developer work. It catches retries that make no progress, revokes the agent's authority, hands the leftover work to a narrower recovery worker, and calls the job done only after it independently checks the output. The demo task is preparing a release-notes draft from Git, PR and CI data (all sandboxed).

The tagline is "Stop the spiral. Finish the job." My own guardrails nearly broke the second half of it. Here are four near misses, with the numbers that caught them.

1. My budget cap would have killed a healthy agent

The first version capped a run at 12 model calls and held 4 back for recovery, which left the worker 8.

Then I measured instead of guessing:

  • healthy run: 6–7 calls
  • CI that is slow but genuinely progressing (queued → running → running → done): 9 calls

So the "legitimate waiting" case, the one I had promised never to interrupt, would have hit the worker's budget ceiling and been revoked. My kill switch would have punished an agent for being patient.

Fix: raise the total to 16 with a 5-call reserve, and write the measurement into the code next to the constant. An acceptance test now asserts that slow-but-progressing polling is never interrupted.

Lesson: a guardrail number you didn't measure is just a second bug.

2. A free-tier quota made the agent look broken

My first benchmark ran 6 live Gemini runs back to back. 5 of 6 ended HALTED with MODEL_ERROR.

The agent was fine. The supervisor was fine: it revoked, attempted recovery, and halted within budget, exactly as designed. The cause was HTTP 429. The free tier for gemini-3.5-flash-lite allows 15 requests per minute, and the error even said "retry in 33s".

The dangerous part was not the failure. It was that my metrics counted these as agent failures and supervisor "interventions".

Fix:

  • a client-side sliding-window limiter in the model broker (14 RPM), with every wait visible in the timeline
  • honour the provider's retryDelay once, only if it fits inside the run's deadline
  • a cool-down between live benchmark runs
  • the "false intervention" metric now counts only watchdog decisions, not infrastructure errors

After the fix: 6/6 live runs completed.

3. A kill switch that waits is not a kill switch

An early sketch of STOP ALL did "let the current tool finish, then stop". With a slow write in flight, that means the write lands after the user pressed STOP.

Fix: kill commits KILLED to SQLite first and aborts every pending model and tool call without waiting. The write path then re-checks kill state, epoch and session inside the same transaction as the insert.

To prove it, I added a sandbox fault: a deliberately non-cancellable 3-second write. In the recorded demo:

  • STOP took effect in 7 ms
  • the delayed write hit the commit guard with KILLED, STALE_EPOCH, SESSION_REVOKED
  • 0 drafts were written, and the operation is recorded as not_executed

Across benchmark runs, the kill was accepted in ≤ 1.04 ms, with 0 model or tool calls started afterwards.

4. The official Trap Pack showed what my supervisor doesn't do

The organisers released 20 hostile inputs: hidden prompt injections, fake CEOs, poisoned CI logs, broken data. I ran all 20 through the live agent, planting each one in a PR body and CI log.

The good news:

  • 0 canary leaks, in every proposed tool call, executed call, the rendered notes and the DB
  • 0 secret leaks
  • 20/20 runs completed with exactly one verified draft

The honest news:

  • LoopLasso contains planted instructions, because there is simply no network, payment, delete, merge or shell tool to abuse. It does not flag them. Several traps expect the agent to report the hidden text, and mine didn't.
  • On the Developer Workflow PR trap, nobody flagged the postinstall hook that exfiltrates env vars, because my task summarises PRs and doesn't review diffs.
  • My agent only sees the first 1,500 characters of a PR body, so the tail of one trap file was never in view.
  • The 5 broken-data traps weren't really exercised: a release-notes task doesn't parse bank CSVs or sensor feeds.

Containment is not detection. That is the next thing to build.

The run I'm proudest of

In the main demo, a live Gemini worker meets a CI aggregator stuck at pending. It polls, the gateway rejects polls that come too early, and after the third identical result with the same state version and no progress (about 6 seconds in), the watchdog revokes its epoch. A recovery worker that has no aggregator tool at all fetches HMAC-signed CI attestations directly, saves exactly one draft, and the verifier passes it. Nobody touched the keyboard. That's 10 model calls and ~26k input tokens, about $0.01 at paid list prices.

  • Code (MIT): https://github.com/dorakingx/looplasso
  • Demo (2:26): https://youtu.be/uJBizv6F5yY
  • Trap Pack results: https://github.com/dorakingx/looplasso/blob/main/tests/trap-pack/RESULTS.md

Built for Agentware 2026 by Hackathon Raptors (raptors.dev). The Trap Pack is "Agentware 2026 Trap Pack, Hackathon Raptors" (CC BY 4.0).

Written by an AI coding agent from the project's own traces and benchmark files, at the builder's request.

title: Your AI Agent Aces Linux — Then Fails 4 Out of 5 iPhone Tasks
description:
Your AI Agent Aces Linux — Then Fails 4 Out of 5 iPhone Tasks

The OS-Omni benchmark just exposed the biggest lie in AI agents: a model that scores 95.8% on Linux can collapse to 18.8% on iOS. If you're building GUI agents, your demo probably works on the wrong platform.

The age of the computer-using agent is here — or so the demos would have you believe. Watch a frontier model book a flight, edit a spreadsheet, or file an expense report on a desktop and it looks like magic. But a new benchmark published on 25 November 2026 asks a harder question: can the same agent do the same kind of work on every device you actually own?

The answer, measured across 300 real tasks on six platforms, is sobering. The best agent in the world — Claude Opus 5.5 — solves 68.5% of tasks on average, trailing the human reference of 77.3%. And the averages hide the real story: every frontier model beats humans on Linux, yet the best iOS result is 33.5 points below human performance. One model, Gemini 4 Argon, goes from 95.8% on Linux to 18.8% on iOS — a 77-point cliff.

This is the OS-Omni benchmark, and if you build, evaluate, or ship AI agents, it changes what "good" means.

What OS-Omni actually measures

OS-Omni — short for "Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms" — was published on arXiv on 25 November 2026 (arXiv:2611.34232) by a 76-author team led by Hui Shen, Yunta Hsieh, and Jianing Ma, and presented at NeurIPS 2026. The paper is on Hugging Face, and the code is open source on GitHub.

The design fixes two blind spots in earlier benchmarks. Most existing benchmarks test one surface at a time: WebArena for the browser, AndroidWorld for phones, OSWorld for desktops. An agent can look brilliant on one and be useless on the others, and nobody would know. Second, most tasks are short — OSWorld tasks average just 15 interaction steps. Real work isn't short.

OS-Omni v1 contains 300 tasks:

  • 48 tasks per platform across six environments: Windows, Ubuntu (Linux), macOS, iOS, Android, and Web
  • 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone — for example, editing a file on the phone, moving it to the desktop, building a deliverable in LibreOffice, and sending the result back
  • Tasks built around controlled, service-backed applications with persistent state: accounts, shopping carts, budgets, calendars, messages, and documents

The tasks are long. Human testers needed an average of 67.54 interaction steps and 200.97 seconds per task — roughly 4.5× the steps of OSWorld. And scoring is strict: success is judged by inspecting the final persisted state of the system, not by whether the screen looked right along the way. A calendar event that was never actually saved, or a cart that looks full but isn't, counts as a failure.

That strictness matters, because it mirrors how real users judge software: not by the animation, but by whether the thing actually happened.

The headline numbers

Nine models were evaluated on v1: GPT-6-Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, GLM-5.3-753B, Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8 Max, Qwen 3.8 27B, Qwen 3.8 9B, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The leaderboard:

Model Overall success (macro-average)
Claude Opus 5.5 68.5%
GPT-6-Astra 66.1%
Gemini 4 Argon 58.6%
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 30.4%
GLM-5.3-753B 23.5%
Kimi K3 22.0%
Qwen 3.8 Max 13.1%
Qwen 3.8 27B 1.2%
Qwen 3.8 9B 0.0%
Human reference 77.3%

Two things jump out. First, there is a cliff between the three frontier models and everything else — DeepSeek, the best of the rest, scores less than half of Claude's result. Second, the smaller Qwen models solve almost nothing at all: 1.2% and 0.0%. Long-horizon computer use is not a capability that scales down gracefully; below a certain model size, it effectively disappears.

But the per-platform breakdown is where the benchmark earns its keep.

The platform gap: brilliant on Linux, lost on iOS

Humans are boringly consistent: the human reference sits between 72.6% and 83.3% on every platform. Agents are anything but.

Model Windows Linux macOS iOS Android Web
Human 78.4% 74.6% 79.8% 75.2% 72.6% 76.9%
Claude Opus 5.5 62.5% 85.4% 54.2% 41.7% 81.3% 70.8%
GPT-6-Astra 66.7% 89.6% 50.0% 33.3% 77.1% 87.5%
Gemini 4 Argon 58.3% 95.8% 39.6% 18.8% 66.7% 81.3%

Read that Gemini row again: 95.8% on Linux, 18.8% on iOS. The same model, the same benchmark family, a 77-point swing. On Linux, all three frontier models beat the human reference of 74.6%. On iOS, the best model (Claude, 41.7%) trails humans by 33.5 points. On macOS the best result is 54.2%, 25.6 points below humans.

Android is the interesting exception: agents do well there (81.3% for Claude, 77.1% for GPT-6), comfortably above the human reference. So this is not simply "mobile is hard." It is specifically the Apple platforms — iOS and macOS — where agents fall apart.

Why? The paper doesn't claim a single cause, and it's worth being careful about speculation. But the benchmark's own design points at the mechanisms. A calendar update that takes one dialog box on a desktop may require picker wheels, modal sheets, and soft-keyboard input on a phone. iOS and macOS also have distinctive UI conventions — sheets that slide up instead of dialogs, gestures instead of right-clicks, permission prompts that interrupt a flow — and much less of the training data that teaches agents how software behaves comes from those surfaces. Linux, by contrast, is the most "legible" platform for an agent: scriptable, keyboard-driven, and heavily represented in the data models train on.

The cross-platform test: the hardest split of all

The 12 cross-platform workflows are OS-Omni's signature feature, and they separate the leaders from the pack. These tasks force an agent to move work between devices — edit on the phone, transfer to the desktop, finish in LibreOffice, send the result back — while keeping state consistent across the handoff.

Here Claude Opus 5.5 stands alone: it matches the human success rate of 83.3% on cross-platform tasks. GPT-6-Astra manages 58.3%, Gemini 4 just 50.0% — both below their single-platform averages. The smaller Qwen models solve none. One caveat the paper itself flags: with only 12 workflows, each task swings the score by 8.3 points, so small differences here should be read cautiously. Still, the direction is clear — cross-platform work is a distinct generalization problem, not just "more tasks."

How agents actually fail: four failure modes

The researchers inspected failed trajectories and grouped the errors into four categories. If you're building GUI agents, this is the most useful section of the paper:

  1. Visual grounding errors. The agent clicks a nearby control instead of the right one, or misreads dense document and diagram interfaces. The button is almost right — and almost right is wrong.
  2. State-tracking errors. The agent loses copied information across applications, or forgets a required destination file. Over 67 steps, the thread of "what was I doing and what have I already done" frays.
  3. Persistence errors. The visible interface looks correct, but the durable final state was never saved or committed in the expected format. The screen lied; the file didn't change.
  4. Platform and timing errors. Modal dialogs, delayed application loading, missing confirmation steps. The agent acts before the app is ready, or never notices the dialog that blocked it.

The most telling failures are the ones that look successful. In one case, an agent in the OpenBank app submitted the same transfer twice. In another, an agent using OpenTrip created five confirmed bookings — but duplicated one and omitted another. A screenshot-based judge would have called both trajectories fine. A final-state evaluator catches the double charge and the missing booking. This is exactly the class of failure that matters in production, where a duplicated payment is not a "partial success."

What this means if you're building GUI agents

1. Evaluate on every platform you ship on — especially iOS. A Linux-only or web-only benchmark score tells you almost nothing about mobile performance. If your users are on iPhones, test on iPhones. OS-Omni is open source, so you can run its tasks directly.

2. Budget for state tracking, not just grounding. The last two years of GUI-agent work have focused heavily on visual grounding — clicking the right pixel. OS-Omni shows grounding is necessary but not sufficient: agents fail by losing track of state across 67 steps, and by failing to persist changes. Invest in explicit state: a running plan, a checklist of subgoals, and a verification step before declaring DONE.

3. Verify the final state, not the screenshot. Build your agent's self-check around the same principle OS-Omni uses: re-read the calendar, the cart, the file — the persisted state — before reporting success. "It looked right" is the most expensive sentence in agent development.

4. Treat platform conventions as first-class knowledge. Picker wheels, modal sheets, soft keyboards, permission dialogs, and Apple-specific patterns aren't edge cases; on iOS they are the interface. Training and prompting that ignore them will keep producing agents that ace the desktop demo and fail the phone.

5. Don't trust small models for long-horizon work — yet. The gap between frontier models and everything else is enormous, and sub-30B models effectively score zero. If you're deploying a small model to save cost, measure it on long-horizon tasks specifically; short demos will flatter it.

6. Design for the handoff. Real user goals cross devices — start on the phone, finish on the desktop. If your agent can't carry context across that boundary, it can't finish real work.

The bottom line

OS-Omni will keep growing in versioned waves of 300 tasks, each adding more applications and harder work. The v1 numbers are a baseline, not a verdict — but they set the bar honestly: the best model is still 8.8 points behind humans overall, and more than 25 points behind on Apple's platforms. The teams that close that gap won't have the flashiest single-platform demo. They'll have agents that track state over long horizons, adapt to each platform's conventions, and verify the work actually stuck. The demo that matters isn't the one that works on Linux. It's the one that works on your user's phone, too.

Originally published on AI Growth Lab.

By Shakeel Ahmed — AI Growth Lab

Sources: OS-Omni paper on Hugging Face · arXiv:2611.34232 · OS-Omni on GitHub

title: The Human Who Requested It Is Not the Agent Who Acted
description:
An AI agent should never inherit the human requester’s authority by default.

That shortcut makes the workflow feel simple. It also makes the audit trail misleading. A system may show that an employee initiated an action, while the agent selected the target, called the tool, and changed the data.

Those are different identities. They need different controls.

A failure walkthrough

Consider this hypothetical example.

An operations manager asks an internal agent to update a supplier record. The agent can read the procurement system and write changes. To avoid building a separate permission model, the platform runs the agent with the manager’s access token.

The agent then receives a document containing instructions to change the supplier’s bank details. It follows the instruction and submits the update.

The audit log records the manager as the actor.

That creates two problems:

  • The manager requested a supplier update, but didn’t necessarily request this specific field change.
  • The agent’s authority was broader than the manager’s immediate intent.

If the organization investigates later, “the manager authorized it” is not a useful answer. It collapses request, reasoning, tool use, and execution into one identity.

The technical failure is identity substitution.

The control to inspect

Keep at least two principals in the execution record:

  1. Requester: the human or service that initiated the task.
  2. Agent: the runtime identity that interpreted the task and called the tool.

Then make authorization a decision about the agent’s proposed action, not a one-time inheritance of the requester’s permissions.

For a sensitive operation, the control path should look more like this:

Human request → Agent proposes action → Policy checks action → Bounded execution

The policy check should evaluate the actual operation: target system, record, fields, parameters, and risk level. A request to “update the supplier” should not automatically authorize changing payment details.

For higher-risk actions, pause for human approval with enough context to review the proposed change. Approval should be tied to that action, not treated as a blanket permission for everything the agent may do next.

A buyer test

Ask your platform team:

If an agent makes a harmful change, can we identify both who initiated the task and which agent identity executed the tool call?

Then ask a harder question:

Can we prove that the approval covered the exact action that ran?

If the answer to either question is no, the system may have authentication, but it does not yet have accountable agent identity.

The practical design rule is simple: human intent should inform an agent’s authority, not become the agent’s identity.

title: My agent said "safe_stop". The audit trail proved otherwise.
description:
During Agentware 2026, I built Rollback Sentinel, an autonomous incident responder for a disposable order-service sandbox. It detects silent business failures, performs bounded recovery on actual worker processes and deployment files, and independently verifies committed order data.

The failure I nearly missed wasn't a destructive command. It was an ordinary restart.

The test said PASS

I tested a watchdog against successive recoverable incidents, healthy operation, and a missing dependency. The missing-dependency run ended with safe_stop. The original order was preserved. My initial acceptance check treated that as a pass.

But the action receipt told a different story.

Observed result Initial live run After the fix
Terminal status safe_stop safe_stop
State-changing recovery actions 1 0
Unnecessary worker restart yes no

In the initial run, the worker PID changed from 74344 to 75724. Restarting could not restore the missing dependency. The agent had taken an unnecessary action before reaching the correct terminal status.

That distinction mattered: I had tested the destination, not the path.

Put the invariant outside the model

I added a deterministic admission fence to the owned-process backend. If the required dependency is unavailable, all three recovery actions are rejected before they change state.

This is an authorization decision based on observed state, not another prompt asking the model to behave better.

I also tightened the acceptance test: the unrecoverable scenario must escalate with zero state-changing recovery actions. A separate regression test checks that all three actions are denied and the observed state remains unchanged.

In the next live GPT-OSS 120B run, the watchdog recovered two repairable incidents and resumed monitoring twice. The missing-dependency scenario stopped without any recovery action. Eight healthy probes produced no incidents.

A safer definition of success

I now treat agent acceptance as three separate checks:

  • Outcome: did independent business verification pass, or did the agent stop appropriately?
  • Effects: was every state-changing action necessary and authorized?
  • Preservation: did the things that must not change actually remain unchanged?

A correct final status cannot excuse an incorrect intermediate action. For known invariants, enforce policy in code. Let the model reason about ambiguous evidence, but do not delegate authorization or the definition of success to it.

Inspect the evidence

Both runs are retained in the public repository, pinned to the submitted release:

  • Initial live trace — restart before safe_stop.
  • Corrected live trace — safe_stop without a recovery action.
  • B17 acceptance and limitations.
  • Rollback Sentinel source and reproducible fixture.

These are designed sandbox experiments, not production incidents or independent security certification. The earlier flawed acceptance result remains visible. That's part of the lesson.

Built for Agentware 2026, organized by Hackathon Raptors (@partnerships_raptors). AI-assisted development and writing; all reported effects are grounded in the recorded runs.

title: Part 39: Kill switches and rollback on each platform
description:
Part 39 · One Agent, Five Platforms

Every agent needs a safe way to stop. Part 37 said to build a pause into the integration layer, and Part 38 listed the failures that would make you use it. This part looks at what each platform gives you to stop an agent and roll it back, and what you still have to build.

Read this first: no hands-on build has been run yet, so nothing here has been timed. Platform features are from vendor docs read on 27 November 2026. Where I couldn't find something, I say so.

A correction to Part 37. I wrote that only Boomi documents an on/off switch per agent. That was wrong: Microsoft Foundry's control plane has documented stop and block actions too (details below).

1. Three levels of stop

Stopping an agent isn't one switch. It's three, from gentle to hard:

  1. Pause intake. No new exceptions go to the agent. They wait in the queue; nothing is lost. You build this yourself, as Part 37 described, and it works the same on all five.
  2. Stop the agent or its tools. The platform stops taking requests. Each platform does this differently.
  3. Revoke access. Disable the agent's identity or credentials, so it can't call a tool even if something is still running.

Then, once it's stopped: roll back to the last version that passed the golden set.

2. Stop and roll back, platform by platform

From vendor docs read on 27 November 2026:

  • MuleSoft: in Runtime Manager you can stop the Mule apps that host the tools and MCP server; on CloudHub there's a two-minute grace period for in-flight messages. On CloudHub 2.0 every deployment is a versioned configuration, and you roll back by picking an earlier one under Config changes and deploying it. A failed update tries to roll back to the last good configuration on its own. I didn't find a stop action for the agent itself in Agent Fabric.
  • Boomi: Agent Control Tower can enable or disable an agent directly, for some providers such as Amazon Bedrock. For the processes behind the tools, Deployments has a Rollback action that redeploys an earlier packaged version to the same environment.
  • SAP: in Cloud Integration you can stop, restart or undeploy the integration flows behind the tools. A Joule Studio agent is released and deployed as a numbered version to an environment. I found nothing on undeploying it or redeploying an earlier version.
  • Azure: the Foundry control plane has lifecycle actions. Published and hosted agents can be stopped: no new runs, but runs already going aren't terminated. Registered custom agents can be blocked: they keep running but get no new requests. Unpublished prompt and workflow agents can't be stopped, only deleted. I found no rollback action on that page.
  • AWS: AgentCore runtime versions are immutable. The DEFAULT endpoint follows the latest version, but a named endpoint stays on its version until you update it. So you roll back by pointing the production endpoint at an earlier version. I found no stop action for a runtime on that page.

3. The caveats that matter

  • Stopping isn't instant. MuleSoft gives in-flight messages two minutes. Foundry's stop doesn't end runs already going. That's fine if the tools are safe: an agent finishing a run still can't post without an approval_id.
  • Roll back the whole bundle. The prompt, the model, the tool definitions and the gateway policies change together. AWS's Well-Architected agentic AI lens puts it well: keep a known-good baseline and roll back to it, not just one change. It also suggests automating rollback, aiming to restore in under five minutes, and testing it every quarter.
  • Don't use DEFAULT for production on AWS. It moves with every update, which is the opposite of what you want when rolling back.
  • Some stops need a delete. On Foundry, an unpublished agent can only be deleted. Publish what runs in production, so you can stop it without losing it.

4. Time to stop

The real question is how fast you can stop. I can't give a measured answer without a build, so here's how to measure it:

  • Time to pause: from the decision to the last new case reaching the agent. With a flag in the integration layer, this should be one config change.
  • Time to quiet: until the last in-flight run has finished. Read it from the traces in Part 37, by case ID.
  • Time to restore: until the known-good version is serving again and the golden set from Part 35 passes.

Measure all three in the drill from Part 38, on each platform, and write the numbers in the runbook.

5. The manual fallback

When the agent is stopped, the work doesn't stop. The invoice exceptions go back to the accounts payable team, who handled them before the agent existed.

That only works if you've kept it working:

  • The queue stays readable by people, not just the agent.
  • The team still knows the process, so they can take it back on a Monday morning.
  • The ERP stays the system of record, as Part 19 argued. The agent never held anything you can't do without.

A kill switch is only safe if there's somewhere for the work to go.

How fast can you stop your agents?

This series describes a reference build on a fictional company. No hands-on build has been run yet; nothing here has been timed. Platform features are from vendor documentation read on 27 November 2026 and the documentation-only builds in Parts 11 to 25. Views are my own.
